text:
"If only one kind of person can afford to be there [in the City] it becomes a mono-culture over time"

Klein & Thompson make this point again and again in Abundance about cities. Cities are the engines of technological progress. Economic mobility is spread out when ordinary people can move to places and be around the growth. And that it's an indictment when firemen cannot afford to live in cities they protect.

"Everything is downstream of housing" or "It's a housing story"

All of those things are true and yet I find a small pebble of distinction in my thinking, perhaps only in emphasis. And yet it feels significant.

To me, the indictment of the city is that people cannot STAY in the City. Or rather, the "one kind of person who can afford to be there" is the childless person, whether single or married.

A 23 year old investment banker, nurse, teacher, fireman or even a barista can all generally afford to live in the City ... so long as they are single and willing to have roommates. The newness of the housing and the neighborhood will vary (probably only the banker can live alone) but there is still housing for most.

But the problem comes as people get older and, naturally, want to advance to the next stage in life. When you're young and single, you're more likely to tolerate lower levels of cleanliness, smaller spaces, or a neighborhood that is still transitional. In fact, those are the things that make the City exciting.

But, only some careers have the wage potential to move from "Living with friends in that somewhat sketchy, but fun, place" to "Having your own place in the neighborhood you like." And that's where the bankers, doctors, and engineers really separate themselves.

But the gap becomes a chasm when people think about having children. A two-income couple who makes $400,000 can live like kings in NY or SF. They might be in a small 2BR, but you can afford an apartment or condo in any neighborhood in any City in the US.

Having children either means someone stops working, or they pay an eye-watering amount for childcare. And when it comes to school, while you can afford a payment on a $1.5MM house ... you (probably) cannot afford tuition at $30,000 for 2 kids ... so the schools need to be "good enough."

Again, this applies to couples who have "made it." The nurses and teachers and fireman have long since moved to Jersey or Texas.

I don't think there's any specific disagreement between what I'm saying and Klein/Thompson. Derek wrote a great article last year about the childless City (which I contributed a quote to). But I think the emphasis of the City being a place where people are unable to STAY provides a bit better framework both for what is wrong, what needs to be fixed ... but also WHY people oppose change.

I'm still organizing my thoughts on the book and how, specifically, conservatives who also love the City can join or differentiate parts of the Abundance agenda.

But for now, I think the distinction lies in the emphasis around children and families.

I think the *goal* of the City should be to create places where ambitious, creative, people move in, have kids and STAY. Babies are not a byproduct. They are the goal.

text:
Most Texans think Texas history starts at the Alamo.
1836.The Texas Revolution. Sam Houston. Independence.

But Texas civilization started long before that.

The first permanent city in Texas wasn’t Austin, Dallas, Houston, or even San Antonio.

It was Ysleta.

Founded in 1680 along the Rio Grande near present-day El Paso.

That’s nearly 100 years before the American Revolution and more than 150 years before the Alamo.

While the East Coast colonies were still struggling to survive, there were already permanent communities in Texas.

When Ysleta was founded, Texas wasn’t a state. It wasn’t a republic. It wasn’t even really Texas yet. It was a remote frontier on the edge of civilization.

The people who built Ysleta weren’t politicians or planners. They were families fleeing violence during the Pueblo Revolt in New Mexico. They traveled hundreds of miles south looking for a place to survive.

No roads.
No infrastructure.
No government programs.
No guarantees.

They built homes by hand. They dug irrigation systems from the Rio Grande. They planted crops in desert soil. They created a permanent community where nothing had existed before.

At the center of that settlement stood the Ysleta Mission, which still exists today — one of the oldest continuously operating religious sites in America.

Think about that for a minute.

While George Washington hadn’t even been born yet, Texans were already building permanent towns.

Texas didn’t begin with government.

It began with people willing to build something permanent in a hard place.

Small frontier communities like Ysleta laid the foundation for everything Texas would become — long before oilfields, skyscrapers, highways, and modern cities.

More than 300 years later, Ysleta still exists.

Empires have come and gone.
Borders have changed.
Governments have changed.

But that first Texas community is still standing.

Before the Alamo…

Before the Rangers…

Before the Republic…

Before the State…

There was Ysleta.

The first city in Texas.

Most Texans have never even heard of it.

Once again, corruption and ego triumphed over common sense... leaving our great beautiful city to continue rotting in the sun.

Maybe I should just move to Antarctica? At this point, that seems easier than trying to build a life for myself in San Francisco. Yes, we have one of the most beautiful cities in the world. We also have billionaire tech office glass skyscrapers and rooftop night clubs. But walk across the street and the next thing you know, you are back in the dark ages... women giving birth on the sidewalk, stillborns in the porta potty waste pool next to City Hall, evil men living in the sewer, people jumping off rooftops, women going missing, elders being targeted and kids trying to play on playgrounds surrounded by 20+ people using fentanyl . The fentanyl bazaar at 7th and Market looks like a scene from a failed civilization... Every corner tells the story of what happens when you vote blue no matter who.

Honestly, I’m starting to think an underground cave with some MREs in the McMurdo Dry Valleys of Antarctica doesn’t sound so bad. No corruption, no fentanyl, no chaos, no Obama... just peace and survival. Down there, at least the cold has integrity. Maybe that’s what it takes to live an honest life again... In San Francisco the warmth feels fake, smiles feel bought and the city I once loved is on life support and everybody is suggesting to pull the plug.

The sidewalks are lined with tents and memorial candles, and every block feels like a crime scene no one cares to solve. I’ve watched the same politicians who caused this crisis stage photo ops in front of temporarily cleaned up alleys, only for the encampments to return hours later. When San Francisco got cleaned up for President Xi of China, the refentanylization happened overnight. I’ve intervened in robberies, stopped assaults, defended our last few grocery stores and stood between criminals and innocent people... not because I wanted to but because chaos and lawlessness has become rampant and if we don't stand up for our community nobody will. The police are limited, our judges are immoral, the nonprofits are rich and the people are either suffering or dead.

They have built an empire on misery by taking advantage of the everyday kindness and love of California Families and they will never let it end because too many of their friends profit from it. We The People are being exploited while Democrats benefit from the suffering of the less fortunate on the streets. The Republican Party is far from perfect, but at least we can improve upon the Republican Party and update our system. The democrat system is corruption. Our own local and state government is the problem.

So here we are again... another headline, another failure, another chance for redemption thrown away. The National Guard could have really helped stop the bleeding, even if only for a moment. But the people in charge would rather let the city burn than admit they failed. Maybe one day, San Francisco will remember what it means to protect its own. Until then, those of us who still care will keep fighting the good fight and when the time comes, we will vote red, not out of hate, but out of love and the survival of everything we know and love.

I’ve come to believe that President Trump leads in true New York City fashion... the kind of wall street smart pragmatism that even the most seasoned career politicians can’t even comprehend. When everyone in San Francisco screamed “don’t send in the National Guard,” he said OKAY and didn’t. Why waste time, money and manpower on a city that spits on the very people trying to save it? You don’t pour resources into a failing enterprise that refuses to fix itself. You let it learn the hard way and when it’s finally humbled enough to ask for help, then you rebuild it properly.

I believe President Trump made a rare miscalculation or perhaps listened to the wrong advisor or billionaire when it came to San Francisco. Pulling back the National Guard from San Francisco is not the correct move at this moment in time. The real families of San Francisco... the parents, the workers, the people who still hold onto hope in this once great beautiful American city very much so want the National Guard to come in. We are all sick and tired of watching our world class neighborhoods rot while corrupt politicians and nonprofits benefit off the chaos. 

We are not asking for occupation... We are asking for protection, order and the restoration of dignity. The San Francisco Bay Area needs a top to bottom quality of life update. If Trump had called me, the National Guard would be in San Francisco right now.

San Francisco STILL needs The National Guard.

Respectfully.

text:
Thoughts From a Native Californian
"California doesn’t need saving—it needs remembering."
By R.G. Ryan

I am a native Californian, born upon the fertile soil of the Pajaro Valley in Santa Cruz County. And I am troubled—go ahead and throw in embarrassed, ashamed, distraught—by what I see in the state I love.

California still calls itself progressive, but progress, by definition, moves forward toward measurable improvement. Yet after fifteen years of de facto one-party rule, our schools continue to underperform, our cities deteriorate, and our tax base erodes. If the destination of progress is renewal, we seem to be traveling the opposite way. When Sacramento’s version of “progress” leaves cities broken and families fleeing, maybe it’s time to redefine the word.

What troubles me most is the moral inversion hiding beneath our rhetoric. When every failure is someone else’s fault, reform becomes heresy. We’re told these policies express compassion and inclusion. Yet compassion that bankrupts common sense isn’t compassion—it’s negligence dressed in virtue.

Real compassion measures itself in outcomes, not applause.

Real progress accepts course correction as a sign of maturity, not betrayal.

California doesn’t need saving, it needs remembering. Remembering what once made it magnetic: freedom as responsibility, compassion anchored in common sense, progress measured by what endures. We were builders and dreamers. Pragmatic, daring, convinced that effort could rewrite a life. Somewhere along the way, we traded craftsmanship for convenience and virtue for virtue-signaling. To remember isn’t nostalgia; it’s recovery. If California can reclaim the spirit that prized work over words and results over rhetoric, it won’t need redemption. It will simply recognize itself again.
_______________
R.G. Ryan is a novelist, musician, and essayist whose work explores the intersection of faith, culture, and human responsibility. A native of California’s Central Coast, he writes about the places—and the values—that shape us.

text:
La fertilité est fondamentalement mimétique : on veut des enfants parce qu’on en voit autour de nous. Quand on voit des enfants/bébés c’est assez irrésistible !

Israël démontre ce mécanisme : exposition constante aux familles nombreuses -> désir mimétique d’en avoir soi-même. Les communautés Haredi dont la fertilité élevée contamine progressivement le reste de la société israélienne.

Le danger c’est un cercle vicieux mortel dans les pays à basse fertilité :
Moins d’enfants -> Moins d’exposition sociale aux bébés -> Moins de désir d’enfants -> Encore moins de naissances -> Vieillissement accéléré -> Société de plus en plus hostile aux familles (infrastructures, normes, attentes) -> Encore moins d’enfants !

La Corée du Sud (TFR 0,8), Taïwan (0,7) et le Japon illustrent cette spirale : dans les grandes villes croiser un enfant devient exceptionnel. Les « childless cities » deviennent la norme. Quand toute votre cohorte est sans enfant……. avoir un bébé devient un acte socialement déviant plutôt que normal.

La société devient même hostile aux enfants : zones « no kids » dans les avions, hôtels « garantis sans enfants », invisibilisation croissante dans l’espace public. L’intolérance sociétale aux enfants accélère leur raréfaction.

Briser ce cercle vicieux exige des interventions culturelles massives (comme en Géorgie) ET structurelles (logement, garde d’enfants, transferts). Mais plus on attend plus c’est difficile : la norme sociale pro-famille s’évapore génération après génération !

Sans enfants pas d’avenir. Agissons avant qu’il ne soit trop tard !!

text:
Iranians & Foreign Nationals Flee to Armenia as Border Crossings Surge Amid Escalating Iran–Israel Conflict & Growing Regional Uncertainty 🇦🇲🇮🇷
➖➖➖
Amid escalating military tensions between Iran and Israel, hundreds of Iranians and foreign nationals have entered Armenia in recent days through the Meghri and Agarak checkpoints in the southern Syunik Province, seeking safety and stability. Reports from the border indicate a steady influx of people, both by car and on foot, many of whom are grappling with soaring transportation costs and fuel shortages.

According to Ashot Aramyan, head of a local tourism organization in Meghri, the town has seen a sharp increase in foreign visitors in recent days, primarily due to the escalating conflict. Most of the travelers are citizens of China, India, Germany, Russia, and Iran, many of whom are exiting Iran by land because of restrictions on air travel. Among them are employees of embassies and international companies operating in Iran.

“Despite the large flow, most visitors stay just one night, which allows for a steady rotation and makes it possible to accommodate everyone,” Aramyan told Public Radio of Armenia. He added that the customs checkpoint in Meghri is functioning smoothly, with no significant delays thanks to efficient coordination by the staff.

On June 18, CivilNet correspondent Hasmik Hovhannisyan, reporting from Meghri, described the scene as chaotic and emotionally charged. Iranians arriving at the border are being asked to pay up to $300 per person for taxi rides to Yerevan—more than ten times the usual fare of approximately 10,000 drams ($25). “It’s very expensive to get from Tehran to Yerevan,” one traveler told CivilNet. “There’s a shortage of gasoline, and many of us had to overcome great difficulty just to reach the border.”

Similar reports from the Agarak checkpoint suggest that pressure on border crossings is increasing by the day. Iranians, along with citizens of other countries and ethnic Armenians, are struggling to secure transportation from the border to other parts of Armenia. Taxi drivers are demanding between $300 and $350 for a ride to the capital, a sum well beyond what most arriving families can afford.

Among the arrivals are ethnic Armenian families fleeing the conflict zone. One mother, who spoke to Azatutyun, said she came with her children after Israeli airstrikes intensified near their home. “Tehran and other cities are emptying out. People are afraid, and they’re moving wherever they can find safety,” she said. “We had great difficulty even reaching the checkpoint. There’s no fuel, and finding money is impossible.”

The humanitarian situation is being closely monitored.

UN World Food Program personnel were seen at the Agarak crossing on June 17, though Azatutyun noted a lack of visible Armenian government representatives on site. Meanwhile, long lines of Iranian-registered trucks have built up on the Armenian side of the border, indicating a potential bottleneck in the flow of goods and people.

The Armenian government, while not declaring a state of emergency, is preparing for possible consequences of the regional conflict. Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan addressed the matter during a parliamentary Q&A session on June 18, confirming that contingency plans are being developed.

“All potential issues are under daily monitoring,” Grigoryan said. “Yes, we are considering refugee flows, logistical disruptions, and energy issues. These scenarios might become necessary at any moment, or not at all, but they must be ready.”

He emphasized the need for a coordinated and proactive response, noting preparations for temporary housing, population displacement, and social support mechanisms.

“These questions are being addressed by a consolidated inter-agency task force,” he said, declining to reveal further details due to the sensitive nature of the planning.

For communities like Kamiane, regular support covers immediate needs—and reminds families that even the smallest villages are not forgotten. #ChefsForUkraine

text:
I once owned a music school. It was a thriving little place that employed several teachers and nearly 100 students. When COVID happened, we shut down for the initial “two weeks to flatten the curve.” Then I reopened. We offered online lessons. Families could choose masks if they wanted. My incredible teachers, from both sides of the political aisle, never stopped showing up to work. I became a publicly outspoken advocate against the illegal government mandates. I spoke up for the rights of small business-owners to remain open and run their businesses how they saw fit without fear of government interference or being shut down for “noncompliance”

But student attendance never truly recovered. 

I kept that school open far longer than I should have from a financial standpoint. But I was not going to roll over while the government destroyed small businesses, livelihoods, the arts, and people’s sense of normal through fear, pressure, and overreach. 

That experience fundamentally changed me.

And it’s exactly why I refuse to quietly accept what is happening with our dog Lucy.

When the government oversteps, acts unjustly, and attempts to destroy the lives people have worked so hard to build, I fight. 

I will not be bullied or intimidated by the government, or by petty neighbors who think they should have the right to dictate how my family should live.

This isn’t about rebellion, stubbornness, or me being “out of touch,” as one neighbor texted me. This is about standing against powers that overstep and bullies who attempt to rule through fear, pressure, and intimidation.

It’s about teaching our children that it is not only acceptable, but right, to stand up for yourself—especially when there is a much larger principle at stake.

This is about preserving freedoms, exposing the holes in laws and systems that can be weaponized against ordinary families, and fighting to ensure future generations still have the privilege of pursuing the American dream and the rights that come with it.

Lucy, that scraggly, beautiful pearl from the desert who became our family’s protector and guardian of our flocks has become a symbol of something far bigger than herself.

Watching people rally around our family and this cause has been a hopeful reminder that Americans still stand up for what is just and worth protecting. I truly believe something meaningful and beautiful will come from it.

We just want our dog back. We just want to live in peace. And now, we want to prevent others from suffering as we have. 

#savelucy

text:
Her name was Rattanbai Petit.

Everyone called her Ruttie.

She was born on February 20, 1900 in Bombay into the Petit family, one of the wealthiest Parsi families in India. Her grandfather had built some of the first cotton mills in the country. She grew up in a home where ministers, poets and lawyers came for dinner.

Bombay society called her the Flower of Bombay.

In the summer of 1916 a lawyer named Mohammad Ali Jinnah came to spend the summer with her family in Darjeeling. He was 40 years old. She was 16.

They discovered they shared the same interests. Books, horses, nationalism and a restless curiosity about the world.

Jinnah asked her father for her hand in marriage. Sir Dinshaw Petit, who considered Jinnah a close friend, was furious. He had Jinnah legally barred from communicating with Ruttie while she remained a minor.

They met in secret anyway and decided to wait.

On her 18th birthday her family held a grand banquet at the Taj Mahal Hotel. After her father’s speech Ruttie stood up and told the room she had accepted Jinnah’s proposal and they would be married shortly.

She sat down to thundering silence.

She converted to Islam on April 19, 1918 and they married the same day at his home in Malabar Hill. She brought with her only her pets from her old life.

Her Parsi community ostracised her completely. Her father did not speak to her for years.

Their daughter Dina was born in 1919. Then Jinnah’s political life consumed everything. He was travelling, campaigning, negotiating.

Ruttie was left alone in large houses.

She developed chronic colitis. She withdrew into books and the company of a few loyal friends. By 1927 they had effectively separated.

In early 1928 she moved into a suite at the Taj Mahal Hotel in Bombay, alone. Her health continued to fail.

On the night of February 19, 1929 she was too weak to say more than a few words to her friend Kanji who sat with her.

What she said was, “If I die, look after my cats and don’t give them away.”

She died in her sleep on February 20, 1929.

It was her 29th birthday.

Jinnah was in Delhi when her father called him. He returned to Bombay. As her coffin was lowered into the grave, the man known for never showing emotion in public broke down and wept openly.

He kept all her clothes, ornaments and photographs packed in boxes for the rest of his life. In August 1947 he visited her grave one last time before leaving for Pakistan.

He never returned to India.

She gave up her family, her community and her religion for a man who gave her a life but not enough of himself to fill it.

She was 29 years old.

Follow for stories India deserves to remember.

text:
USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN 78) is finally home. The supercarrier, with nearly 4,500 Sailors aboard, pulled into Naval Station Norfolk on Saturday, greeted by hundreds of families and friends after completing a grueling 326-day combat deployment. The well-deserved homecoming capped the longest deployment in more than five decades, which was extended multiple times to support operations across two continents and combatant commands.

Ford, the world’s largest and most advanced aircraft carrier, departed Virginia almost a year ago for, what was at the time, a routine deployment to Europe. The deployment turned out to be anything but when Ford was redirected to the Caribbean in November ahead of Operation Absolute Resolve. Following the successful extraction of President Nicolas Maduro out of Venezuela, and despite pushback from top Navy brass to come home, the CSG crossed the Atlantic again to project power and pressure from the eastern Mediterranean and northern Red Sea during Operation Epic Fury against Iran. Overall, Ford sailed over 57,000 nautical miles, logged more than 5,700 flight hours, and conducted 12,000+ aircraft launches. Upon arrival in Norfolk, Carrier Strike Group 12 was presented with the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a military unit can receive.

Catch up on the latest in this week's @thewarzonewire carrier tracker: https://t.co/SMWx9YQ8qw

My heart goes out to the affected families, the management of the schools, and the entire communities of Yawota, Esiele, and surrounding areas during this anxious period.

An attack on our schools is an attack on our future. Our children should be in classrooms learning in safety, not living in fear. No parent should have to endure the trauma of not knowing the whereabouts of their child.

I commend the Oyo State Police Command, the I.G, and other security agencies for launching rescue operations, and I urge them to intensify efforts to ensure the safe and immediate return of all those abducted.

I also call on the Oyo State Government to work closely with security agencies and local communities to strengthen security around our schools, particularly in rural areas that are more vulnerable to criminal attacks.

To the affected families, please remain hopeful. My thoughts and prayers and that of the entire state are with you. We stand with you and share in your pain.

As a people, we must unite against all forms of criminality and continue to support lawful efforts to keep our communities safe.

May Almighty God protect our children and grant their safe return.

OH

These are the forces that drive urban populations down. When nations industrialize, they essentially leave the medieval era. Yeah, there were fires and wheels and smithys and cobblers but there was no automation or mass production. 

Even now, good luck making a living in rural America. Unless you're in one of a handful of industries that thrive there, you've got to live in a metro area to make money. And metro areas multiply your expenses and lower the affordability of kids.

text:
Data from e61 Institute shows that young women in Australia out-earn young men by 7-8% on a per hour basis, for those working more than 30 hours per week. The premium earned by young women prevails until their early 30s, and then neutralises during their 30s. During the last decade, young women have seen the largest growth in wages relative to men of any age cohort. And most of this growth for young women came during the last term of Coalition government, from 2019 to 2022. Australian women also have lower unemployment rates than men. A number of cities in the US and UK also display higher hourly earnings for young women compared to young men (aligning to the overall Australian experience).

Drivers of this positive wage gap for young women include significantly superior tertiary education which feeds directly into early-career job access and pay trajectories (there are 64% more female graduates in Australia than male graduates), preferential treatment and quotas for females in a wide range of professions and careers, a sector shift towards services and the “care-sector” (such as strong growth in the National Disability Insurance Scheme), explicit government support for lifting female wages in comparison to male wages (such as the Aged Care and Childcare sectors plus the “gender undervaluation review” by Fair Work Commission), and metro areas display higher wages gaps for young women in comparison to outer/regional/remote areas.

When young women exceed the earnings of young men, there are a few knock-on effects for relationships, birth rates, sustainability, and the health of our society:
- Relationship formation slows. Females typically aim up (i.e. hypergamy) with a desire for a high-earning male. With fewer options available, abundant disposable income and high opportunity cost of their time, women become more selective and they delay coupling up. Couples with a higher earning woman are less stable, and have lower satisfaction.
- More women (and men) remain single, and eventually become involuntarily childless for their entire life. There are relatively more high-achieving women (from an economic perspective), and they tend to pair with high-achieving men. When there are fewer men tracking to stable and well-paid roles, then this delays the formation of long-term relationships.
- Fertility timing gets pushed out, which directly results in fewer children. Later partnering and economic uncertainty correlates with delayed childbearing, causing fewer total births.
- Social trust and wellbeing fall. Boys and young men have been discriminated against throughout their education, while seeing girls and young women elevated. When young men perceive fewer pathways to economic status, stability, and family formation, then it spills into disengagement (from education, work, and civic life).

The Australian media overwhelmingly amplifies a false narrative of a “gender pay gap” that harms women. Most of these estimates ignore the difficult and dangerous conditions faced by men (95% of workplace deaths are male), the long commutes and discomfort of workplaces, fewer work-from-home options for men, the unpaid hours worked by men, the lower security and higher risks that men face in comparison to women.

Young women from their teens to their early thirties are outearning young men, in stark contrast to the loud media headlines. This is symptomatic of an excessive focus on economics over non-financial and intangible factors, short-termism versus long-term sustainability, and an all-time low birth rate. 

Instead of accelerating into a cul-de-sac, we need to rethink education, careers, and the insanely high cost of housing: reduce the over-investment into tertiary studies early in adulthood; prioritise having children when male and female bodies are younger (with healthier children as a result); reorient from an emphasis on pre-kids careers to planning for post-kids careers; giving both men and women workplace flexibility to care for their own children (which comes with lower pay); cherishing the unique but different roles that mothers and fathers contribute; plus uplifting families as the key social institution for future generations.

It isn’t.

In Papua New Guinea - and in most developing nations - this tactic is standard political practice.

In our capital city, Port Moresby, we have three Open Seats and one Governor’s seat. Over the past 10–15 years, Members of Parliament and aspiring candidates have routinely transported thousands of their own people from their home provinces, settled them on land purchased near electorates they were contesting, and reshaped the voter base.

Come election time, they already had the numbers.

Another common tactic is flying voters back to their provinces during every election cycle so they can vote where it benefits a candidate most.

Demographic engineering is not new. It’s how power is secured in unstable or developing political systems.

What we’ve seen under the Biden administration - combined with the explosion of Sanctuary Cities - is the same concept executed at a much larger, more organized, and more sophisticated scale.

Now stack the variables.

You have a culture where millions of Americans abort children with no hesitation, framed as “healthcare.”

You have rapidly growing immigrant populations who overwhelmingly vote Democrat because the policy incentives align with their immediate interests.

You have millions of illegal immigrants imported into the country, many dependent on government benefits and political protection - creating a clear loyalty structure.

And on top of that, you still have millions of Americans who vote Democrat purely because the party promises free handouts.

Meanwhile, the one group expected to carry the country forward - working-class, conservative, pro-family Americans - are having fewer children, delaying families, or opting out altogether.

Demographics decide nations.

Politics is downstream from population.

text:
History may not repeat itself, but it rhymes...

Parallels between ancient empire collapse and modern fertility patterns:

Wealth and fertility inversion

- Roman and Greek elites had fewer children than lower classes, despite greater resources to support large families
- Today, higher income and education levels correlate strongly with lower fertility across virtually all countries
- In both eras, wealth enables choice, and choice often means fewer children

Urban versus rural divide

- Ancient cities like Rome and Athens showed lower fertility than surrounding countryside
- Modern fertility decline is most pronounced in cities, with rural areas maintaining higher birth rates
- Urban living increases costs, reduces space, and shifts social norms away from large families in both contexts

Marriage delays and avoidance

- Augustus penalized unmarried Romans because bachelorhood had become common among elites
- Modern marriage rates have declined sharply, with average age at first marriage rising by nearly a decade since the 1960s in many countries
- Both periods show a weakening of social pressure to marry young and reproduce

Moralistic framing by commentators

- Polybius blamed Greek decline on greed, laziness, and love of luxury
- Modern discourse often frames low fertility as resulting from selfishness, careerism, or hedonism
- In both cases, structural factors like economics and urbanization get less attention than moral narratives

Policy responses with limited success

- Augustus offered tax breaks and legal privileges for parents of three or more children
- Modern pronatalist policies (parental leave, child tax credits, housing subsidies) have shown modest effects at best
- Neither ancient nor modern incentives have reversed underlying trends once established

Elite anxiety exceeding actual crisis

- Roman laws targeted senators and equestrians specifically, suggesting the "problem" was concentrated at the top
- Modern fertility discourse is often loudest among educated commentators whose own class shows the steepest decline
- Both periods show ruling classes worried about reproducing themselves while broader populations maintained higher fertility longer

Luxury and opportunity cost

- Ancient writers noted that parents limited children to preserve wealth for fewer heirs
- Modern parents cite costs of childcare, education, housing, and lifestyle maintenance as reasons for smaller families
- Children shift from economic assets (labor, old-age support) to expensive investments in both transitions

Cultural shifts in life purpose

- Hellenistic philosophy emphasized personal fulfillment, self-cultivation, and withdrawal from civic duty
- Modern individualism prioritizes self-actualization, career achievement, and personal freedom
- Both represent a turn inward, away from family lineage as the primary source of meaning

Gender dynamics

- Roman women with three children gained legal independence from male guardians, suggesting childlessness offered women certain freedoms
- Modern fertility decline tracks closely with women's access to education, employment, and reproductive autonomy
- In both cases, expanded options for women correlate with reduced childbearing

Migration as demographic compensation

- Greek mainland population declined partly as people emigrated to opportunity in Hellenistic kingdoms
- Modern low-fertility countries increasingly rely on immigration to maintain population and workforce
- Both scenarios involve population movement masking or offsetting native fertility decline

text:
John makes a great point about taxes mostly affecting company formation, and this exact analogy also applies to young people having children in the City. The real issue is formation, scaling, and staying power for both companies and families. If a City is not good for the long term, people will either leave now, leave later, or forgo.

The City is perfect for certain kinds of companies and people. As a small company, if you need access to highly specialized, highly paid, mission-critical staff and you need to be in person, it absolutely makes sense to be in NYC, San Francisco @garrytan, El Segundo @JoshuaSteinman, etc. You benefit disproportionately from the density of talent and other similar companies.

The same goes for young ambitious people. Being in Manhattan when you are 22 to 26 is fantastic. You are going to work hard, be around other ambitious peers, and be near the most successful capital and companies.

But no real company stops at a few dozen employees, and most people want to have kids at some point.

Once you scale to hundreds or thousands of employees, you need an entirely different labor force: middle management, operations, customer support, finance, HR, junior engineers, factory workers, and others. These are people who are essential to the firm but not paid founder or partner salaries. These are precisely the people who are most sensitive to housing costs, school quality, and taxes.

Your company has committed, culturally and operationally, to value in-person work. If you have chosen a city where the very employees you need to scale cannot afford to stay, and where the families you need to retain face eye-watering housing costs or long commutes, then at that point the 14% tax is no longer just expensive. It actively undermines your ability to function as an in-person organization.

That is not a hypothetical problem. It shows up as constant churn, remote exemptions, satellite offices, or quiet relocations ... even among the successful startups. The company may keep its HQ in NY/SF but the growth engine moves elsewhere. And Now founders and management have to be on the road.

This is where the analogy to families becomes unavoidable.

Cities like New York increasingly function as revolving doors. They are excellent at attracting young adults and early-stage companies. They are terrible at retaining them once life becomes more complex. Families that do manage to stay are disproportionately wealthy, and policy increasingly treats them as the solution by raising costs on the small, shrinking base of families who have not yet left.

But that gets the causality backwards.

The problem is not that wealthy families (or valuable companies) are insufficiently taxed. The problem is that the city cannot attract and retain enough families in the first place. Just as with companies, the real loss is not the people who leave. It is the families and firms that never come, or never scale, because the math no longer works.

A city built on constant inflows of young people and young companies looks vibrant in the short run. In the long run, it hollows out its middle: fewer children, fewer stable neighborhoods, and fewer institutions with continuity. Schools degrade further, housing prices rise faster, and the tax base becomes narrower and more volatile, prompting still higher taxes on those who remain.

So it's not a story about tax rates, it is about compounding decisions over time and reduced quality of broad services. When a city prices out the middle layers of companies and families alike, it does not just lose people. It loses duration, depth, and institutional memory.

The real policy question, then, is not “Will the wealthy leave?” It is whether the city can become a place where companies can scale and families can stay. Without that, the revolving door keeps spinning, no matter how strong the city’s natural advantages may be.

TLDR: Cities need to be designed to keep the "missing middle" both of housing and management ... for families

⚡ Every advanced economy on Earth has entered a synchronized demographic collapse.

That is the underlying force that creates the pattern.

Let me break it open for you.

1.  Birth rates in developed countries collapsed from 1970–2020

This is the root cause.

Across OECD nations, fertility fell to:
•Japan: 1.2
•South Korea: 0.72
•Italy: 1.24
•Germany: 1.4
•Spain: 1.2
•Switzerland: 1.4
•Canada: 1.47
•UK: 1.56
•USA (white non-Hispanic): 1.58

These numbers are far below replacement (2.1).

This isn’t cultural or racial.
This is economic-demographic gravity.

Once fertility falls below ~1.6 for more than 20–30 years, the curve does not recover without migration.

This is math, not ideology.

2.  A shrinking workforce breaks the pension system, the healthcare system, and the tax base

When the population pyramid inverts, more old than young, governments face fiscal collapse.

To avoid that collapse, countries import working-age adults.

This is why the trend is synchronized across:
•Switzerland
•Australia
•Austria
•Germany
•Canada
•Sweden
•Spain
•UK

The type of immigrant varies, but the phenomenon is identical.

3.  Migrants are filling age gaps, not replacing populations

Look deeper and you’ll see:

The median age of migrants to OECD countries is typically 25–34.

The median age of native populations is 42–48.

This is backfilling a demographic crater created by 50 years of below-replacement birth rates.

If this did not happen, these economies would experience:
•GDP contraction
•pension insolvency
•collapsing housing markets
•labor shortages
•shrinking tax bases
•accelerated national decline

Migration is the stopgap.

It is not the cause of the collapse.
It is the response to the collapse.

4.  The real “coordinator” is something much more boring and much more powerful:

demographic arithmetic

Birth rates drop.
Population ages.
Governments panic.
Migration spikes.

Every OECD country followed the same economic trajectory and therefore hit the same demographic wall.

That is why the pattern is synchronized.

5.  Why this chart feels alarming to people

Because the rate of change is historically fast.

Humans evolved for slow demographic drift, not 30-year composition shifts.

The brain interprets rapid change as threat.

The Deepest Layer:

What this really is about is civilizational entropy.

Every advanced society eventually hits the fertility–prosperity inversion:
•more prosperity →
•more education →
•more urbanization →
•higher cost of raising children →
•later marriage →
•fewer children

This is the same phenomenon that hit:
•ancient Rome
•classical Athens
•Qing China’s elites
•late medieval merchant cities

The modern version is just global and fast.

The real cause is that advanced civilizations eventually consume their own capacity to reproduce themselves.

text:
“Canada’s housing crisis is not just locking people out of homeownership. It is delaying—and in many cases erasing—the milestones that define adult life for its next generation.

Our country is facing a milestone recession: a broad, intergenerational collapse in the ability to hit the benchmarks that once signalled independence and progress in adulthood.

Young people are staying in school longer, in part because entry-level wages are weak and job markets are uncertain. They’re staying at home longer because even with decent incomes, market rents are unaffordable. They’re delaying partnerships, marriage, and children—because a life of their own still feels out of reach. And when they finally do begin to start their adult lives, they often do it far from the cities they grew up in—because that’s where housing is available and affordable, if you don’t have an inheritance.

Many still go on to have children. But they do so later, and have fewer children than they had hoped for, and under greater stress. Housing is not the only reason for Canada’s record-low fertility rate, but it is a significant one, compounded by a deeper cultural sentiment: that the future feels less secure, less free, and less worth betting on.

A generation raised to believe they would do better than their parents is instead learning to shrink their expectations. That shrinkage—of time, of space, of possibility—is what makes this moment so corrosive. The promise of Canada was that each generation could build more than the one before. That promise is breaking. Not all at once—but in thousands of delayed decisions, deferred dreams, and invisible compromises that always put our youth last. It’s hollowing out our culture.”

Now show all these images of destroyed cities, thousands of deaths of civilians and our children to all those who justify the russians. Or to those who say that the Ukrainian strikes on russian military airfields are terror. 

Destruction of the aggressor's aircraft, which have been killing Ukrainians daily for several years now, committing countless war crimes and aggression - IS THIS TERROR?

A world of vile, immoral and inhuman hypocrites, whose souls are blacker than soot.

And it is precisely in this hypocrisy that the root of global evil lies.
Those who remain silent about Mariupol and hundreds of other cities and towns, but are outraged by the military airfield where the planes that committed all this were destroyed, are not pacifists or adherents of peace, but accomplices of murder. Those who shout that they do not want a third world war, but have never called on Russia to stop bombing Ukrainian cities, choose the side of violence, not peace.

Ukraine did not start this war.
Ukraine defends its right to live.

And every Ukrainian strike on a missile depot, on an airfield from which murderers take off, on a command post of those who give orders to bomb peaceful cities - This is defense, this is the right to life. 

While someone demands to “understand Russia”, Ukrainians bury their loved ones every day, for the sole reason that Russia started the war, and it can also end it.

An elderly woman, who was pulled out from under the rubble by rescuers and who spent two days under a concrete slab next to the body of her dead neighbor. 
Will she be an “aggressor” if she says: “I want those who dropped this bomb on us to never take off again”? 

A father, mother and their daughter, left without a home, without work, without school and heat - are they terrorists if they pray that the enemy airfield from which the missile took off no longer exists? 

Is a paramedic who has stopped the bleeding of children wounded by shelling hundreds of times a war criminal if he says: “If we destroy the enemy positions, fewer children will die”?

A schoolgirl, who has studied in a basement for over a year, will she become a “radical” if she writes an essay: “I dream that killer drones will no longer fly over us”? 

And at this moment, everyone who lives in warmth, safety and well-being, but condemns those who defend their right to life, loses the moral right to talk about humanity.

A Ukrainian who demands the destruction of a military airfield from which planes take off every day, killing his people, is not a terrorist. He is a man who does not want to die.
A mother who screams to the whole world: "Help us survive!" is not an instigator of conflict. She is the voice of those who survived hell.

So stop shifting responsibility.
Stop comparing defense with attack.
Stop devaluing other people's pain.

Peace begins with honesty.
With recognition: who is destroying and who is protecting.
And only then can we talk about peace - real, not imaginary.

text:
Thoughts on Japan’s Declining Birthrate

I wanted to share my thoughts on Japan’s declining birthrate, but as I looked into it, I realized how many complex factors are involved. It turned out to be a longer discussion than I expected, but I’ve broken it down into key points, so feel free to read through if you’re interested.

Fewer People Are Getting Married

One major factor behind Japan’s declining birthrate is that fewer people are getting married. In the past, marriage was the norm, and being single was quite rare. Today, however, staying single is no longer unusual, and more people are choosing not to marry.

One reason for this decline is the shift from arranged marriages to love marriages. In the past, families or matchmakers played a significant role in helping people find a spouse, but now, individuals are expected to find a partner on their own. This change has made it more difficult for some people to get married, especially those who have limited opportunities for romantic relationships.

Additionally, work pressures and economic uncertainty have led many people to delay marriage, and some end up remaining single as a result. As society becomes more accepting of staying single, the number of people who never marry may continue to rise.

Even Married Couples Are Having Fewer Children

Even among those who do get married, more couples are choosing not to have children or are limiting themselves to just one. In the past, it was common to have three or four siblings, but today, one or two children per family has become the norm. In 2024, Japan recorded 720,000 births, the lowest number since World War II.

This is not just a matter of changing personal preferences—economic factors play a significant role. Raising a child requires both time and money, and many couples feel that they simply can’t afford to have more children. This is especially true in urban areas, where the cost of living and education is particularly high. As a result, more couples are making the difficult decision that “one child is the limit” or even deciding not to have children at all.

Furthermore, compared to the past, the amount of money spent on each child has increased. Parents today want to provide their children with the best possible environment, investing heavily in education, extracurricular activities, and other aspects of child-rearing. This increased financial burden makes larger families less feasible.

In addition, as more young people move to big cities, birthrates tend to decline even further. The high cost of living in urban areas makes raising children more challenging than in rural areas. Encouraging people to stay in regional areas might help stabilize birthrates to some extent.

Higher Education and Rising Child-Rearing Costs

Another key factor is the increasing emphasis on higher education, which has made raising children even more expensive. In the past, not every child was expected to go to university, but today, higher education is seen as essential. As a result, the financial burden on parents has grown significantly.

At the same time, the rising university enrollment rate has contributed to delayed marriage and childbirth. With longer years spent in education, people are entering the workforce later, which in turn pushes back the timing of marriage and parenthood. Many people eventually decide that having children is not a priority.

Given these high costs, it’s no surprise that many couples feel that “one child is the limit” or even decide not to have children at all.

The Impact of the “Lost Generation” and the Rise of Non-Regular Employment

Economic insecurity is another major factor driving Japan’s low birthrate. The so-called “Lost Generation” — those born in the 1970s — were supposed to become parents in the 1990s and 2000s. However, many missed their opportunity due to economic hardship.

text:
Why Red States Have Much Higher Birthrates than Blue States
With lessons for Democrats and low fertility countries everywhere!

In the 2024 US presidential election, one of the most prominent features was the very large family gap between states won by Trump and states won by Harris -- red states have far higher fertility. X user Charlie Smirkley observed that “The hypothetical 0% Trump share state would have a TFR of 1.04. For a state with a 100% Trump share, the TFR would be 2.20.”

Given this large and persistent difference, Democratic states really need to need to boost birth rates or else be left behind politically. But what is behind this enormous gap? There are several factors that matter a great deal for birthrates, and Republicans do much better on all these factors than Democrats. Let’s explore:

Pronatal Beliefs
The first driver of birthrates is simply fertility preferences: How many children do people want to have? This in turn is driven by views around children. How important are families? Are low birthrates a problem or a good thing?

I showed in a recent thread how beliefs around children have a big impact on fertility.
https://t.co/zGVcDRLEqt
In 2023, Pew Research surveyed Americans about their views around family, and they asked several questions about pronatal views, such as whether people having fewer children is negative or positive. It turns out that there are big differences between Republicans and Democrats, with Republicans having markedly more positive views about the importance of children for America’s future.

This is area where things can really change. A lot of people do not yet grasp that low birthrates are a serious problem. When they do, many will want to do their part by having more children.

Religiosity
Overwhelmingly, studies show a strong positive relationship between religious belief and attendance, and fertility.
https://t.co/PDgaxUQd22

Is there a difference in religiosity between Democrats and Republicans? Yes, a big one! Republicans are much more likely to have religious belief than Democrats and are more likely to attend religious services.

Density and housing type
In general, density and crowding are quite negative for birthrates. This is plain both from a review of the literature around fertility and from maps of fertility around the around the world.
https://t.co/0qxZlMvNPS
https://t.co/zehjWlSRga
Given the large ‘land gap’ between Democrats and Republicans, where Democrats tend to crowd in and around cities while Republicans tend to spread out across the land, it is no surprise that the latter would have much higher birthrates.
Republican areas tend to have much cheaper housing because of less expensive land and because they tend to have fewer restrictions on building. But also, in cities where Democrats tend to live there is a high prevalence of apartment living, which is itself less favorable to family life.

Marriage
Until about 1980, there was little difference between Republicans and Democrats in marriage rates. Both tended to marry at very high rates. But these days, less than half of Democrats ages 30-50 are married, while more than 2/3 of Republican are.
This matters greatly for fertility, since people who are married are much more likely to have children than those who are not.

Lessons for Blue States and Low Birthrate Countries
What can blue states (and low birthrate countries) learn from red states about how to have higher birthrates?

· Develop pronatal belief. That means building awareness of low birthrates as a problem and speaking positively rather than negatively about population. People really do adjust their fertility preferences according to these ideas!
· Value religion more. Faiths should not be dismissed backwards, especially in a world of plunging birthrates. They are often the biggest driver of family formation.
· Build more housing, but of a type that is right for families. Mainly that means opening new land for more suburbs. A lot of blue states, such as California and Oregon, have plenty of unused land, but they prohibit building on it.
https://t.co/vbJNnzLmEn
· Encourage marriage in culture. University of Maryland economist Melissa Kearney explains that those left rarely want to talk about the benefits of marriage for families, because such talk is coded as right-wing. That taboo is costly and needs to be discarded.

Republican leaning states in the US are doing comparatively well demographically and may come to dominate Democrat leaning states if these trends continue. It would be better for those states and better for America if they could raise their fertility, by following those states that already have this figured out.

Meanwhile, countries struggling with low birthrates would be well advised to follow the red state model to higher birthrates.

Shares are greatly appreciated!

On October 6th 2021, the firm published an analysis titled "Crisis or Opportunity? What China's 3rd Child Policy Means for Consumer Investors," examining the potential effects of China's shift to a three-child policy on consumer behavior and market opportunities.

The analysis highlighted several key points:

1. Demographic Shifts: China's declining birth rates and aging population have prompted policy changes aimed at encouraging larger families. However, factors such as the high cost of urban living, demanding work schedules, and changing societal norms have led many couples to opt for fewer children.

2. Consumer Market Opportunities: Despite the challenges in reversing declining birth rates, L Catterton identified growth prospects in specific consumer segments:

Post-90s Mothers: This demographic, representing around 60% of new mothers in China, exhibits a preference for premium, health-focused products, indicating potential for high-end maternity and childcare brands.

Lower-Tier Cities: With over 80% of China's newborns expected to come from third- to fifth-tier cities, there are opportunities for brands to cater to the unique preferences and price sensitivities of consumers in these regions.

Global Expansion: Chinese brands leveraging efficient supply chains to offer competitively priced products internationally can tap into global markets, especially in sectors like children's apparel.
