quote.text:
LA to SF on FSD + Tesla Q1 2026 Call.

✅ Listen to the full 1-hour Tesla 2026 Q1 shareholders call while Tesla self-driving (FSD) drives our Cybertruck over 500 miles (800 km) from the Los Angeles area to the San Francisco Bay Area, hands- and feet-free the entire way.

✅ Over 9 hours of flawless self-driving on city streets and highways, including Hollywood and Los Angeles (video sped up 9.6x to match audio).

✅ The Cybertruck handled the complete route on Tesla self-driving (FSD): Joshua Tree → Loma Linda → Tesla Diner in Hollywood → all the way home to the San Francisco Bay Area.

✅ We stopped every couple of hours for breaks, food, and walking the pup, using the time for easy Supercharger stops.

✅ Elon Musk and Tesla executives (Vaibhav Taneja, Ashok Elluswamy, Lars Moravy, Michael Snyder, and Travis Axelrod) answered shareholder and analyst questions on FSD (supervised & unsupervised), Robotaxi, Optimus, Energy, HW3/AI4/AI5, Europe rollout, and more.

I only intervened a couple of times to reposition in parking spots and adjusted the speed profile (Chill ↔ Standard ↔ Hurry) as needed.

Here's the full transcript:

(00:00) Travis Axelrod: Good afternoon, everyone and welcome to Tesla's first quarter 2026 Q&A webcast.  

(00:04) My name is Travis Axelrod, Head of Investor Relations, and I'm joined today by Elon Musk, Vaibhav Taneja and a number of other executives.  

(00:15) Our Q1 results were announced at about 3:00 PM Central Time. In the update deck, we published at the same link as this webcast.  

(00:22) During this call, we will discuss our business outlook and make forward-looking statements. These comments are based on our predictions and expectations as of today.  

(00:30) Actual events or results could differ materially due to a number of risks and uncertainties, including those mentioned in our most recent filings with the SEC.  

(00:40) During the question and answer portion of today's call, please limit yourself to one question and one follow up. Please use the raise hand button to join the question queue.  

(00:50) Before we jump into Q&A, Elon has some opening remarks. Elon.  

(00:54) Elon Musk: Thank you. So I think we've got a very exciting year ahead of us with 2026.  

(00:59) We're going to be substantially increasing our investments in the future. So we should expect to see a significant, very significant, increase in capital expenditures.  

(01:10) But I think well justified for a substantially increased future revenue stream. And obviously Tesla's not alone in this.  

(01:20) I think you've seen most, if not all, certainly the major technology companies substantially increasing their capital investments and we're going to be doing the same. I think it's going to pay off in a very big way.  

(01:37) So we're investing in and improving our core technologies, battery powertrain, AI software, AI training, chip design, manufacturing expense, you know, laying the groundwork for significantly increased manufacturing production.  

(01:52) We are also strengthening our supply chain across the board, batteries, energy, AI, silicon and everything and laying the groundwork, like I said, for what we expect to be a significant increase in vehicle production in the future and of course, a very significant increase.  

(02:18) Well, actually releasing Optimus, but increasing our internal production for testing and then probably being able to have Optimus be useful outside of Tesla sometime next year.  

(02:33) As you've heard me say a few times, I think Optimus will be our biggest product, not just Tesla's biggest product ever, but probably the biggest product ever.  

(02:46) And I remain convinced of that conclusion.  

(02:51) On our vehicle side, it's always I think worth noting that a Tesla car is incredible value for money and they're all autonomy ready.  

(03:03) Depending on what part of the world you're in, the supervised full self-driving is getting extremely good.  

(03:12) We have just started production of Cybercab and we'll begin production of our semi-truck soon.  

(03:22) Now I should say whenever you have a new product with a completely new supply chain, new everything, it's always a stretched out S curve.  

(03:34) So you should expect that initial production of Cybercab and Semi will be very slow, but then ramping up and going kind of exponential towards the end of the year and totally next year.  

(03:52) And in fact, we'll be ramping up production of all vehicles and all factories to the best of our ability through the balance of this year.  

(04:02) On the energy front, the United States and the whole world will need a lot of energy storage to meet growing electricity demand.  

(04:12) Demand for our Megapack is very strong and we're excited to begin production of Megapack 3 later this year in our new world class factory outside Houston.  

(04:24) For full Self driving and Robotaxi, version 14.3 was a major architectural update. And we have a whole pipeline of major improvements to full self-driving that we believe will lead to unsupervised full self-driving being available anywhere in the world that it is legal to do so.  

(04:47) And then there's version 15, hopefully later this year, probably by the end of this year, but certainly by early next year.  

(05:02) And that will be a complete overhaul of the software architecture and we'll run on AI4. And that at that point we're really just increasing the safety level of FSD above human safety level even more.  

(05:20) Meaning, I think even within version 14, we're significantly safer than a human. But V15 will take that to another level.  

(05:31) We've expanded Robotaxi to Dallas and Houston using the same software as Austin and the Bay Area.  

(05:44) And the limiting factor for expansion is really rigorous validation, making sure things are completely safe. We don't want to have a single accident or injury with the expansion of Robotaxi and we have, to the credit of the team, not had a single one to date.  

(06:02) And then Optimus, we're preparing Fremont for startup production later this year with Optimus, again, totally new supply chain, totally new technology.  

(06:18) So therefore it's the production S curve is always very slow in the beginning, but we'll ramp up to significant numbers next year and we're constructing a second Optimus factory at our Giga Texas location. And that will probably start production around summer next year.  

(06:47) The V3 Optimus design is almost ready to demonstrate. I think we want to just make sure it's like polished, like it works functionally, but there's some aesthetic elements that need to be finalized.  

(07:03) And I think probably middle of this year we should be able to show it off.  

(07:09) We're also a little hesitant to show V3 off because we find our competitors do a frame by frame analysis whenever we release something and copy everything they possibly can.  

(07:19) So I think there's some value to not showing new technology until it's close to production.  

(07:27) Congratulations again to the Tesla AI chip team for taping out AI5. That's going to be a great chip.  

(07:42) I think probably the best AI inference chip for edge compute that exists. And certainly I think unequivocally the best value for money.  

(07:54) The team did a great job and we already have a lot of momentum for designing AI6 and we've begun to discuss ideas for Dojo 3.  

(08:07) So this is all very exciting.  

(08:12) We've also finalized plans for the chip fab. The research chip fab on the Giga Texas campus, and we'll start construction of that this year.  

(08:25) In conclusion, Tesla is working on a lot of large, ambitious projects. They're all very challenging, but I think they're going to be revolutionary.  

(08:38) And this is what the team does best, solve the hardest problems and build amazing products.  

(08:44) And I'd like to thank the Tesla team for all the hard work and thank you to all of our supporters.  

(08:50) Travis Axelrod: Great. Thank you very much, Elon. And Vaibhav also has some opening remarks.  

(08:55) Vaibhav Taneja: Thanks, Travis. So 2026 has had an interesting start, not just for us but I think the world in general.  

(09:01) On the auto business, we have seen a resurgence in demand in EMEA and certain countries like France and Germany showing over 150% quarter over quarter growth in deliveries.  

(09:12) In APEC, we witnessed growth in South Korea and Japan, again in terms of deliveries. Even out here in the US, we have seen a slight growth in terms of quarter over quarter deliveries.  

(09:26) On the order backlog front, we ended the quarter with the highest Q1 order backlog in over 2 years.  

(09:33) Whilst the recent increase in gas prices has had a positive impact on the order rate, this improvement started before the uptrend in gas prices.  

(09:43) This is due to the work done by the Tesla team in bringing more compelling and affordable vehicles to market.  

(09:52) Ten years back when we launched the Model 3 in the US with the promise of a $35,000 starting price, which if you adjust today for inflation, translates to about $48,000 in today's dollar terms.  

(10:04) The starting price of Model 3 today is way less than that [it's $36k], while the product is way more compelling from where it started.  

(10:13) Given the setup, we are focused on increasing our overall production volume, something that we already started in Q1.  

(10:18) This volume increase is evidenced by the Giga Berlin reaching a record output of over 61,000 units in Q1.  

(10:30) We plan to keep growing volumes further, not just in Berlin, but across all our factories.  

(10:37) Our biggest limiter continues to be our battery pack capacity and we are actively working on resolving that.  

(10:44) Auto margins, excluding credits, improved sequentially from 17.9% to 19.2%.  

(10:49) Note that we have had certain one time benefits from warranty [as well?] down, around 230 million, and some relief on tariffs.  

(10:56) We have not realized any benefit from the recent Supreme Court ruling on iPad tariffs as there is still a lot of uncertainty around the final outcome.  

(11:05) Both tariffs and sustained high interest rates continue to add to our automotive cost. Interest rate subvention costs are recognized upfront.  

(11:18) If interest rates continue to rise, our cost of subvention will continue to impact auto margins.  

(11:24) On the FSD adoption front, we continue to see improvement, reaching nearly 1.3 million paid customers globally.  

(11:32) The bulk of the growth came from subscriptions while upfront purchases only increased 7% as we removed the purchase option in some markets in Q1.  

(11:44) We recently received approvals for FSD in Netherlands. This sets up as well for EU wide approval later in Q2 and you know we are just gated by how the regulators go about it.  

(11:54) Additionally, we have also received approvals in China.  

(12:05) The broader approval is still not there, but we are working with the regulators in the country and we are hoping that we can get approval by Q3.  

(12:14) With these approvals coming through, we expect the broader adoption of the software in the existing fleet and incremental demand for our vehicles.  

(12:21) With all this in mind, we have evolved our vehicle sales strategy where we now emphasize FSD as a product and vehicle as only the delivery mechanism.  

(12:29) As we have noted previously, the energy storage business is inherently lumpy tied to customer deployment timelines.  

(12:41) In Q1, we deployed 68.8 GW hour of energy storage, a 38% sequential decline.  

(12:49) However, we still expect 2026 deployments to be higher than 2025.  

(12:55) We set yet another record with gross margins in this business over 39.5% due to some one time benefits from certain tariff recognitions of more than 250 million from certain tariffs which were paid in prior quarters. On a normalized basis, we continue to expect energy compression from here with increasing competition and tariff impacts.  

(13:20) As previously discussed, tariffs in this business can have outsize impacts as most of the battery cells are procured from China.  

(13:28) Our order backlog for this business is robust and we are doing our best to build not just based on existing demand, but also on expected demand.  

(13:37) Services and others improved sequentially from 8.8% to 9.2%.  

(13:48) This includes a collection of efforts meant to support our customers like service centers, used cars, paid supercharging, parts sales, insurance, and even our Robotaxi business.  

(13:57) We are making deliberate investments in the infrastructure to help the Robotaxi in the future.  

(14:04) We grew the Robotaxi fleet quarter over quarter and we expect to keep ramping the fleet as we accelerate and get into other geographies.  

(14:13) On operating expenses side, we did increase sequentially from a full quarter stock based compensation expense for the 2025 CEO compensation plan for which one milestone is still deemed probable.  

(14:24) Additionally, our spend on AI related initiatives including expense on development of our own AI5 chip and new products like Cybercab, Semi, Optimus, and Megablock, etc. continue to be at elevated levels and we expect this trend to continue for the full year 2026.  

(14:48) Net income was impacted from mark to market charges on our Bitcoin holdings which depreciated 22% as compared to the last quarter and the unfavorable impact of FX primarily from our large intercompany borrowings.  

(14:56) On free cash flow, we ended the quarter with just over 1.4 billion.  

(15:12) As Elon mentioned, we are in a very big capital investment phase which is going to start now and would last a couple of years.  

(15:20) So based on that, our current expectation for 2026 is over 25 billion of CapEx.  

(15:31) And, you know, just to remind you, we are paying for six factories which we're going to go into operation. Some have already started, some would go into operation later part of this year.  

(15:42) We are further increasing our investment in AI related initiatives including the AI infrastructure to support Robotaxi and the launch of Optimus.  

(15:55) We have already started placing orders for the research semiconductor fab in Austin and for solar manufacturing equipment.  

(16:03) While this may seem a lot and we will have the impact of negative free cash flow for the rest of the year, we believe this is the right strategy to position the company for the next era. We'll make such investments in a very capital efficient manner.  

(16:18) We are actively working on a mission of building a future of amazing abundance.  

(16:24) However, that requires not just a lot of investment but an immense amount of execution.  

(16:30) The future is going to be great and the whole Tesla team is rising to the occasion to make this a reality.  

(16:35) I would like to end by thanking the Tesla team, our customers, investors, and vendors for having confidence in us on this journey. Thanks.  

(16:45) Travis Axelrod: Thank you very much, Vaibhav. Now we're going to go to investor questions, starting with questions from https://t.co/ixsRFvSu4b.  

(16:49) The first question is when will we have the Optimus 3 reveal, which we already touched on. But the rest of the question is when will Optimus production start? Since we ended the model X and S production earlier this mid year.  

(17:01) And then what's the expected Optimus production rate exiting this year and what are the initial targeted skills?  

(17:17) Elon Musk: Well, as I was saying, what we've found is that when we've unveiled various software versions, various Optimus versions, we found out how competitors literally do a frame by frame analysis and copy everything we're doing.  

(17:29) So I think we want to push the Optimus 3 unveil maybe closer to production, somewhere around the late July or August timeframe.  

(17:45) And I mean, just to inject some reality into these questions, since these questions are not, you know, the square root of this question does not fully understand what happens with the production line.  

(17:54) The last S and X production will be in early May, but you have to look at the entire upstream portion of the production line.  

(18:07) So you have to start with, you know, cells, battery packs, you know, motor production, all the parts production.  

(18:17) And so we've been dismantling the S and X production line from the more base level parts to... As you get to most larger sub assemblies, you start dismantling the line from the small parts first, not from the final assembly first.  

(18:33) So the final assembly line that'll be dismantled next month, after the last of the S and X vehicles are done. Now you can't dismantle some gigantic production line overnight.  

(18:49) It takes at least a few months to do so. And then you've got to install a new production line and you've got to provide all of the wiring and communication and test out the machines of the new production line for Optimus.  

(19:10) So that also takes several months.  

(19:22) So frankly, if we're able to go from stopping production on one line, dismantling that entire line, reinstalling a whole new line and turning that on in a matter of four months, that is an insanely fast speed!  

(19:36) I don't think any other company on earth has ever done that before.  

(19:46) Just to put things into perspective and inject some reality into the situation here.  

(19:54) I don't know what the production rate of Optimus will be this year. It is impossible to predict these things.  

(20:01) When you have a brand new product in an entire new production line and you have 10,000 unique items, all of which have to go right to ramp production, it'll move as fast as the least lucky, slowest, dumbest part in the entire 10,000.  

(20:24) And this is Optimus, a completely new product with a completely new production line.  

(20:33) So it's just literally impossible to predict except that I think it will be quite slow for us as we iron out the 10,000 plus unique items that have to be sold for Optimus to reach volume production.  

(20:52) Initial skills will be... Obviously we're going to start with simple skills in the factory and then build up from there.  

(21:06) Travis Axelrod: Great. Thank you, Elon.  

(21:14) The next question is what milestones are you targeting for unsupervised FSD and Robotaxi expansion beyond Austin this year? And how will that drive recurring revenue?  

(21:24) Elon Musk: Well, we certainly hope to have unsupervised FSD or slash Robotaxi operating in a dozen or so states by the end of this year.  

(21:49) Initially, you know, we're taking a very cautious approach to the rollout here.  

(22:03) We haven't had any injuries and certainly no fatalities to date with the unsupervised FSD and Robotaxi expansion. We want to keep it that way.  

(22:14) And so, yeah, I think probably unsupervised FSD or Robotaxi revenue will not be super material this year, but I do think it will be material probably in a significant way next year.  

(22:38) Travis Axelrod: Great. Thank you very much.  

(22:47) The next question is when do you expect FSD unsupervised to reach customer cars?  

(22:51) Elon Musk: I'm just guessing here, but probably in the fourth quarter [of 2026]. It's not simple to release this to everyone, everywhere, all at once.  

(23:07) Because we do want to make sure that there are not unique situations in a city that... A particularly complex intersection or, you know, actually they tend to be places where where people get into accidents a lot because they're just, you know, perhaps there's an unsafe intersection or bad road markings or a lot of weather challenges.  

(23:34) So I think we would release unsupervised [FSD] gradually to the customer fleet as we feel like a particular geography is confirmed to be safe.  

(23:47) Travis Axelrod: Great. And the next question is how will hardware 3 cars reach unsupervised FSD?  

(24:03) Elon Musk: Unfortunately, hardware 3, I wish it were otherwise, but hardware 3 simply does not have the capability to achieve unsupervised FSD.  

(24:13) We did think at one point it would have that, but relative to hardware 4 it has only one eighth the memory bandwidth of hardware 4.  

(24:24) And memory bandwidth is one of the key elements needed for unsupervised FSD. And it's just generally a thing that's needed for AI, if you're doing an order aggressive transformer, memory bandwidth is the troll point.  

(24:43) So for customers that have bought FSD, what we're offering is essentially a trade-in, like a discounted trade-in, for cars that have AI4 hardware.  

(24:55) And then we'll also be offering the ability to upgrade the car to replace the computer. And you also need to replace the cameras, unfortunately, to go to hardware 4.  

(25:15) So to do this efficiently, we're going to have to set up like kind of micro factories or small factories in major metropolitan areas in order to do it efficiently.  

(25:31) Because if it's done just at the service center, it is extremely slow to do so and inefficient.  

(25:41) So we basically need like many production lines to make the change.  

(25:48) And I do think over time it's going to make sense for us to convert all hardware 3 cars to hardware 4, because that's what enables them to enter the Robotaxi fleet and have unsupervised FSD.  

(26:03) Ashok Elluswamy: And for what it's worth, in the meantime, we are going to also release a V14 version for hardware 3.  

(26:12) This will be a distilled version of the same V14 software that we released for hardware 4. And people should be able to start the drives from park state and basically have all the features that V14 for hardware 4 has and that's expected to come end of June.  

(26:28) Travis Axelrod: Great, thank you very much.  

(26:36) The next question is what enabled you to finish the AI5 tape out early and were there any changes to the original vision?  

(26:40) Last week, Elon said AI5 will go into Optimus and the supercomputer, but one month ago he said it would go into the Robotaxi. Has AI5 been dropped from the vehicle road map?  

(26:51) Elon Musk: Well, the reason AI5 tape out finished early was because the team worked incredibly hard to make it happen.  

(27:00) And just over time we gathered a lot of momentum. But we did have to work every weekend for six months straight, including every holiday.  

(27:13) So it was a lot of sacrifice by a team and I was there of course myself every weekend.  

(27:23) And fortunately we didn't encounter any major... We didn't make any major mistakes that, at least that we're aware of, that required pushing out the tape out.  

(27:33) So the team just did a great job and worked incredibly hard, is the reason.  

(27:40) Yeah, I do expect that AI5 will go into Optimus and into the data center because it's looking like we'll be able to achieve unsupervised self driving with AI4 that is far greater than human safety levels.  

(27:58) Which means it's certainly not immediately needed in the car.  

(28:08) At some point I think it will make sense for us to switch to AI5 in the car, but there's not a pressing issue to do so.  

(28:23) But at some point the AI4 hardware is going to get like so old that the only reason they're keeping the factory open is for AI4.  

(28:35) We are planning an AI4 upgrade to use newer generation RAM. So it'll go from 16 gigabytes to I think 32 gigabytes per SoC, so a total of 64 gigabytes. And probably a 10% increase in compute and sort of into trillions of operations per second and in memory bandwidth.  

(29:01) So that's AI4.1 or AI4+ probably goes into production next year.  

(29:24) I think it depends on... Samsung's doing the modifications for us. So it sort of depends on when they're able to finish that, finish those modifications and bring it to production.  

1/4

text:
Maboko Island-Kisumu's perfect hideout
Maboko Island Resort (Camp Tom) 
This beautiful Island  measures around 5 acres and is located offshore the Seme area. Seme is about an hour and a half drive from Kisumu City.
It has a main block that is made up of three self-contained suites that are well furnished.
At the center of Maboko is a helipad for the helicopters commuting to and from the island.
The common mode of transportation to the island, however, typically involves the use of a powerboat.
Situated South-West of Kisumu County, accessed via the Kisumu-Bondo Road, the Island provides a perfect escape for anyone who wants to get away from the hustle and bustle of the city life. The Maboko Islands Resort (Camp Tom) inside it provides you with such a destination. Being a new facility for travelers seeking an escape, the resort offers a perfect retreat conducive for team building, tranquility and or to rejuvenate the tired body and soul.
Story goes that long time ago, there were Tanzanians from Musoma who used to live on the island. And the island used to have a high population of hippos, and because of this, the Tanzanians therefore called the place “Maboko” meaning place of many hippos. Maboko is from the Swahili word “Kiboko” for hippo. The Tanzanians eventually moved to their motherland, Tanzania leaving the island to the current local inhabitants.
ACCESS
To get to Maboko Island Resort, there are three available options to use:
Use private or public transport from Kisumu through the Bondo road to Obambo, a distance of approximately 20 km. From Obambo, hitch a motorbike ride to Ogal Beach. This should take you to “Camp David” which is the boarding terminal to Camp Tom (Maboko Island Resort). Camp Tom has a secure parking space for guests. There are boats here that will take the passengers to the resort.
From Kisumu City, board a speed boat/yacht from Kisumu Yacht Club or Hippo Point (as may be advised by the Resort). This should take you straight to the resort. The journey is approximately 20 minutes to 1 hour depending on which boat is used.
You can as well choose to fly in straight in to the resort using a chopper. The resort has two helipads to cater for its flying guests.
ACCOMMODATION
Maboko Island Resort offers its guests three unique accommodation options:
Stay in the main house: provides the guests with the best scenic and uninterrupted view of Lake Victoria, Homa Hills, Ndere Island, Kisumu City and Sondu Miriu Hydro Power Project. The main house is a three bedroomed mansion with a kitchenette for a self-catering option. All rooms are ensuite. The house has two balconies in the upper floor.
 Stay at the lakeshore chalets: located straight at Lake Victoria’s edge, these chalets gives the guests the freshest breeze from Lake Victoria. They come in five pairs of two-unit houses (conjoined to offer families with kids their privacy) and also 4 single unit lake houses.
POINT TO NOTE: Maboko Island Resort is the greenest resort destination in the Lake Victoria waters. Both in terms of the green flora (the four fig trees are always green all year round and provides the perfect shades from the hot Kisumu sun) and the fact that the chalets and the main house are all powered by the radiant Kisumu sun through the solar lighting systems.
THINGS TO DO
Fishing: Catch your own dinner! The resort offers a range of fishing excursions to suit individual tastes and style, both line fishing by the shores and out on the great lake, either alone or with experts. Marine safety and security is permanently on standby.
Kayaks and jetski are available on request for the high adrenaline and more adventurous guests.
Lake excursions are also a huge attraction, visit the various islands or just go round and round the lake with your boats, away from Maboko Island, stroll amongst tropical vegetation to the marine reserve viewpoint to experience the benign mix of flora and fauna. Walking in an abundance of exotic shrubs, giant land tortoises and flying foxes in a perpetual natural habitat
Tour of Local Attraction Sites: Kenya Wildlife Impala Sanctuary, Dunga Beach, The Equator at Maseno, Kit Mikayi, Kisumu Museum, River Yala Falls, Luanda Magere Grave Site, Ruma National Park, Abindu Caves, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga & Tom Mboya Mausoleums, Kogello Village etc. are some of the surrounding attractions around Lake Victoria.
Dinner by the Shore: Your stay will not be complete without a romantic dinner by the shore under the stars with serenity and personalized service. Enjoy the sound of the splashing waves and the beauty of Lake Victoria over Maboko in the evening and at night. Dinner on the balcony of your room can be arranged on request.

text:
Opening Up the Universe of Pro-Natal Policy
For years, countries have been focusing on the same handful policies, like baby bonuses, paid family leave and subsidized childcare to address falling fertility. Meanwhile, a range of policies that could work better are mostly ignored.

Financial subsidies alone aren’t enough
In the United States, the discussion of low birthrates is quite new, at least on the political scene. But some European countries have been dealing with this problem for fifty years or more.

Policies that offer financial incentives for people to have kids, from subsidized childcare to various tax credits, are being talked about in the United States. But countries like Germany, Sweden and Finland have had family policies like these for a generation, and still have fertility well below replacement. The fertility rate in 2023 was just 1.39 births per woman in Germany, 1.45 in Sweden and 1.26 in Finland.

Policies like baby bonuses and other financial incentives are a good thing for families, but they don’t work that well at raising fertility.

Why don’t these financial incentives raise birthrates that much? Because money isn’t the main driver for fertility. If it were, birthrates would be soaring right now, as the world has gotten much richer in the last few generations. Instead, birthrates are the lowest they have ever been.

Meanwhile there is a whole array of pronatal policy options that nobody is talking about! To raise birthrates, here are some other things governments should consider:

1. Pronatal Communication
Is it strange for a government to encourage people to have kids?
In fact, governments and political leaders already give plenty of messages around childbearing, and those messages are implicitly negative.

Stop environmental catastrophizing
The most anti-family message is the idea that Earth is overpopulated and faces environmental catastrophe. That objectively is not true. The population density of the United States is 98 people per square mile, which is more than double the global population density of 41 people per square mile. And yet, most of America (and likewise most of the world) is sparsely populated!
The carrying capacity of America and the world is many times higher than the number of people currently alive.

As for the environment, it is getting better, not worse. Air and water pollution is decreasing every year, tree cover is increasing worldwide, and the shift to sustainable energy is happening fast.

Yet much of today’s environmentalism is based on the deeply misanthropic idea that humanity is bad, a scourge on the planet. This is the core philosophy of antinatalism.

And it is widespread in schools!

Get antinatal messages out of schools
One of the first steps policy steps to solve the low fertility crisis is to stop teaching population control messages to kids. Kids in schools everywhere are taught that we face the threat of overpopulation, even though fertility rates have been below replacement for a long time.

An organization called Population Connection, founded by antinatal extremist Paul R. Ehrlich, has been active in schools for decades, scaring children about the perils of overpopulation even as the data show birthrates are plummeting. President John Seager recently bragged, “Our materials are integrated into the classroom. We have about 50,000 teachers who reach about 3 million students every year.”

I documented how Population Connection is propagandizing American and Canadian children in this expose’:
https://t.co/m4z4PjtL7R
Another organization called Negative Population Growth hands out scholarships to students who write essays and make posters about overpopulation. Here are two scholarship-winning posters.
If these posters were from the 1970s that would be one thing. But these posters were just made recently! Kids are still getting antinatal propaganda, even with birth rates at record lows in the United States and around the world.

Is there any organization in America telling kids the truth, that birthrates are too low, and we need more children? I don’t know of any!

Anti-natal messaging worked too well, and pronatal messaging will work too!
The idea that you can just encourage people to have more kids seems way too simple. Why would that work? Life is too complicated.

And yet all over the world, countries urged people to have fewer children over the last 50 years, and that was incredibly effective. I wrote about how population control messages caused large families to disappear in Korea, virtually overnight.
https://t.co/Tmbykmeq1N
If population control propaganda in East Asia teaches us anything, it is that messaging about families has a powerful impact on family size.

Meanwhile, celebrating large families can boost fertility, by raising the status of motherhood. I wrote about how this happened in Mongolia and elsewhere in the world.
https://t.co/g25opoWrsV
Parents crave status and validation for their efforts more than money. And leaders can give that, by celebrating parents at every opportunity and even giving awards and honors to mothers of many children.

Awareness is key
How can you convert people to pronatalism? How can you persuade people to believe in bigger families?

The first step is to tell the truth. When people learn that fertility is far below replacement, they get that this is a serious problem. Most people just don’t know yet.

In fact, the greatest fertility turnarounds in history were driven by awareness of the problem, followed by a cultural shift toward pronatalism. I wrote about these cases!
https://t.co/OSQSpfzNFk

2. Sex-Ed that teaches people about age-based fertility decline, and not merely how to avoid pregnancy
These days, it is far more common to end up childless when you wanted children, than to end up with more kids than you wanted. Yet almost all sex-ed is teaching young people how to avoid pregnancy.

What most people do not learn is how short the fertility window is, and how crucial it is to find a partner early enough to have children.

It would be easy and incredibly valuable to educate young people on how fertility falls with age. Then they can plan early enough to have children before it’s too late.

I discuss that in this post:
https://t.co/o99PahhNRU

3. To fix the housing crisis and help families: lower immigration levels and build the right kind of housing
There is a shortage of housing in the United States. But especially, there is a shortage of family friendly housing such as single-family homes.

The first step to fixing housing and thereby fertility is to bring immigration down to more sustainable levels. In countries like the US, extremely high immigration has produced a housing shortage. Housing increases slowly, and very high immigration can overwhelm the supply, causing soaring prices for everyone. I wrote about that problem here.
https://t.co/ztXy3PzGFc

A second policy step is to remove restrictions that prevent horizontal expansion of housing. A policy that leads to building more single-family homes will be pronatal. This includes:

· Removing “smart growth” restrictions designed to fight ‘urban sprawl.’ Many cities are ringed by urban growth boundaries to stop suburbs, even though there is space for new subdivisions.
· Releasing federal and state lands for development.

This thread looks at how important it is to open new land for building from a pronatalist perspective.
https://t.co/vbJNnzLUtV

Meanwhile, it is important not to try to solve a housing crisis the way East Asia has, by building giant towers of apartments. The lowest fertility rates in the world, 0.5 in parts of Seoul, and 0.4 in parts of Shanghai, are found where people live in apartment blocks in high-density urban cores.

Consider these three posts exploring how high-rise apartment towers tend to exhibit low fertility, even when they are cheap and abundant.
https://t.co/AAJsnI5ZyJ
https://t.co/RpvdrUr8Ks
https://t.co/yCqOGg7s9f
It is particularly important for long-term fertility to get housing type right, because housing stock once built persists for a very long time. In Korea and China, all that high-density urbanism will drag down fertility for generations to come. We should avoid following their lead.

Rules that favor building houses over apartments are almost certainly a good idea, fertility-wise. Fertility tends to fall sharply as the apartment fraction in a city increases.
Everyone knows we need more housing. Yet almost nobody talks about housing type, even though that matters hugely for fertility.

4. How to Fix Childcare
There is an easy way to increase the supply of childcare while reducing the cost. Quite simply, childcare across the country should be deregulated, in two ways:

· Increase the number of children allowed per staff member.
· Remove degree requirements on childcare workers.

Gorry et al. (2017) found that a one-infant increase per staff member is associated with costs that are lower by 9% to 20% while removing degree requirements is associated with costs that are lower by 25% to 46%. Childcare quality was not hurt by these changes.

5. Religious Freedom
The impact of religious belief and practice on fertility is undeniable. Faith groups confer a strong fertility advantage. Many studies show the strong relationship between religiosity and fertility, as I document in this thread.
https://t.co/PDgaxUQKRA
While governments cannot and should not push faith on anyone, they can protect religious freedom and foster a climate of tolerance that allows a variety of faith groups to thrive and coexist peacefully. School choice and a right to homeschool are examples of policies that support religious freedom.

Religious freedom should extend to small religious groups that are outside of the mainstream. As futurist Robin Hanson explained in a recent podcast, we need ‘cultural experimentation.’ High fertility groups like the Amish and the Haredim are bright spots in a bleak demographic landscape, and we benefit from cultural variety.

6. Incentivize Marriage
Birth rates are more than twice as high for married women as for unmarried women of the same age and this gap is increasing.

Marriage can be incentivized through a variety of policies, especially in the tax structure. Marriage penalties can be eliminated and the tax benefits to marriage can be increased.

7. Reduce Medically Unnecessary C-sections, which Limit Future Fertility
An underdiscussed cause of lower birthrates is the excessive use of C-sections, at rates far above what is medically necessary.

Demographer Lyman Stone has explained that that C-sections reduce future fertility in two ways:
· Studies find the ability to conceive is reduced after a C-section, due to scar tissue in the uterus.
· Doctors advise women to avoid becoming pregnant again after 2-3 C-sections, because of the risk of a uterine tear.

I explain the negative fertility impact of excessive C-sections, across countries and US states in a thread:
https://t.co/NZXPrO0k1N
Incentive structures should be changed. Often doctors perform unnecessary C-sections because they can make more money than with vaginal deliveries. This can cost a woman her future fertility. Medical boards should get involved also, to ensure that individual doctors are not performing C-sections above the medically appropriate rate.

There it is! A whole range of effective policies to raise fertility rates, that hardly anyone talks about!

Please share! And follow @MoreBirths for more.

text:
Excessive Immigration Hurts Birthrates
When migration overwhelms the housing supply, fertility plummets

Housing costs are a big barrier to having kids in the US and other countries. Where immigration exceeds the ability to add housing, young people are priced out.

The building industry can’t keep up
Immigration can bring a lot of benefits, but there are also costs, and housing shortages are often one of them. Housing limitations are a big reason why excessively high immigration rates are not feasible. The housing stock of a country increases gradually, but immigration can overwhelm housing suddenly. @ElonMusk explained the problem back in January:

Housing shortages related to very high immigration are already occurring in the United States. Even though US fertility has been below replacement for 50 years, there aren't enough houses for families that want them.

House Affordability is a Causal Factor for Birthrates
The relationship between housing affordability and fertility rates has been well established in numerous studies. This can easily be seen among US states. Where homes are more affordable in relation to incomes, fertility is higher.

When homes are too expensive, young people are often stuck living with their parents. As demographer Lyman Stone showed in a study across many countries for the Institute of Family Studies, when young couples live with their parents, they tend to have far fewer children.

For fertility, it is crucial for young people to start living independently early in adulthood, but this is very hard to do when there is a housing shortage.

The Case of Canada
Canada offers a cautionary tale of what happens when immigration overwhelms the housing supply. No country in the world has higher net-migration per capita than Canada.

Meanwhile, fertility in Canada has plummeted to just 1.25 births per woman in 2023, meaning Canada has by far the lowest fertility among Anglosphere countries and one of the lowest fertility rates in the world. Why is fertility in Canada suddenly so low?

The lack of sufficient housing is surely a big reason. Home prices have tripled just since 2000, and housing has become the top political issue in Canada, pushing a generation of young people to the right.

Making matters worse, much of the housing being built in Canada is small apartments in high-rise towers. These are generally anti-natal. Canada really needs more of the single-family homes most sought after by people wanting children. The supply of those is much harder to increase.

While falling fertility in Canada has multiple causes, the immigration-driven housing crisis is a big one. Canada is an extreme case, but this effect is seen in other countries too. In New Zealand, which has the second highest per-capita migration rates, fertility fell from 2.0 to 1.5 since 2015. In the UK, it fell from 1.77 to 1.43 over the same time period. In these cases too, immigration-led housing shortages seem to be a major part of the story.

What about East Asia
What about East Asian countries like Korea, China and Japan? They have very little immigration and yet have extremely low birthrates. Don't they undermine this argument?

First, low fertility has multiple drivers. A range of factors have an impact including cultural ones, and it is a mistake to distill birthrates down to just one cause. But second, within-country migration is massive in these countries, contributing to a similar housing dynamic locally.

Even though Korea, China and Japan are all depopulating and have low international immigration, they have extremely high rates of migration from rural areas to a few fashionable cities. The result is similar: young adults are priced out of housing and end up living with their parents, or else they live in tiny apartments. Fertility is exceptionally low in cities like Seoul, Shanghai and Tokyo, compared to the respective countries as a whole.

Everyone can’t live in the same place
When everyone tries to move to the same places, whether within countries or across borders, it is negative for birthrates by creating both crowding and local housing shortages. From a fertility perspective, geographic dispersion is much more pro-natal.

One of the great challenges for solving the global fertility crisis is figuring out how to have economic dynamism that is geographically spread out across many regions and countries. Networked communication can help. The economic benefits of migration will be short-lived if birthrates are so low.

Please share this and follow @MoreBirths for more on the low fertility crisis and its solutions.

text:
This is the most important chart to understand for America's future, both economically and politically.

The federal budget will go out of control even if we have no wars or recessions for the next 30 years. We felt the consequences of the huge deficit spending spike in 2020:

-The worst inflation wave in four decades, leaving typical households worse off today than they were five years ago.
-Interest rate hikes that have put a family home out of reach for young couples across the country, not just in coastal cities. That means fewer children, dimming the nation's future.
-Interest rates have also made payments to cover the national debt surge to the highest levels (relative to the economy) in generations. This will be an anchor around our feet.

We're set to have larger and larger deficits as federal spending grows on autopilot every year. That means more inflationary pressure, keeping the cost of living high and making it harder to bring interest rates down.

The problem isn't a lack of revenue, but the relentless growth of government.

Congress has refused to do real budgeting for too long. America can't afford for its leaders to sleepwalk their way to a national bankruptcy.

It's time to get serious...

text:
Understanding Kenya's key population ratios: 

The dependency ratio, the child dependency ratio, and the old-age dependency ratio tell us the proportion of unproductive versus productive populations in the country.  

The dependency ratio highlights the burden of children aged 0-14 years and the elderly of 65+ years placed on the working population of 15-64 years.  It tells us how many unproductive people there are for every 100 productive ones. 
In the chart below, it is represented by the size of the dot. Kenya has a total dependency ratio of 75.2%, meaning for every 100 working-age individuals, there are 75 dependents.

To understand what's going on in the counties, let's look at the chart below, which is divided into four quadrants. The dotted lines represent the national averages. The x-axis is the old-age dependency ratio (elderly age 65+ depending on those aged 15-64), and the y-axis is the child dependency ratio (children aged 0-14 depending on the working aged 15-64).

Bottom left: These are counties like Nairobi, Mombasa, Kiambu, Uasin Gishu, Nakuru, and Kajiado. Nairobi has the lowest child dependency ratio and also the lowest age dependency ratio. Ideally, it means, there are fewer children to working age population and a lower ratio of the elderly population. Since these are major cities and towns, we obviously expect very few elderly people since Kenyans retire in rural areas. These counties also tend to have the lowest fertility rates, which explains the lower number of children. This is the best spot to be. 

Bottom right: These counties have higher old-age dependency ratios but lower than average child dependency ratios. Most of them are Mt. Kenya counties, which have the lowest fertility rates in the country. As we've also seen before, they also have the highest life expectancies. Murang'a has the highest age dependency ratio of 14.3%, meaning there are around 14 elderly persons to be supported by 100 working-age people. For comparison, Japan has an old age dependency ratio of 51%. 

Top right: Other than Siaya, Kitui, and Vihiga, the rest in this category are average. These are mostly the Western, Rift, and Nyanza counties.  They hover between an age dependency ratio of 6% and 9% and a child dependency ratio of 70% and 90%.  In these counties, a hundred working-age people support between 70 to 90 children and 6 to 9 old people. Siaya, Kitui, and Vihiga have between 11 and 14 elderly people to support, in addition to around 70 to 80 children.

Top left: These counties have a lower number of the elderly but have a disproportionately high number of children. Counties in this quadrant tend to have high fertility rates. The highest is Mandera, where 100 working-age people support around 128 children. Others are Wajir, West Pokot, Narok, Samburu, Tana River, Migori, Isiolo, Marsabit, Turkana, and Garissa.  

To sum up, lower dependency ratios can be found around major cities and Central Kenya. In these counties, the working-age population can comfortably support the non-working-age population. The old-age dependency in Central does not appear large enough to be burdensome. Counties with the highest burden are mostly in the ASALs. Nationally, our dependency ratio is considered high but is expected to ease as children grow up and join the workforce.

text:
Difficult Questions for Solving the Fertility Crisis
A discussion with arguably the greatest family thinker of our time

I was fortunate to have a great hour-long sit-down with @BradWilcoxIFS in the beautiful courtyard of the Rayburn House Office Building in DC yesterday, following a speech he gave. University of Virginia Professor Brad Wilcox is (among many other things) a founder of the Institute for Family Studies which has produced some of the most important work on issues that impact family formation.

Although Wilcox’s first focus is on marriage, our conversation covered a whole range of issues around birthrates.

I think the most interesting part of our discussion was where we hit snags. As we talked, we ran into some difficult problems where we do not yet have great answers. If we can figure these out, we can go a long way toward solving the fertility crisis.

(1) How can we address the density problem and incentivize people to spread out more?

Urbanization is a big root of the birthrate crisis. Cities are magnets for both economic and social reasons, but cities end up having incredibly low birthrates.

In Asia the problem is especially acute. Cities like Shanghai, Beijing, and Seoul all have fertility rates far below 1 birth per woman, as density, the entertainments of city life and the predominance of large apartment towers all conspire to hurt family formation. Yet even as rural areas empty out, cities become ever more crowded. Young people are drawn to urban cores, and then have very few children there.

In many countries struggling with too-low birthrates, including Japan, Korea, Spain and the United States, there are vast areas that sit neglected, where housing is cheap and space for families is abundant.

How can we encourage people, governments, and companies to spread out, and form new towns and especially to revitalize towns and smaller cities that are already there?

This is not a new problem but a very old one. For example, London has been a population sink for rural England throughout history. In theory the pressures to urbanize should be less because of communication networks and the Internet, but densification continues in most countries.

Wilcox suggested work-from-home and self-driving cars (enabling longer commutes) as two things that will help. True! But overall, we have no good answers to this so far.

(2) How can we introduce pro-family content into schools?

In his speech that preceded our conversation, entitled The Closing of the American Heart about the decline of marriage in America, Wilcox emphasized the need to teach young people both about the value of marriage and fertility time constraints.

We agree that education of young people is in a way the most obvious starting point for turning around the birthrate crisis. But as University of Maryland economist Melissa Kearney has noted, there is a taboo about talking about the value of marriage, even as its benefits for families are extraordinary.

How we persuade educators to teach pro-marriage and pro-natal content in high schools in colleges given the present political and social climate?

A difficult problem indeed!

(3) How can we get the left of the political spectrum to recognize and focus on the birthrate crisis?

Where are the left-wing pronatalists, I ask. Wilcox mentions Matthew Yglesias and I do admit that the author of One Billion Americans surely qualifies. But there don't seem to be a lot of others on the left. When I attended the Natalism Conference in Austin, Texas in December, I found myself wishing the political slant of most pronatalists wasn’t so obvious!

If pronatalism becomes coded as right-wing (and that is happening already) then left will be decidedly uninterested. That is a big problem when a majority of young women vote left.

We are already seeing a big political divide on birthrates, a divide that didn’t exist a generation ago.

(4) Who will lead the kinds of large scale pronatal movements we need and what organizations will appear to advocate pronatalism?

Given the civilizational impacts of collapsing fertility, it is surely the most under-emphasized problem in the world today. There are thousands of organizations and hundreds of billions of dollars dedicated to environmental issues but what organizations and prominent leaders are dedicated to solving the truly existential low fertility crisis?

The Institute for Family Studies just launched a Pronatalism Initiative led by brilliant demographer Lyman Stone, but Wilcox tells me that is still just a one-man policy shop. I was surprised to learn IFS overall consists of just a few full-timers -- surely there should be hundreds at least! Can Professor Wilcox lead something much, much bigger? He tells me his plate is full, but we can only hope!

Where are the prominent pronatal leaders in the English-speaking world? If a young person is interested in helping to solve the low birthrate crisis, where can they even go right now? There should be several big pronatalist organizations, representing every perspective and political persuasion, to help turn things around.

So, consider these to be some of the great problems to solve at the center of the birthrate crisis. This is not an exhaustive list, but it is already a lot to work on. Make progress on any of these and you will make the world of the future a much, much better place!

text:
What You Build Becomes Your Housing Stock
In America and around the world, an increasing share of the housing stock is antifamily (small apartments), which will drive down birthrates for generations
(Please share!)

This week, I visited new apartment buildings in Bethesda and Rockville in Maryland, one after the other, and discovered a shocking fact:
Essentially 100% of the new apartments being built in urban areas are antifamily. In each of the recently built residential towers I visited, I found that not a single unit has 3 bedrooms. Thousands of new housing units, and none that are family friendly. I posted about that.

@mattyglesias responded to me with a logical fallacy at the heart of the pro-densification argument:
“DC is full of single-family rowhouses occupied by groups of childless roommates.
The easiest way to increase the supply of family sized housing is to build some more tall 1br/2br apartment towers so the childless people can live and open up family-sized dwellings.”
– Matt Yglesias

Nobody said anything about banning apartments, just keeping zoning rules already in place. (Although now that Yglesias has brought it up, I wonder if he may be onto something!)

But the idea that you increase the supply of family friendly homes by some sleight of hand that doesn’t involve literally adding more of them is nonsense.

Building some more tall 1br and 2br apartment towers will increase the supply of family sized housing by (and bear with me because this part involves some math) -- 0 units!

No, Matthew Yglesias, the easiest (and only) way to increase the supply of family sized housing is to build… family sized housing.

Hardly anyone moves from a single-family home or townhome into an apartment
I get what Yglesias is meaning to say. Somehow, if you build thousands of units of tiny apartments then the people living in gentrified, architecturally significant DC rowhouses (and single-family homes) will vacate their more spacious abodes and crowd into these towers, freeing up housing for young people trying to start families.

Now since I am a DC native and Yglesias is not (true!), I will speak ex cathedra: That is not happening.

My current single-family neighborhood in the DC suburbs has tons of elderly people who still are not leaving, even into their eighties and beyond. I know several elderly widows in my neighborhood still holding onto spacious four- and five-bedroom single family homes all by themselves.

If anyone can come up with incentives to get empty-nesters to vacate their large suburban homes and move into newly built 1-bedroom apartments in high-rises so that young families can move in, that would be great. (Seriously, there is a terrible mismatch. Baby boomers are far more likely to own single family homes than their children who need them.)

But for now, people voluntarily downsizing after enjoying big houses is not much of thing. And so, the ones targeted for all this new apartment housing that has no space for children are Millennials and Gen Z. That is no doubt a big factor in the low fertility crisis we now see.

If you build anti-natal housing, that becomes your housing stock basically forever
In the last few years, we have been treated to the shocking news of some incredibly low fertility numbers. The latest figures are that fertility is only around 0.5 or 0.6 births per woman in cities like Seoul, Shanghai, and Beijing. Places like Vancouver, Tokyo and Manhattan are falling below 1.0 and Washington D.C. proper is not doing much better.

Housing matters greatly for fertility and what gets built will last for generations. East Asian cities have been rapidly erecting huge apartment blocks for a decades, and now almost all their housing stock consists of apartments in towers.

China is a prime example. China ended their one child policy in 2016, only to find that birthrates keep falling. Hardly anyone in China is having two or three kids, even though that is allowed now. Obviously big shifts in culture and work explain a lot of that. But if a Chinese couple wanted a house with a yard to accommodate a large family, where would they go?

Now in many American cities there is a strong push to build more apartments. As Bobby Fijan, a large-scale apartment developer and influential urbanist explains, virtually none of the apartment stock that is being built today is suitable for families. New three-bedroom apartments are unheard of. But even two bedrooms are just a fraction of units in most new buildings, with most of new apartments being studios and one-bedroom apartments!
This way of building will prove catastrophic because future generations will be stuck with a housing stock where a large portion is unsuitable for families, much like how the young people in so many East Asian cities are effectively without family-friendly housing options.

Can this be remedied just by adding three-bedroom apartments to the mix? That would help some, and a great way to fix what has been built is to do conversions that combine smaller apartments to make larger, more family friendly ones.

But we should move to a world where all housing that is built is family-friendly, not just some designated portion.

The Baby Boom was partly due to a boom in single family homebuilding

What caused the 1946-1964 Baby Boom? As I have often written, the first cause was a surge in young marriage. But an interconnected cause was a huge boom in the building of pro-family housing (with an assist from good financing).

Records show there was a surge in the issuance of building permits after the war and suburbs sprung up after WWII ringing every major US city. This new housing stock in the form of single-family homes was just the thing to support young couples having large families.

Better still, generation after generation of Americans benefitted from this new pro-family suburban housing stock (including, I would guess, most of the libertarian economists now advocating for urban high rises). American fertility has remained consistently higher than in Europe in no small part because of this housing advantage.

If you build high-rises, that crowds out other building
The claim that building apartment towers doesn’t affect those who need family housing is just untrue. All building has opportunity costs and the ability of the United States and other countries to build housing is not without limit. The availability tradespeople, materials and financing are finite. Most developed countries are building too few housing units, and a primary constraint is the raw capacity of the building sector, which has not had the efficiency gains seen in other areas of manufacturing.

Therefore, when the building sector is focused on building studios and one-bedrooms in towers, it has much less ability to build single family homes.

(As an aside: Maybe prefabricated houses will help fill the demand for single family homes with a yard. Can those scale up? Modern prefab houses are far nicer than those of yesteryear, the much-derided trailers.)

Not NIMBY or YIMBY, but GIMBY
The apartment share of housing is strongly correlated with low fertility in cities around the world. I plotted the fertility rate against the fraction of the population in cities and countries living in apartments and the result is remarkable: The type of housing stock matters dramatically for fertility rates. This means that as the apartment share of housing rises, you will move rightward on that curve toward lower fertility.

It turns out that the NIMBY folks (Not In My Backyard) and the YIMBY folks (Yes, In My Backyard – meaning urban infill with apartment blocks) are both wrong. The YIMBY folks are right that we need to build more, but they want to build a type of housing that is totally unsuitable for families in a time of collapsing birthrates.

J. Sanilac here on X has coined a term we all need to adopt: GIMBY: Grass In My Backyard. That means being pro-homebuilding and pro-fixing the housing shortage, but with the expectation that homes should be suitable for families and have a yard of some kind. The yard doesn’t have to be big, and it doesn’t even have to be grass -- sand and cacti are ok if you are out West! But there should be a patch of ground for kids to play on that is their own.

Libertarian types and urbanists who think it is oppression not to be able to build infinity high-rises should spend time contemplating the birthrate collapse happening in East Asia. Korea, Japan and China have built apartment towers seemingly without limit, and now they all face a demographic winter. Building GIMBY-style will help us avoid that outcome. And there is still a lot of work to do to open up space for building horizontally, both close to cores and further out.

Please follow @MoreBirths for more on how we can fix the low birthrate crisis.

text:
The core claim of courtyard urbanism is that courtyard block development is one of the most effective ways to add family housing in high-cost cities because it makes large, livable apartments easier to design, finance, and deliver.

The evidence is both formal and historical. For thousands of years, cities have used shallow buildings, shared party walls, and interior courtyards to create dense housing with light, air, privacy, and usable outdoor space. In a contemporary courtyard block, these same principles make it possible to produce family-sized apartments with abundant daylight, cross-ventilation, generous floor plans, and direct access to patios, balconies, terraces, play areas, gardens, and shared yards, WITHOUT requiring every family to buy and maintain a detached house on scarce, expensive urban land.

Courtyard housing has appeared repeatedly during periods of urban expansion, from ancient Rome to the great apartment districts of late-19th- and early-20th-century Europe. The last major flourishing of this form came when Western European cities were facing rapid urban growth and rising demand for better housing in the city.

text:
The problem with single-family housing in very high-cost parts of cities is that we're using very expensive land to house too few households.

In high-demand parts of the city, even a modest single-family home on a standard lot can sell for well over $1M (like this one that just went up around us). That means one household is carrying the full cost of very costly urban land. 

Apartments are so useful because they spread that land cost across many households, which is often the only way middle-income families can realistically afford to live in these locations.

Take a ~5,000 sq ft site worth about $1.4M.
Today , that site might hold two single-family homes selling for $1M+ each. If each home has 4 bedrooms, that is about 8 bedrooms total.

But if the same site were built as a 5–6 story courtyard-style apartment building, it could potentially support 10–16 homes (mix of larger and smaller apartments). 

Consider the relative land cost per bedroom:

Single-family scenario
Two homes on a ~5,000 sq ft site
Land value: ~$1.4M
About 8 bedrooms total
….roughly $175,000 in land cost per bedroom

Mid-rise apartment scenario
Same ~$1.4M land cost spread across 12 units
Assume mostly 3-bedroom units
About 36 bedrooms total
….roughly $39,000 in land cost per bedroom

That is about a 4–5x difference in land cost per bedroom before even getting into building efficiency, shared infrastructure, or reduced parking.

AND with the right building form (shallow floor plates, dual-aspect layouts, accessible shared courtyards, real foyers, family-sized kitchens, and usable green space) apartments can be nice family homes.

text:
hi I am agnostic about the relationship between urbanization and fertility.

My understanding is that normal urban density levels are NOT negatively correlated with fertility when you control for housing size (ie, women living in 4BDs in the city are having as many kids as women living in 4BDs in the suburbs).

And I suspect that all cities need to do to increase the number of families with young kids  is to add enough family-sized housing to meet demand and bring down cost of a 3BD+.

That said, I do think there is a plausible secondary effect. If the centers of economic and cultural life (cities) become more visibly and functionally family-friendly, then having children may begin to feel more compatible & aspirational within a wider range of adult lifestyles, leading to more births. 

Ie, currently society tells adults that becoming a parent means moving away from centers of society, and buying a house with a  yard in a drive-everywhere suburb. For many 20 somethings, that sounds baaad. It did for me -- I watched my mom spend her 30s and 40s driving me and my three sisters around suburban W Michigan, and I wanted nothing to do with that. 

Obviously, suburban parenting appeals to many adults and that's wonderful.  (and there is a wide variety of suburbs, some requiring less car time than others) The problem is not the suburbs. Problem is that, for many adults who prefer cities, the urban alternative is artificially constrained because regulations and design culture restricts development of  3BD+ in small buildings with yard access.

Hence, my argument that cities should legalize and facilitate more family-friendly development in cities to accommodate the substantial share of adult population who prefers to raise kids in the city, if they can find suitable housing.

More broadly, I am interested in restoring the "complete life cycle, multigenerational" character of cities. Great civilizations have historically unfolded in cities where people lived over many generations, forming deep ties with local communities and institutions.  That multi-generational character has been broken in 20th century America, as a combination of bad urban development and car culture has pushed middle class families into suburbs.

It would be great for cities, for families, and for the country generally if more families had the option of staying in cities.

In other words, I am not trying to solve the fertility problem. I'm trying to solve a deeper civilizational problem, which is that our economic, cultural, and political centers of society do not accommodate residents across the life cycle.

quote.text:
“Cities shouldn’t just be great for the ambitious and adventurous at 25. They should be places where those same people can build a life at 35, too.”

This is so on point. Many Americans rightly think cities aren’t for families…but that’s because we stopped BUILDING them for families.

And while I do appreciate much of the YIMBY message (net good), I also think we need to be critical about what KIND of housing we are building. Not all housing is good housing. 

A city of only multi-family apartment buildings (as they’re built today) isn’t a city. It’s a collection of human storage units. 

That’s not to say big apartments are bad. But that ONLY big apartments are bad (which is virtually all new housing construction outside of suburban homes). 

Cities need design, beauty and humanity etched into every nook and cranny we can. And part of that beauty and humanity is incorporating children and families. 

Anecdotal, but something I’ve noticed holds generally true: If you make a place cool for kids and their parents (where both enjoy being there) it suddenly becomes a place for everyone—even the teens, singles and empty-nesters. I think there is something about having children around that can be life-giving and wholesome and bring out the best in people. 

To conclude: 

1) Hardware dictates what kind of software can run, and we’ve built hardware that’s incompatible for families in our cities.  

2) The built world is the human habitat. We shouldn’t treat it so flippantly as to simply say “anything that adds housing is good”. We actually do need GOOD housing. 

That doesn’t make it easy, and we shouldn’t be puritanical about it. There are real obstacles and limitations, and progress isn’t linear. But it SHOULD be the vision.
