text:
Something is breaking in America’s cities, and you can see it in empty classrooms.

New York City lost 22,000 students in one year. Chicago is down nearly 22 percent since 2011. Houston lost 8,300 students this year alone. Denver, Seattle, San Francisco, all bleeding families. Parents are not staging protests. They are just quietly leaving.

This is what abandonment looks like in real life. Working parents pulling their kids out because the schools feel unsafe, chaotic, or useless. Kids falling behind in reading and math. Districts admitting enrollment is collapsing while insisting everything is fine.

Nearly half of New York’s public school students can’t read or do math at grade level. Let that sink in. That is not a political talking point. That is a human disaster.

So families do what families always do. They protect their children. They choose charters. They choose homeschooling. They choose online schools. They scrape together money for private schools. Not because they hate public education, but because they love their kids more than they trust the system.

And what do cities do in response? They hire marketing firms to “recruit” students like customers. More kids means more funding. Fewer kids means budget cuts. So now school districts are competing for bodies instead of fixing what is broken.

This is the quiet collapse no one wants to name. Not war, not riots. Just parents walking away from a system that stopped working for their children.

You don’t lose 117,000 students in New York since 2019 because of birth rates alone. You lose them because trust is gone.

When families flee your schools, it means something deeper than policy failed.

I see lots of folks who are all in a lather about the possibility that President Trump might invoke the Insurrection Act, painting it as an unheard-of and completely improper use of Presidential power and a misuse of Federal troops on US soil …

… well, except for the following times Federal troops were called out in the past.

Best to all,

w.
===

 Chronological list (1794–1992, 33 instances)

1794‑09‑25 – George Washington – Whiskey Rebellion in western Pennsylvania; Washington called forth militia to suppress armed resistance to the federal whiskey excise tax.

1799‑03‑12 – John Adams – Fries’s Rebellion in eastern Pennsylvania; federal troops and militia used to put down tax‑resistance uprising over a federal property tax.

1808‑04‑19 – Thomas Jefferson – Pervasive violations of the Embargo Act of 1807 around Lake Champlain, Vermont; invoked to try to stop widespread smuggling tied to cross‑border trade with Canada.

1831‑02‑10 – Andrew Jackson – Border dispute with Mexico in what is now the Arkansas‑Texas border area; proclamation issued, but dispute resolved before troops used.

1831‑08‑24 – Andrew Jackson – Nat Turner’s slave rebellion in Southampton County, Virginia; federal artillery and Marines deployed in support of state forces without formal compliance with Insurrection Act procedures, later endorsed by Jackson.

1834‑01‑28 – Andrew Jackson – Violent labor dispute among Irish canal workers on the Chesapeake & Ohio Canal in Maryland; Jackson ordered federal troops to aid in law enforcement after a state request, but did not issue the required Insurrection Act proclamation.

1861‑04‑15 – Abraham Lincoln – Secession of multiple Southern states at the outbreak of the Civil War; Lincoln called forth militia and invoked the statutory framework that included the Insurrection Act to suppress rebellion and enforce federal law.

1871‑10‑17 – Ulysses S. Grant – Ku Klux Klan–related terrorism in South Carolina during Reconstruction; after warning proclamations, Grant invoked expanded 1871 Insurrection Act powers, deployed troops, and suspended habeas corpus in designated counties.

1873‑05‑22 – Ulysses S. Grant – Post‑election violence and the Colfax Massacre in Louisiana following the contested 1872 gubernatorial election; proclamation issued under the Insurrection Act amid widespread rural violence, with no major new troop deployments beyond existing Reconstruction forces.

1874‑05‑15 – Ulysses S. Grant – Brooks‑Baxter War in Arkansas over the disputed 1872 gubernatorial election; Grant invoked the Act to order Brooks’s supporters to disperse after the legislature recognized Baxter, relying on existing federal troops as a buffer.

1874‑09‑15 – Ulysses S. Grant – White supremacist coup in New Orleans, Louisiana (part of the same long‑running election dispute); Grant invoked the Act and sent federal troops who expelled insurgents from the city and restored the recognized government.

1874‑12‑21 – Ulysses S. Grant – Vicksburg Massacre in Warren County, Mississippi; after a Black sheriff was deposed and groups of Black residents were killed by white mobs, Grant invoked the Act and deployed troops to prevent further violence and restore the elected sheriff.

1876‑10‑17 – Ulysses S. Grant – Armed “rifle club” paramilitaries in South Carolina threatening the 1876 state elections; Grant issued an Insurrection Act proclamation and reinforced federal troops already in state to help secure the election period.

1877‑07‑18 (and 07‑21, 07‑23) – Rutherford B. Hayes – Great Railroad Strike of 1877; at multiple governors’ requests, Hayes invoked the Act and sent federal troops to Martinsburg, West Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania, to help reopen rail traffic and suppress associated violence.

1878‑10‑07 – Rutherford B. Hayes – Lincoln County War in New Mexico Territory; at the territorial governor’s request, Hayes invoked the Act so troops already in the territory could intervene in a violent factional conflict.

1882‑05‑03 – Chester A. Arthur – Arizona Territory raids and violent lawlessness, including cattle theft gangs and Chiricahua Apache raids; Arthur issued an Insurrection Act proclamation authorizing federal troops in the territory to help suppress both.

1885‑11‑07 – Grover Cleveland – Anti‑Chinese violence in Washington Territory, especially the Tacoma Riot of 1885 and related events in Seattle; Cleveland invoked the Act at the territorial governor’s request and deployed troops to Seattle to protect remaining Chinese residents.

1886‑02‑09 – Grover Cleveland – Continued anti‑Chinese violence in Seattle, Washington Territory; Cleveland again used the Insurrection Act framework to send troops to protect Chinese residents from expulsion by armed white mobs.

1894‑07‑08 (and 07‑09) – Grover Cleveland – Pullman Strike, initially in Chicago and then spreading to multiple states; Cleveland invoked the Act after sending troops on July 3, and then extended it to numerous states and territories where the railway strike disrupted interstate commerce and mail.

1914‑04‑28 – Woodrow Wilson – Colorado Coalfield War, including the Ludlow Massacre; after the governor requested federal aid, Wilson invoked the Act and deployed federal troops to replace Colorado National Guard forces and restore order.

1921‑08‑30 – Warren G. Harding – Battle of Blair Mountain in West Virginia; Harding invoked the Act at the governor’s request and sent federal troops and an Army air unit to end the large‑scale armed miners’ uprising.

1932‑07‑28 – Herbert Hoover (but not legally) – Bonus Army incident in Washington, D.C.; General Douglas MacArthur, contrary to Hoover’s limited instructions, used troops as if the Insurrection Act or martial law had been invoked to expel World War I veterans and their families, even though no proper invocation occurred.

1943‑06‑21 – Franklin D. Roosevelt – 1943 Detroit race riot; Roosevelt invoked the Insurrection Act and sent federal troops to Detroit to halt deadly racial violence and restore order.

1957‑09‑23 – Dwight D. Eisenhower – Little Rock Crisis, Arkansas; Eisenhower invoked the Act, federalized the Arkansas National Guard (ordering it to stand down), and deployed the 101st Airborne Division to enforce desegregation at Central High School.

1962‑09‑30 – John F. Kennedy – Ole Miss riot in Oxford, Mississippi; Kennedy invoked the Act to deploy federal troops to protect James Meredith’s enrollment at the University of Mississippi and to crush a violent segregationist mob attack on federal officers and observers.

1963‑06‑11 – John F. Kennedy – “Stand in the Schoolhouse Door” at the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa; Kennedy invoked the Act, federalized the Alabama National Guard, and used it to compel Governor George Wallace to allow two Black students to enroll.

1963‑09‑10 – John F. Kennedy – Continued resistance to school desegregation across Alabama; Kennedy again invoked the Act, federalized the Alabama Guard, and ordered it to cease blocking Black students’ attendance at public schools statewide.

1965‑03‑20 – Lyndon B. Johnson – Selma‑to‑Montgomery voting‑rights march in Alabama; Johnson invoked the Act and federalized the Alabama National Guard to protect marchers after prior attacks by state and local forces and mobs.

1967‑07‑24 – Lyndon B. Johnson – 1967 Detroit riot; after days of deadly urban unrest and an overwhelmed state response, Johnson invoked the Act at the governor’s request and sent federal troops to assist the National Guard and police.

1968‑04‑05 (and 04‑07) – Lyndon B. Johnson – Post‑assassination riots following the murder of Martin Luther King Jr.; Johnson invoked the Act to deploy troops in Washington, D.C. (April 5) and then again to send troops to Chicago and Baltimore (April 7) to quell widespread urban rioting.

1987‑11‑24 – Ronald Reagan – Atlanta federal prison (U.S. Penitentiary) detainee uprising involving Cuban detainees; Reagan invoked the Insurrection Act but relied on federal law enforcement, with advice from a small Army special forces element, rather than large troop deployment.

1989‑09‑20 – George H. W. Bush – Post–Hurricane Hugo lawlessness and looting in the U.S. Virgin Islands; Bush invoked the Act (nominally at the territorial governor’s request, though that request was later disputed) and deployed federal troops to help restore order.

1992‑05‑01 – George H. W. Bush – Los Angeles riots after acquittals in the Rodney King beating case; at the California governor’s request, Bush invoked the Act and sent federal troops and federalized National Guard forces to support riot control, though much of the violence had already been reduced by the time they arrived.

text:
Almost every urban school district is facing a large, structural budget deficit due to declining enrollment and the end of COVID stimulus funds that requires very tough political decisions like Seattle made this week, else bankruptcy and/or state takeover looms.

Some districts will be able to address their deficits through job cuts in the near term, but almost all will eventually need to close schools, perhaps the most politically fraught action possible. School boards that refuse to do so won't be financially viable.

The enrollment decline in urban districts is almost universal and driven by a number of factors including bad demographics, rising housing prices that force low income families to the suburbs, growing preference for charters and home school, and chronic absenteeism.

Even growing metropolitan areas see their urban district shrinking. Houston ISD is -13% from 2019; Austin ISD is -9%. The school choice movement in red states will exacerbate this trend.

This trend has been brewing for years, but federal stimulus funding since 2020 has masked over the problem. With these funds ending this year, districts are waking up to 4 years of rising costs and falling enrollment with no backstop.

Districts all knew this fiscal cliff was coming, yet almost none prepared for it. The difficulty of government to address a crisis in advance is universal. School boards must make some very unpopular decisions. The question is whether they will.

text:
Seattle, one of the wealthiest, best educated cities in the WORLD cannot get its public schools out of a death spiral. 

The frustrating thing here is that SPS is acting as if closing schools is the “hard but good” thing to do, whereas it’s actually the easy but very bad option. 

What’s hard and needed is rebuilding enrollment (and thus revenue) and building trust with the state to get needed additional funding. 

Closing schools is going to alienate parents who are going to leave for private schools snd suburbs. The families that are most mobile are also the lowest cost to serve. 

This is an exact repeat of the closure of the HCC/gifted program. An extremely high margin program that brought in far more revenue than it cost, creating resources to serve disadvantaged kids. Destroyed forever due to ideology and laziness.  

The school district is currently in virtual default. It is borrowing money from its own capital funds, a loan that can never get repaid without enrollment growth. Closing schools will simply accelerate the inevitable descent into full receivership.

text:
Now the recriminations begin
Tina Faulk The Spectator Australia 19 October 2023 

Despite the promised week of silent mourning for the defeat of the Voice to Parliament, the recriminations and blame-to-be-laid are in full throttle – or should that be voice? The Leader of the Opposition is first in line to be bucketed by the Yes campaign, with complaints that Dutton refused to give bi-partisan support etc. These noises continue now that he has ‘gone back on proposing another referendum’.
This is the howl of insanity. If every state, along with the Northern Territory, voted with a resounding ‘No’ (including South Australia, the hoped-for swing state to which the Prime Minister gave such careful attention, sending back the second largest negative vote) why would Peter Dutton promise more of the same in years to come?
As someone guilty of handing out ‘No’ flyers in Sydney’s multicultural, multi-lingual Ryde, I saw firsthand how the campaign proceeded, and how – to the shame of Australia’s elites – it divided us along class and economic lines. As was expected, affluent and well-educated Teal seats returned ‘Yes’ votes, while – in stark contrast – Western Sydney voted ‘No’.
Perhaps that should have been ‘mayoh’ Mandarin Chinese for ‘no’ because that was what was being murmured as Asian families lined up on Saturday carrying babies and parking strollers as middle-class white women pressed ‘Yes’ voting cards into over-full hands.
While ‘Yes’ corflutes were everywhere to be seen, not just at voting places, I didn’t see a single ‘No’ corflute anywhere except at the voting place. Shirts and buttons imploring ‘Yes’ votes were in abundance, but I didn’t see a single shirt or ‘No’ button outside the polling places. Perhaps this was because ‘No’ campaigners, like ‘No’ voters, felt the need to be discreet, were elderly, or coy about their voting preferences. One white-haired ‘No’ campaigner gamely handed out flyers from his mobility scooter while his dog seated beside him.
In Balmain, in the Prime Minister’s seat of Grayndler, just down Victoria Road from Top Ryde, the story was the same… Not a single ‘No’ corflute could be found outside Rozelle Public School during the usual lively Rozelle Markets. There were, however, more well-dressed and well-spoken white people, many with dogs, wearing ‘Yes’ tops and buttons.
You couldn’t help but see how this untimely and unwarranted referendum has brought the cracks and fissures of civil society into the public view.
This buried the notion of ‘we are one but we are many’ and ‘you are, I am, we are Australian’. This referendum demonstrated that the gaps have grown wider, not just in remote and rural committees of both black and white Australians, but between people in our east coast cities.
In the week before the voting started, I sat at an informal lunch table with colleagues, one of whom suddenly commented, ‘It’s migrants, the multiculturals, they won’t vote ‘Yes’.’
All eyes in the group turned towards me – their owners tending to have family names that started with ‘Mac’ or ‘O’, but the speaker was correct. Migrants who have to work harder than most Anglo-Celtic Australia would ever envisage cannot, and should not, be expected to vote for communities however deserving, of which they have little knowledge or understanding. Family comes first, and it always will.
In the hard-scrapple outer western suburbs, as the price of food rises alarmingly and parents have to decide whether the purchase of school shoes can be delayed another term, no one has time or inclination to think about much beyond the next week or the next payday.
Amid all the recriminations, wailing, and gnashing of teeth, two things came together for me from Saturday 14 – the day some commentators are now calling ‘Black Saturday’.
The first was a ‘Yes’-wearing voter who swanned past, deep in conversation with her friend, as she asserted, ‘I just don’t think they should have lit up the Opera House sails in blue and white.’ The second was the elderly Asian man, carrying his grandchild, who, after a quick surreptitious glance around, gave me a quick thumbs up as he walked from the polling place.
Australians need to heal from this division. Let’s hope it doesn’t take too long.

text:
Why IS a 3 bedroom/1 bath (a type of home nobody wants anymore) the most common housing type in SF?

As with many answers about housing in SF, it involves an earthquake, a building boom, and subsequent poor regulations that froze the city in time, making it more expensive and kicking families to the suburbs.

Nearly half of SF's housing was built before 1940. There are two types of old homes here, and both ended up as 3/1s.

1) Victorians: The 1906 earthquake destroyed 80% of the city. Large Victorian homes that survived outside the fire line (Western Addition, Hayes Valley, Mission, Castro, Haight) got rapidly subdivided into flats to house 200,000+ displaced residents. A 5-bed, 2-bath home became two or three units, each inheriting one bathroom. I've lived in 2 different homes like this.

2) Post-quake builds. Most of the rest of the city was rebuilt fast and cheap with identical 2-bed, 1-bath homes with a garage on a 25' x 120' lot. Many families later converted the dining room to a third bedroom. You see 10s of thousands of these in the Sunset, Richmond, and Excelsior, built from the 1920s-1940s when the city was growing 20-25% per decade (picture 1 below). The biggest homebuilder in the US during that time was Doelger Homes, who was building 2 houses per day for years in SF.

You can still see the split by neighborhood. Victorian subdivided flats dominate the Western Addition, Haight, Noe Valley, and the Mission. Doelger-era 3/1s fill the Sunset, Richmond, and Excelsior.

Ok that makes sense but why are they STILL 3/1s 100 years later? Because preferences changed and the housing didn't, because the city doesn't really let you change housing.

Until the 50's/60's, one bathroom for a family of six was normal... people bathed once or twice a week. Many homes didn't have showers. Kids shared rooms. The Brady Bunch had six kids sharing two bedrooms and one bathroom (the source of many fights!), and that was considered a normal middle-class home. 

Nobody builds like that anymore. In 2024, >95% of homes built in the US had 2 or more bathrooms. The 3/1 is basically extinct in new homes, but SF is full of them.

People want more space! In 1950, the average home had 300 square feet per person. In 2025, it's about 900 (image 2)!

Everywhere else, people added bathrooms and houses were built differently. In Pittsburgh, I addeed 2 bathrooms to a 40's era 3/1 I owned and massively increased its value. 

In SF, the housing has barely changed. A few reasons:

1. Rent control. ~1/2 of the units in SF are rent-controlled with annual increases capped (recently at 1.4%). No landlord is spending $50-80k on a bathroom addition they can't recoup.

2. Permitting. Adding a bathroom takes 6-12 months just for approval. I added one to a rental a few years ago. It took 16 months, costing me over $100k in opportunity cost alone. Then opening your walls invites inspectors to flag other issues (often predating your ownership) that snowball costs.

3. We barely build new housing. SF completed only about 1,600 net new units in 2024, well below the pace needed to meet demand. So the old 3/1 stock barely gets diluted by new construction that meets modern standards.

No incentive (rent control) + limited ability (byzantine permitting) + almost no new supply = a city frozen in its post-earthquake floor plans.

SF ranks last among the 50 largest US cities in percentage of households with children. There are many reasons for this, but the housing stock is a big reason. Three bedrooms sounds fine until you realize there's one bathroom and no practical way to add another.

We've been house hunting for a while, and the demand for family-ready homes is insane. Hundreds of people at open houses for anything that works for a small family. Friends end up moving to the suburbs because they can't find a home that fits.

Pricing data seems to confirm it. I couldn't find the granular data I was looking for but did some poking - I looked at homes on the same block with similar sizes in the sunset... a 3/2 sells for $1.5-1.7M while a 3/1 on the same block goes for $1.2-1.4M. A $300k+ premium for a second bathroom. I only did a cursory search here, so if someone has better data please share!

Multi-unit buildings trade at a massive discount too. It's very common for people to live in a multi-unit as if it were one home. Two units with separate entrances and kitchens when the inspector comes, then you add a door or hallway between the units and get rid of the kitchen afterwards. Extremely wasteful, but extremely common. 

The city won't let you merge units, so many end up this way as semi-merged. The city's position is basically that you can't merge anything even a chopped-up 1906 emergency subdivision that was never meant to be subdivided.

This has been in the news recently because a young family bought a 4-unit that was living as a 1 unit, and now are being asked to carve it back to a 4 unit (image 3).

The biggest fix is building more housing... but we should also simplify permitting for bathroom additions and stop treating unit mergers like a crime, especially for buildings that were originally single-family homes. Let two 3/1 flats become one 4-bed, 3-bath home!

Would be good for keeping families in the city.

People who want 15 minute cities don’t mind bringing crime, homeless, and mass migration into every neighborhood.  They just don’t want families to be able to escape their control by moving to the suburbs and driving their kids to good schools.

A lot of cities, and even the Road to Housing, gives credit by the number of units built, or the number of affordable units built … which means that three 400sf Studio is prioritized over one 1200sf 3BR. It should be tied to square footage, not face rents and not number added.

And affordable rents as a % of AMI, are way easier to hit for studios than they are for family size units.

Studio units are very good for capturing young people who want to move into a city to work. The disadvantage is that they are unable to be for people who want to advance into the next life stage. Which means that workers either need to choose between not having children or moving to the suburbs.

text:
The 1950s were a defining era for automobiles in America, shaping the way people lived, moved, and interacted with one another. This post-World War II decade saw an unprecedented surge in economic prosperity, which led to a boom in consumerism and a newfound fascination with cars. During this golden age, automobiles became symbols of freedom, status, and the American dream, profoundly impacting public perception, pop culture, and government policies.

The 1950s witnessed a significant shift in the American lifestyle, with more people moving to the suburbs, seeking space and privacy away from the bustling city centers. Owning an automobile became a necessity for many families as it facilitated commutes to work, allowed for leisurely drives, and provided access to the burgeoning highway system. Cars represented more than just a mode of transportation; they embodied individuality and personal expression.

Car culture flourished during this time, giving rise to a fascination with drive-in theaters, drive-thru restaurants, and car clubs. Teenagers embraced the newfound freedom offered by automobiles, making cars an integral part of their social lives. Carhop restaurants and diners became popular, and cruising became a favorite pastime for young people, cruising down the main streets of their towns on Friday nights in their flashy vehicles.

Cars also found their way into various aspects of pop culture during the 1950s. Hollywood played a significant role in promoting car enthusiasm through iconic films like "Rebel Without a Cause" (1955), featuring James Dean, which showcased the rebellious and carefree spirit often associated with teenage drivers of the era.

Automobiles also found a prominent place in music, with songs like "Hot Rod Race" by Arkie Shibley and "Maybellene" by Chuck Berry glorifying the allure of fast cars and the open road. These tunes, filled with themes of romance, adventure, and freedom, resonated with the youth and further ingrained cars into the cultural fabric.

The government also played a crucial role in shaping the automotive landscape during the 1950s. The construction of the Interstate Highway System, initiated by President Dwight D. Eisenhower, began in the mid-1950s and had a profound impact on car travel. The expansive network of highways not only made long-distance travel more convenient but also facilitated suburbanization and the growth of car-dependent communities.

Moreover, the automotive industry thrived during this period, driven by the "Big Three" automakers: General Motors, Ford, and Chrysler. Their cars showcased innovative designs, advanced technology, and powerful V8 engines. These companies were often at the forefront of developing new trends, which intensified the public's interest in owning the latest and greatest cars.

The 1950s was a transformative period for automobiles in America, shaping not only the way people traveled but also their lifestyle, culture, and aspirations. The legacy of this decade can still be felt today, as classic car enthusiasts and nostalgia seekers continue to cherish the remaining models of these iconic vehicles and the memories they evoke of a bygone era.

text:
My wife asked me to quit my job so she could “focus on her career.”

Now she wants me back after leaving me for her boss.

When I met Vanessa, she was still struggling to build her career.

I was already financially stable, owned a small house, and had a decent job in IT.

Back then, I genuinely believed marriage was about supporting each other through different seasons of life.

So when she got accepted into a competitive corporate program in another city, I encouraged her to go for it.

Even when people warned me it would change her.

For the first few years, everything seemed fine.

I handled most of the responsibilities at home while she climbed higher professionally.

Long hours.

Business trips.

Networking events.

I supported all of it proudly.

Then she got promoted again.

text:
Ok, I’m sorry, but I really need to do this. 

Disclaimer: If you’re easily offended, especially when you’re told you need to leave where you are now and come to Israel, you can keep scrolling. 

I’m serious. Keep scrolling. 

You’re still here? Fantastic. 

We need to talk.  

I just got off my 7th call today with a potential oleh who wants to move to Israel. And this is just a normal day. 

Every day, I have anywhere between five and ten meetings or calls about Aliyah. 

I have some things I need to tell you. 

Let’s just start from the end. 

- You don’t need to speak Hebrew fluently to live in Israel. Fact. 
- You don’t need to lower your quality of life in Israel. Fact. 
- You don’t need to cut your salary in half. Fact. 
- You can afford to live in Israel especially if you’re open to living in places other than Jerusalem, Tel Aviv, or Ra’anana. Fact.

Anyone who tells you otherwise is lying. 

“I heard from people that it’s hard to make a living there!”

If one more person tells me that…

Tell me, this person who told you that, where do they live? 

What’s that? They live in America? And you think their opinion on Israel and how “Hard” it is to live here is accurate? You don’t think that maybe they are a bit biased being that they decided to stay there?

Or maybe you heard it from someone who tried to make Aliyah and failed? Do you think they’re objective? 

Are there people who struggle here? Sure. Do you know of a place where no one struggles? 

The people who can’t make it here are the exception to the rule. If you’re smart, hard working, and resourceful, you can make as much money here or more than you make there.  

Yes, you read that right. 

In 99% of professions, you can make great money here. If you’re a doctor or lawyer making zillions of dollars there, we’re gonna have to find you a solution here. But almost all other professions? You can do just fine here! 

If you’re in tech? That means engineers, sales, marketing, and countless other professions, you can make very good money here. 

I want to pause here for a second and make a confession. 

I have known Nefesh B’Nefesh since day one. I’m super close with the management team there. But I had no idea, until last week, how insanely helpful  their website is. 

They have endless resources there and I’d strongly recommend you follow them on social media and spend some significant time on their site. Chances are, you’ll get 90% of your questions answered. 

There is; however, a catch. 

The chances of you getting a job offer before coming to Israel are slim to none. It’s happened but it’s uncommon.  

Now I get it, getting on a plane without a job waiting for you is scary. I agree. It is.

That being said, there are people here waiting for you, like yours truly, people who will do whatever they can to help you have a soft landing. There is, however, a leap of faith needed. 

If you’re going to wait for the day that everything is lined up, everything is perfect, well, you’ll never come to Israel. 

There are tens of thousands of families who came here with minimal savings, no job lined up, barely any Hebrew, and no network, and they’re living fantastic lives across Israel. You will be no different.

And now let’s talk about the elephant in the room. 

You’re like the nerd who can’t read the room and overstays his welcome at a party where he is not wanted. I’m sorry that’s harsh, but it’s true. 

You are not wanted or welcome in Australia. The UK doesn’t want you there. Europe doesn’t want you! Canada has spoken and Jews are no longer welcome. The same is true for the United States. 

“Stop with the hysteria, Hillel. Things are not so bad here.”

Let me ask you a question. 

If you’re walking in the street and you see a pit 100 feet in front of you, would you say “I haven’t fallen yet. The pit doesn’t affect me so I’ll just keep walking, or would you do whatever you can to avoid that pit?”

And yet, I keep hearing intelligent people say to me “Eh. The antisemitism doesn’t affect me so I’ll just stick around.”

I guess the data is lying. 

I guess there’s not an increase of hundreds of percentages in antisemitic events. 

I guess Jews aren’t being harassed openly on the streets. 

I guess half the Democratic Party doesn’t want to cut ties with Israel. 

I guess the mayor of NYC is not an open antisemite. 

I guess all of that is made up and antisemitism isn’t a problem because you don’t think it affects you. 

Do you even hear yourself? 

“This isn’t Germany, Hillel. Stop it!”

Oh, really? It isn’t. 

Let’s play a game. 

Can you name a single thing that happened before the holocaust that has not happened today?

Windows being shattered? Synagogues being vandalized? Jews being harassed on campuses? Jews being assaulted in the streets? Openly antisemitic politicians gaining power? Jewish businesses being boycotted? 

Go ahead, name me one thing that happened before the holocaust that has not happened today. 

I’ll wait…

Listen, you don’t have to take my word for it. I asked my great aunt who survived three concentration camps how she would compare the antisemitism she saw before the holocaust and the antisemitism she’s seeing today. 

She answered me with two simple words.

“The same.” 

Her words, not mine. 

I’ve said this before and I will continue to say it over and over.

We all know the story of the man who gets on the roof in the storm where he thinks God will save him. 

They send him a boat and ask him to get in, but he refuses and says God will save him up there. 

They send a helicopter, he refuses to get on and says God will save him.

He then drowns and when he asks God why he didn’t save him, God looks at him confused and says “I didn’t save you? I sent you a boat. I sent you a helicopter. You didn’t get on.”

One day, Jews who decided to stay in the diaspora will face their Creator. They will ask Him “We prayed for the ingathering of the exiles for thousands of years, why didn’t you bring us home?”

God will look at them confused and ask, “I didn’t bring you home? Are you kidding? Is this some sort of joke?! 

I sent you ElAl; literal wings of eagles!! 

I sent you Nefesh B’Nefesh to make it easier. 

I made Israel a paradise. 

I performed open miracles. 

None of that worked so I sent you Mamdani! I made it as clear as I know how that you need to go home. 

You didn’t get on a plane!”

Not offended yet? Hold my beer. 

Yes; all Jews belong in Israel. Every single one. 

No; we do not need Jews in the diaspora. Stop convincing yourself.  

Yes; Israel can accommodate mass Aliyah. Leave that to us. 

No; it won’t be more dangerous if all Jews come home. This is where we belong. 

Yes; Israel will be just fine without American support. We know what happens when we depend on foreign governments. 

“How is Israel safer? You had 10/7!”

Fair question.

On that day, the IDF failed its mission. But a failed mission is still better than no mission at all.

Here there is an army dedicated to your safety, an army that failed on that dark day. 

Who is protecting you there? Who cares about your well-being? I think we both know the answer. No one.

Sure, we have challenges here in Israel, but standing on the side and pointing fingers is not a good look.

Come here, help us from within, bring your skills and talent, help build the future of the Jewish people, because the future of the Jewish people is here, not there, and if you still haven’t figured that out, you’re not paying attention.
  
Now, listen, I get it. Picking up and leaving the place you’ve called home is not so easy. No, it’s not. 

Do you wanna know what else is not easy? Being a Jew.

No one told you it was going to be easy.

For some people, keeping the sabbath is not easy, for others eating kosher might not be easy. 

Since when do we only practice Judaism when it’s easy?

And yes, moving to Israel is a Torah commandment just like keeping Shabbat and eating kosher.

Whether you want to look in the written Torah, the Talmud, or even listen to modern Day Torah scholars, a Jew belongs in Israel.

The Talmud in the Ketubot tractate (Page ק״י) says explicitly that anyone who lives in Israel is like someone who has a God, and anyone who lives outside of Israel is like someone who worships idols. 

That’s a direct quote. 

The Ramban says that a Jew outside of Israel is not really observing the Torah, he’s just practicing for when he comes to Israel. 

Rav Kaniefzky who wasn’t exactly the biggest Zionist said that a street cleaner in Israel is more righteous than a rabbi outside of Israel. 

Listen, if you are a religious Jew and have convinced yourself that you do not belong in Israel, you have seriously lost the plot.

God has given us this country after thousands of years, performed open miracles for us, helped us win wars against countless armies that were infinitely stronger than us, and has facilitated more Torah learning than we’ve ever had in history. 

You belong here and if you disagree, sorry, but you’re not being honest with yourself. All you’re doing is trying to find sources that’ll validate your narrative that you don’t belong in Israel. You do. 

Did you ever stop and ask yourself how it could be that after the ten plagues, 80% of the Israelites stayed in Egypt? 

Did you ever stop and ask yourself how is it that the spies so openly contradicted God? These were 10 of the heads of the tribes, the biggest rabbis of the generation and they simply defied God‘s command to enter the land. 

How? What did they tell themselves?

I think the answer is quite obvious.

The Israelites in Egypt told themselves, “I am Egyptian. I was born here. My parents were born here. My grandparents were born here. I’m not running away.“

But, you’re a slave. You’re persecuted. Leave! 

“Yea, no, we’ll just stay here.”

And what did the spies tell themselves? 

“We are very religious here in the desert. We have the clouds of glory, food coming from the heavens, water coming from rocks, and we have a direct line of communication with God. 

I think I’ll stay here where my kids are sheltered and not going to Israel where I have to build an economy and an army, and my children will be exposed to the secular world.”

God said to them “You don’t get it. Not your job to stay here and be religious. It’s your job to go into the land.”

And they said “Thanks but we’re good. Well stay here in Lakewood, I mean, the desert.”

Same narratives, different generation. 

“I am American. I was born here, my parents were born here, my grandparents were born here. I’ll stay here, I’m not running away. You need us to stay here and lobby on your behalf. We’ll just stay put.”

And then there are the modern Rabbis, the heads of communities, who instead of encouraging their congregation to go home, they tell themselves the same thing the spies told themselves.

“We are very religious here in Brooklyn. Our kids are sheltered. We can be great Jews. In Israel, they’ll be exposed to <Gasp> secular Israelis. No thank you. We’ll stay here where we can be very “Religious.””

Listen, everyone has their circumstances, and some of those circumstances do not permit some people to pick up and come to Israel. I get it.

You have elderly parents, your child needs a special type of education, you have specific medical needs, and on and on. Of course coming to Israel immediately is not feasible for many people.

So those people should, at the very least, start planning. 

However, as a collective, there simply is no excuse for Jews not to come home. 

All the reasons that once existed no longer exist. 

You are not comfortable there anymore, and if you are, you are not paying attention. 

You no longer have to cut your salary in half. 

You no longer have to lower your quality of life. 

You no longer need to know Hebrew to get along here. 

You no longer have to come with millions of dollars to live comfortably here.

All of those were once valid justifications for Jews not to come home. None of that applies today.

I’m getting really tired of speaking to people who tell me that they were told they can’t make it here.

A WARNING TO THE AMERICAN GOVERNMENT, THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY, AND THE PEOPLE OF NIGERIA CONCERNING THE 2027 ELECTIONS

By Kio Amachree President, Worldview International Stockholm, Sweden 18 April 2026
I want to ask the United States Government, the United States Senate, and the international community one question before I set out the facts of this communication.
How does the most powerful government in the history of the world — a government that holds DEA files on a sitting African president, that denied his closest business associate a visa on national security grounds citing intelligence reports linking that associate to Hezbollah financing, that knows about a Swiss court conviction for money laundering connected to the looted assets of a military dictator — look at what is happening to Nigerian citizens every single day and continue to do business as usual?
I am going to answer that question. And I am going to do so by placing before you a record so complete, so documented, and so morally indefensible that no American senator, no State Department official, and no member of the international community will be able to claim, after reading it, that they did not know.

I. WHO I AM

My name is Kio Amachree. I am a Swedish and Nigerian citizen, resident in Stockholm, and President of Worldview International. I am a Christian Nigerian from the Niger Delta — a member of the Kalabari royal dynasty — and I write to you not only as a human rights advocate but as a man who fears for his own life and for the lives of millions of his fellow Nigerians under the government of Bola Ahmed Tinubu.

I am the eldest son of Chief Godfrey Kio Jaja Amachree QC — Nigeria's first indigenous Solicitor-General, first Permanent Secretary of the Federal Ministry of Justice, Acting Attorney-General of Nigeria, and the first African ever to serve as Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations from 1961 to 1966, during which he managed the UN Civilian Operation in the Congo, oversaw all UN Trusteeships and Non-Self-Governing Territories, and flew to Lisbon to negotiate directly with the President of Portugal over the independence of Angola.

My grandfather, Chief Sekin Jaja Amachree, was a delegate to the 1958 Constitutional Conference in London and gave testimony before the Willink Commission of Inquiry advocating for the constitutional protection of Niger Delta minorities.

Dr. Nabo Bekinbo Graham-Douglas SAN — my uncle by marriage, having married Christina Amachree, my father's sister — served as Attorney-General of the Federation of Nigeria in 1972, the highest law office in the land, and was one of the first two Senior Advocates of Nigeria, conferred on 3 April 1975.

Chief Albert Korubo Horsfall — connected to this family through our shared Kalabari royal lineage — served as the first Director-General of the National Intelligence Agency and Director-General of the State Security Service, the only Nigerian in history to have headed two separate national security agencies.

My cousin Dennis Amachree served for nearly three decades as a senior intelligence officer within Nigeria's Department of State Services, rising to Assistant Director of Intelligence and Investigation.

I was educated at Eton College and at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. I worked on Wall Street and in the City of London. I served in Nigeria's National Assembly in 1981 and 1982.

This is who I am. This is the family I come from. And this is the government that has ignored me, threatened me, and left my murdered cousin without justice for seven years.

II. THE KILLING OF MISS IBISIKI AMACHREE AND THE STATE'S TOTAL FAILURE

My cousin Miss Ibisiki Amachree was a PhD holder and a mother of two young children.

In February 2019, she was serving the Federal Republic of Nigeria as an ad-hoc electoral official during the general elections in the Degema/Abonnema axis of Rivers State — the ancestral home of the Amachree family and the seat of the Kalabari royal dynasty. Soldiers of the Nigerian Army discharged live ammunition into a civilian area. Miss Ibisiki Amachree was fatally shot. She died in service to the Nigerian State.

The incident was dismissed as a "stray bullet." No independent inquiry has ever been held. No officer has been publicly named. No prosecution has been brought. No explanation has been provided to this family in seven years.

I have submitted three separate formal legal petitions to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu as Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces — the constitutional office bearing supreme authority over the soldiers who killed her.

First petition — ignored. Second petition — ignored. Third petition — ignored.

I have written three times to Nigeria's national security establishment.

Three times — ignored. Without a single word of response.

In return for these entirely lawful petitions I have received death threats from within the machinery of the Nigerian government.
The eldest son of Africa's first UN Under-Secretary-General. Threatened with death for writing legal letters.
That is who Bola Tinubu is. That is the government you are partnering with.

III. THE SECURITY CATASTROPHE TINUBU PRESIDES OVER AND REFUSES TO CONFRONT

The United States Government designated Nigeria as a Country of Particular Concern under the International Religious Freedom Act. President Trump said publicly that Christianity faces an existential threat in Nigeria. American air strikes have been conducted against terrorist groups on Nigerian soil. These are not the assessments of hostile critics — they are the formal positions of the United States Government itself.

And they are correct.

I am a Christian Nigerian. I say to you plainly and on the record: I fear for my life in Nigeria. I fear for the lives of millions of my fellow Christian Nigerians. And I am not alone in that fear. Every day — not occasionally, not rarely, but every single day — Christian communities across Nigeria's Middle Belt, its North-Central states, its Northeast and Northwest are being attacked, slaughtered, burned out of their homes, and driven from their lands by Islamic terrorist groups operating with what can only be described as structural impunity.

The numbers are not disputed. Nigeria consistently ranks among the top countries in the world for Christian persecution. More Christians have been killed in Nigeria in recent years than in any comparable country on earth. Churches have been burned. Priests have been murdered. Schoolchildren have been abducted from Catholic schools. Entire Christian communities have been ethnically cleansed from lands their families have occupied for generations.

And what has President Bola Ahmed Tinubu done?

Let me tell you what he did in Jos, Plateau State — a city that has become a symbol of the slaughter of Christian communities in Nigeria's Middle Belt.

After one of the most devastating attacks on Christian civilians in recent Nigerian history, President Tinubu travelled to Jos. He landed at the airport. He was there for approximately ten minutes. He then departed — citing, extraordinarily, a lack of electricity at the airport as his reason for leaving. He did not go to the site of the killings. He did not meet the survivors. He did not visit the bereaved. He did not stand on the ground where Nigerian Christians had been slaughtered and declare that his government would protect them.

He got back on his plane and flew away.

That is the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. That is the man to whom the United States is extending counterterrorism cooperation and military training. That is the man the United Kingdom welcomed to Windsor Castle with a 42-gun salute last month. That is the man whose government ignored three formal legal petitions from the eldest son of Africa's first UN Under-Secretary-General and responded to those petitions with death threats.

A man who cannot stay at an airport for more than ten minutes to stand with his murdered citizens is not a counterterrorism partner. He is a man who has abandoned his people to their fate and expects the international community to cover for him while he does it.

IV. THE PROFOUND MORAL CONTRADICTION AT THE HEART OF AMERICAN POLICY

I want to place before the United States Government the full moral weight of the contradiction it is currently maintaining — and I do so not in anger but in the precise, documented language of a man who has spent his life believing in the institutions of the international rules-based order and is now watching those institutions be used to protect the very people they were built to hold accountable.

The United States Government holds DEA files on President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. Those files are the subject of an active Freedom of Information case before a United States federal court — Judge Beryl Howell presiding — with a judicial deadline for disclosure in June 2026. The documented record already in the public domain connects Tinubu to a heroin trafficking network investigated by American federal authorities in the 1990s, and to the forfeiture of funds to the United States Government arising from those investigations.

The United States Government knows this.

The Tinubu administration has awarded a contract worth billions of dollars for the construction of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway to the Chagoury Group — awarded without public tender, without competitive bidding, and without transparency — to a conglomerate whose principal, Gilbert Chagoury, was convicted in Switzerland for money laundering connected to the stolen assets of the late military dictator Sani Abacha. The same Gilbert Chagoury was denied a visa to enter the United States on grounds related to national security, with American intelligence reports linking him to financial networks connected to Hezbollah.

The United States Government knows this too.

So let me ask — directly, on the public record, in language that will not be forgotten — how the Government of the United States reconciles the following.

On one hand: maintaining DEA files on a sitting African president, denying his closest associate a visa on national security grounds citing Hezbollah intelligence, knowing about the Swiss money laundering conviction, knowing about the billions in public contracts awarded without competitive tender to a man it has itself deemed a national security concern.

On the other hand: extending counterterrorism cooperation, military training, intelligence sharing, and diplomatic engagement to that same president's government — while that government kills civilian electoral officials during elections, ignores seven years of formal legal demands for accountability, presides over the daily slaughter of Christian communities, and threatens the lives of those who dare to ask why.

I have spent my entire life playing by the rules. I attended Eton. I studied at Wharton. I worked on Wall Street and in the City of London. I submitted petitions through proper channels. I wrote formal letters. I engaged every legitimate institution available to me. I followed every rule the international order asks of men like me.

And the man with the DEA file got the state dinner at Windsor Castle. And the man with the Swiss money laundering connection got the billion-dollar contract. And the man linked to Hezbollah financing got a place at Nigeria's highest table of power. And I got the death threats.

I want to ask the United States Government plainly: what is the point of playing by the rules anymore if this is how the rules are applied?

I ask that question not for myself alone. I ask it on behalf of every Nigerian Christian being slaughtered in the Middle Belt while their president flies away from the airport after ten minutes. I ask it on behalf of every Nigerian who goes to vote in the hope that their vote will be counted and their life will be protected. I ask it on behalf of Miss Ibisiki Amachree — PhD holder, mother of two — shot dead by Nigerian Army soldiers during an election in 2019, still without justice in 2026.

V. THE WARNING ABOUT 2027

The United States Senate Subcommittee on Africa and Global Health Policy meets on 21 April 2026 — in three days — to discuss counterterrorism in Africa. I am submitting this letter in advance of that hearing and formally request that it be entered into the record.

Consider what the evidence before you establishes.
A government that kills its own electoral officials during a democratic election and faces no accountability — seven years, three petitions, total silence — has received a clear and unambiguous signal that it can do so again.
A government that deploys soldiers against unarmed civilians monitoring a vote and dismisses the killing as a "stray bullet" has established the template for how it will manage inconvenient results in 2027.
A government whose president flies away from the site of a massacre of Christian civilians after ten minutes at an airport has demonstrated to every armed group in Nigeria that the state will not seriously contest their violence.

A government that responds to lawful petitions from the son of Africa's first UN Under-Secretary-General with death threats has made its position on dissent and accountability entirely clear.

And you — the United States Government — are training that government's army, sharing intelligence with its security services, and maintaining diplomatic and commercial relations with its president while all of this is happening and while your own federal courts are preparing to disclose DEA files about that president in June 2026.

If the international community does not use its very considerable leverage now — before the 2027 elections — to demand accountability for the killing of Miss Ibisiki Amachree, to demand an end to the slaughter of Christian communities in Nigeria's Middle Belt, to demand that the Tinubu government answer publicly for its relationship with the Chagoury Group and its connection to the DEA investigations, and to place the entire architecture of Nigerian election security on formal international watch — then the international community will bear a direct share of the moral responsibility for what happens to Nigerian citizens during the 2027 elections.

I am a Christian Nigerian. I fear for my life. Millions of my fellow Nigerians fear for theirs — every day, not theoretically, but with the knowledge that their government will not protect them and that the international community continues to do business with the man responsible for that failure.

VI. WHAT I FORMALLY DEMAND

I demand the following of the United States Government.

That the case of Miss Ibisiki Amachree — shot dead by Nigerian Army soldiers during the 2019 elections, unsolved and unprosecuted after seven years — be raised formally and urgently with the Nigerian government with a demand for a full public account of all steps taken or not taken since February 2019.

That the three ignored petitions submitted to President Tinubu as Commander-in-Chief, and the three ignored communications to Nigeria's national security establishment, be placed on formal international record as documented evidence of institutional impunity at the highest level of the Nigerian State.

That the death threats directed against me as a Swedish citizen and human rights defender be formally noted and that appropriate representations be made to the Nigerian government demanding the guarantee of my safety and the safety of my family.

That the United States Government make public its position on the DEA files pertaining to President Tinubu — particularly in advance of the June 2026 federal court disclosure deadline — and explain how those files are compatible with the ongoing strategic partnership between the two governments.

That accountability for the killing of civilian electoral officials be made a specific and binding condition of any ongoing or future American military training, intelligence cooperation, or defence assistance to Nigeria.

That the systematic slaughter of Christian communities in Nigeria's Middle Belt and North-Central states be raised formally with the Nigerian government as a matter of urgent human rights concern — with specific reference to President Tinubu's conduct at Jos, where he remained at the airport for approximately ten minutes before departing without visiting the site of the killings.

That Nigeria's 2027 election security be placed on formal international watch with immediate effect and that specific mechanisms be established to monitor and document any use of military force against civilian electoral participants.

VII. CONCLUSION

My father gave years of his life to the United Nations. He believed — with every fibre of his distinguished being — that the international order existed to hold power accountable, to protect the innocent, and to ensure that no government could kill its own people with impunity while the world looked on.

His grandniece was shot dead by Nigerian Army soldiers during a democratic election. His eldest son has been threatened with death for asking why. His country's president — a man whose name appears in American DEA files — was welcomed to Windsor Castle with a 42-gun salute while Christian Nigerians are slaughtered daily and their president flies away from airports.

I have petitioned. I have documented. I have warned. I have done everything the international rules-based order asks of men like me.

Now I am asking the international rules-based order to do its job.

The record is before you. The June 2026 federal court deadline is approaching. The 2027 elections are eighteen months away. The slaughter of Christian Nigerians continues today, tomorrow, and every day that this government remains unaccountable to anyone.

You know what is happening in Nigeria. You know who Bola Ahmed Tinubu is. You have always known.

The question is whether you will act on that knowledge before it is too late — or whether history will record that you knew, and chose silence.

I have warned you.

The record will show that I warned you.

Kio Amachree President, Worldview International Eldest Son of Chief Godfrey Kio Jaja Amachree QC First African Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations (1961–1966) Stockholm, Sweden 18 April 2026

text:
The Great Depression, sparked by the Wall Street crash of October 1929, became the worst economic disaster in modern history, devastating the lives of millions across America and the world.

In a matter of weeks, stocks on the New York Stock Exchange lost half their value, and as businesses collapsed, unemployment rose dramatically.

Unemployment jumped from less than three million in 1929 to four million in 1930, eight million in 1931, and twelve and a half million in 1932.

Factories were shut down, farms and homes were lost to foreclosure, mills and mines were abandoned, and people went hungry.

In the Pennsylvania coal fields, three or four families crowded together in one-room shacks and lived on wild weeds, and in Arkansas, families were found inhabiting caves.

In New York City in 1931, there were twenty known cases of starvation, and by 1934, there were 110 deaths caused by hunger.

More than 200,000 vagrant children wandered the country as a result of the breakup of their families.

Meanwhile, America's elite families remained entirely shielded from this catastrophe.

Because of the family's wealth, George H.W. Bush was largely unaffected by the Great Depression, attending Greenwich Country Day School from 1929 to 1937 and then Phillips Academy, an elite private school in Massachusetts.

The financial foundation of the Bush family was rooted in powerful investment banking connections, with patriarch Prescott Bush joining his father-in-law's Wall Street investment firm in 1926, which merged with the British-American banking firm Brown Brothers in 1930.

During the depths of the Depression, Prescott Bush actively attracted wealthy clients to the firm, pitching professional wealth management as the safest way to protect their fortunes.

The family's financial stability was further reinforced by the largesse of the Walker side of the family, who were open in their demonstrations of wealth.

While ordinary Americans were losing everything, the Bush dynasty was consolidating generational privilege, elite schooling, and banking power that would eventually propel two of its members to the presidency.

The Great Depression created a catastrophic divide between America's wealthy elite and its struggling masses, exposing the deep inequalities baked into the nation's economic structure. While millions lost their jobs, homes, and in some cases their lives to hunger, families like the Bushes continued to thrive through banking networks and inherited wealth that were essentially immune to the economic collapse. This contrast had lasting consequences for American society, fueling class resentment, reshaping political alliances, and accelerating demand for government intervention through programs like the New Deal, yet the fundamental wealth gap that allowed elite families to prosper untouched during national catastrophe remained largely intact, setting a precedent for how economic crises tend to hit the poorest hardest while leaving entrenched power structures undisturbed.

The current governor of New York was never elected to the job. She got it because Andrew Cuomo was a predator who resigned in disgrace. Since then, she’s presided over the largest population exodus of any state, a migrant crisis she helped create, a $𝟐𝟔𝟑 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐛𝐮𝐝𝐠𝐞𝐭 she can’t balance, and an approval rating so low that members of her own party are openly plotting to replace her. Here’s the full picture.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝: 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐚 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐧 𝐁𝐮𝐟𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐨 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐆𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐨𝐫’𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧

Born Kathleen Mary Courtney on August 27, 1958, in Buffalo, New York. Her father was a steelworker; the family lived in a 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐫 𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐞𝐥 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐭 when she was young. Irish Catholic, working-class roots — and she talks about it constantly. She graduated from Syracuse University and earned a law degree from Catholic University in D.C., then worked as a corporate lawyer and Capitol Hill aide.

She served on the Hamburg Town Board, then as Erie County Clerk for 4 years. In 2011, she won a special election for Congress in a deep-red district — but lost it a year later when it was redrawn. After two years out of office, Andrew Cuomo plucked her from obscurity to be his running mate in 2014. She was chosen not for her talent but for her geography — a woman from upstate to balance a New York City governor. She served as lieutenant governor for seven years, a job she later admitted was largely ceremonial. “𝘐 𝘥𝘪𝘥𝘯’𝘵 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘢 𝘥𝘦𝘴𝘬 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘊𝘢𝘱𝘪𝘵𝘰𝘭”, she told a reporter.

Then on August 24, 2021, Andrew Cuomo resigned after the New York Attorney General found he had sexually harassed 𝟏𝟏 𝐰𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐧. Just like that, Kathleen Courtney Hochul — the woman nobody chose, nobody vetted, and nobody outside of Western New York had heard of — became the 57th governor of the state of New York. Not by election. By accident.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐍𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐇𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫-𝐔𝐩 𝐒𝐡𝐞 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐝 — 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐁𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐝

One of Hochul’s first acts as governor was to reveal what Cuomo had hidden: the state had undercounted COVID nursing home deaths by 𝟏𝟐,𝟎𝟎𝟎 — bringing the true toll to over 𝟏𝟓,𝟎𝟎𝟎 elderly New Yorkers who died after Cuomo’s administration ordered COVID-positive patients back into nursing facilities (NY AG Report). It was the right thing to do. Cuomo’s cover-up was a scandal of historic proportions.

And then Hochul buried it. When the U.S. House Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic investigated the nursing home deaths, Hochul’s administration 𝐫𝐞𝐟𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐞 𝐚 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 despite 𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐥 𝐫𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐬 from Congress (House Select Subcommittee). She stonewalled a bipartisan investigation into the deaths of 15,000 elderly citizens. The same cover-up she exposed under Cuomo, she perpetuated under her own name. The families of those 𝟏𝟓,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐨𝐫𝐬 never got answers — not from Cuomo and not from Hochul.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐇𝐮𝐬𝐛𝐚𝐧𝐝: 𝐃𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭

Hochul’s husband, 𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐦 𝐇𝐨𝐜𝐡𝐮𝐥 𝐉𝐫., serves as 𝐒𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐨𝐫 𝐕𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐃𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 — a multibillion-dollar hospitality and gaming conglomerate based in Buffalo. Delaware North operates casinos, stadiums, airports, and resorts across the country. The company has spent over $𝟑𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐥𝐨𝐛𝐛𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 Hochul’s office since she became governor (𝘛𝘪𝘮𝘦𝘴 𝘜𝘯𝘪𝘰𝘯).

While her husband collected his salary from Delaware North, Hochul championed the most controversial stadium deal in New York history: a $𝟏.𝟒 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐬𝐮𝐛𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐲 for a new Buffalo Bills stadium — at the time the largest taxpayer contribution to a professional sports facility in American history. Delaware North operates the 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐬’ 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐮𝐦. Her husband’s company directly profits from the deal she pushed through with public money. She has dismissed conflict-of-interest questions as “𝘴𝘦𝘹𝘪𝘴𝘵”.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐢𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐂𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐬: $𝟒.𝟑 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠

When the migrant crisis hit New York in 2022, Hochul initially embraced it. New York was a “sanctuary” state. The city that never sleeps would welcome everyone. Then the bills arrived.

New York has allocated over $𝟒.𝟑 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 for illegal immigrant services — housing, healthcare, food, legal aid (NY Comptroller). At the peak, the city was spending $𝟑𝟕𝟎 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐧𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 to house migrants in hotels — nearly double the $𝟐𝟎𝟕 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐧𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 it spent to shelter its own homeless population. Think about that: illegal immigrants got better accommodations than American citizens sleeping on the streets.

By January 2025, the money ran out. Hochul cut off new funding for migrant services — after years of promising that the federal government would reimburse the state. The reimbursement never came. $𝟒.𝟑 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 of New York taxpayer money, gone. Hotels converted to shelters. Schools overcrowded. Emergency rooms overwhelmed. And when it became politically untenable, she reversed course and pretended she’d been tough on the issue all along.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐨𝐩𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐄𝐱𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐬

People are leaving New York in droves. Between 2024 and 2025, New York lost a net 𝟏𝟑𝟕,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 to other states — the 𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝-𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐫𝐚𝐰 𝐩𝐨𝐩𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐬 of any state in America (U.S. Census). A 𝟒𝟐% of those who left cited housing costs as the primary driver. Families, businesses, and tax revenue are fleeing to Florida, Texas, the Carolinas — anywhere that doesn’t tax you into poverty and then spend your money housing illegal immigrants in hotels.

This isn’t a blip. New York has lost congressional seats in two consecutive redistricting cycles because the population keeps shrinking. The state that was once the center of American gravity is hemorrhaging its own citizens, and Hochul has done nothing to reverse it.

Hochul’s latest state budget is $𝟐𝟔𝟑 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 — the 𝐥𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐧 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐘𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐡𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲. Despite record spending, the state faces a projected deficit exceeding $𝟏𝟎 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (NY Comptroller). text:
Something I've been mulling, inspired by @EjmEj: Tax competitiveness is less about outmigration — though it certainly matters! — than about the dynamics of wealth formation.

Consider how new technologies improve productivity. Yes, existing firms adopt new technologies and make incremental gains over time. The biggest gains, however, come when new firms adopt new business models around the new technology. We saw this with electrification and the internet, we’ve seen this in the advent of remote-first firms, and we’re tentatively starting to see it in the domain of AI.

One can think about location decisions along similar lines, and this is something policymakers in New York City and other high-tax urban jurisdictions need to understand.

There is no question that middle-aged people with mortgages, established professional networks, etc., are sticky. (This is me, plus I don't drive, I hate humidity and change, and I love public transit and museums more than life itself.) They make location decisions in response to big shocks, positive or negative, macro and micro. For example, Covid and the sudden shift in norms around remote work represented a macro shock that made relocating a more attractive option. On the more personal, prosaic side, well-off people often relocate as they plan for retirement or a realization event, or to be closer to children or grandchildren.

Viewed through this lens, you don’t want to limit your analysis to, say, the absolute number of high-income households in a given jurisdiction. (“NYC has more millionaires today than we did a decade ago!”) Rather, you want to look to where the hockey puck is going.

I’d pay close attention to a city’s share of high-income households. Why? Because agglomeration matters, and if other cities are gaining market share while you’re losing it, that is going to shape location decisions for ambitious professionals going forward.

This is why I was so spooked by @EjmEj's excellent new report on the limits of New York’s “Tax the Rich” policy. Consider the shift in "market share" for wealth:

Since 2010, the Empire State’s share of all U.S. millionaire earners has dropped from 12.7% to 8.7%. Yikes.

You might also look to the aggregate capital gains of high-income households. Why? If you set an arbitrary threshold, e.g., households earning over $1M, you lose the distinction between households that are realizing massive capital gains and double-earner, salaried professional households that simply won’t represent the same revenue bonanza.

Lo and behold: In 2010, NY held 14% of the nation’s total capital gains realizations for millionaires, while Florida held 8%. By 2022, they essentially swapped places: Florida rose to 16.7% while New York plummeted to 8.9%.

The data shows that the "apex" of the pyramid—where income is most mobile—is shrinking fastest:

This trend is particularly stark: Between 2015 and 2022, NY’s count of filers earning above $10M decreased by 31% relative to the national total.

Moreover, for those earning $10M+, capital gains and nonwage sources constitute 83% of their income. Unlike wages, this wealth is highly portable and follows the taxpayer’s residence, not their office.

We are left with a revenue base that is incredibly fragile. Just 3,172 households now account for $10 billion in state income tax. On average, every 32 filers in that top bracket represent $100 million in revenue. If just 320 of those families decide the "Tax the Rich" climate is no longer worth it, it blows a $1 billion hole in the budget.

The real danger, though, isn't just who is leaving today; it’s who is deciding not to arrive tomorrow. Ambitious professionals and "remote-first" founders look at where talent is clustering, and if they see a jurisdiction losing its share of the national wealth base, they might conclude the environment is too hostile, unwelcoming, etc. They won't wait for the next tax hike to blow a hole in their own future; they will simply build the next great firms, and the revenue base that comes with them, wherever the puck is actually going.

Prosecutors charged Jorge Luis Tejera, 40, a Venezuelan national, with sex trafficking by force, fraud, and coercion. According to court filings, once migrants entered the country, they were trapped in debt and told they would have to “work it off.” That debt was enforced through extortion tactics, including threats of violence, weapon intimidation, psychological pressure, and threats against victims’ family members. In at least one case, traffickers allegedly used a victim’s child as leverage to force continued compliance.

Authorities say these networks deliberately prey on migrants with limited resources and legal protections, isolating them and using fear to maintain control.

What federal prosecutors are now outlining closely matches what I reported years ago in New York City, when the migrant crisis first escalated. At that time, I warned that gangs were following migrants across borders, embedding themselves in U.S. cities and targeting families living in and around shelters. The reporting focused on criminal exploitation — not migrants themselves — but those warnings were often dismissed or mischaracterized.

Multiple migrant families told me they were being extorted for money shortly after arriving in the city. Witnesses described gang members showing up at migrant shelters, following mothers as they walked their children to school, and demanding payments under threat of harm. Several families told me the same chilling line: “The same people we ran from followed us here.”
Those accounts mirror what prosecutors now allege in the Utah case — that trafficking and extortion networks move with vulnerable populations, enforcing control through fear while victims remain too afraid to report crimes.

Tejera now faces federal charges that could carry decades in prison. The case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations as part of a broader effort to dismantle transnational trafficking organizations.

The indictment underscores a reality many migrants quietly described long before federal charges were filed: these crimes thrive when warnings are ignored and extortion goes unchecked, leaving vulnerable families trapped between fear and silence.

And so I began. On Monday nights we scheduled a series of services that would continue for the next five years. We started in a high school auditorium, and the crowds became so large we had to move to larger facilities.

Hundreds and hundreds of people attended.

The services were totally led by the Spirit, and I listened ever so closely to His voice. People were delivered from serious addictions. Families were reunited. We had "healing lines" and heard testimonies of miracles. But always, always, the services resulted in the salvation of lost souls.

Then something happened. People began to receive miracles, deliverance, and healings right in their seats. No lines for "the laying on of hands." God began to do His work all across the auditorium—so freely that there was not time to hear all of the testimonies.

The press began to take notice. On the front pages of the Toronto Star,  the Toronto Globe and Mail,  and other papers across Canada there were stories of the "Miracle Rallies" we were conducting.

In December 1976 the Globe and Mail  sent a reporter to one of the services to describe in detail what was happening. He wrote of the healings and testimonies and ended the article by quoting me: "I'm not interested in building up Benny Hinn. I'm not and never will be. Jesus is the one. . . to be built up and exalted. We want to reach souls for the Lord Jesus. I want to see souls, souls, souls, souls, souls. People, do you understand that?"

Under the headline, "Does Faith Healing Really Work?"

the Toronto Star  presented four case studies of people who had been healed in our services. He told about a shift worker at the GM plant in Oshawa who had cancer of the throat. "This week, following a checkup at the cancer clinic, he was told there is no trace of malignancy."

He told the story of a Beaverton trucker: "A nonchurch-goer, who had suffered from congestive heart failure and slight emphysema (a lung disease) for seven years, was persuaded by friends to attend a healing crusade. 'I went to the doctor three days later, and he told me he could find nothing wrong,' he says. 'God must have done it.'"

What about their doctors? The reporter quoted one as saying, "Look, there are more things happening in this world than we know about."

Television stations began to film documentaries on what God was doing. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), Global TV, and the huge independent station in Toronto, Channel 9, produced specials. We ran our own weekly television program that was shown in prime time after 60 Minutes  for a year and a half.

Leaving the great city of Toronto in 1979 was not easy for me. It was where I had been saved, healed, and touched by the mighty Spirit of God. The press had nothing but good news to report about the ministry. But again, I promised to follow the leading of the Holy Ghost.

I knew He wanted me to build a church and establish an international ministry. He had told me this years earlier, in 1977. I remember exactly where it happened. I was back in Pittsburgh, riding in a big Yellow Cab when I had a conversation with the Spirit about it. About the ministry He said, "It will touch the world!"

I wondered, "Where will it be? New York? Los Angeles?" But, you know, the Spirit has an amazing way of leading you.
