Thus, in 1922, there were 17 million Arabs occupying an area of 1.29 million square miles that included developed land & land with great resources and wealth, and which included all principal Arab and Islamic centers.

The remaining Mandate of Palestine, however, was only 10,000 square miles.

In other words, 0.02% of the land was mandated for the Jews, and 99.8% of the land was mandated for the Arabs.

The land had become so desolate & ruinous that Zionism found supporters in certain Arab lands.

For example, Dawood Barakat, editor of the Egyptian paper Al-Ahram, wrote: “It is absolutely necessary that an entente be made between the #Zionists and Arabs, because the war of words can only do evil. The Zionists are necessary for the country: The money which they will bring, their knowledge and intelligence, and the industriousness which characterizes them will contribute without doubt to the regeneration of the country.”

Barakat had support from a leading Arab nationalist, Sherif Hussein, who was the guardian of the Islamic Holy Places in Arabia. He foresaw that the return of the Jews to their ancient homeland would resuscitate the Land.

Hussein wrote, “The resources of the country are still virgin soil and will be developed by the Jewish immigrants … The return of these exiles (jaliya) to their homeland will prove materially and spiritually [to be] an experimental school for their brethren who are with them in the fields, factories, trades and in all things connected with toil and labor.”

For centuries before the modern State of Israel was born, there were no “borders,” as the Land was just part of ever-changing vast #imperialist empires.

Even in the decades before Israel’s independence, the borders were certainly not sealed, and many Arab families of “Sham” (Greater #Syria) wandered into Eretz Israel either on accident as they followed their flocks, or on purpose to seek out the expanding employment & economic opportunities in the Land.

Two events led to the massive influx of Arab immigration to Eretz Israel that occurred in the early 20th century.

First was the immigration of European Jews who often arrived on the back of European capital and European technology.

Second, the creation of a British Mandate Government, whose responsibilities legally required Britain (the world’s most powerful empire at the time) to aide in the economic development of Mandatory Palestine, and thus brought with it the British flag, British capital, & British technology (bottom left).

These two events generated a momentum of economic activity that produced in British Mandate Palestine a standard of living previously unknown in the #MiddleEast.

The results were dramatic. The net domestic product per capita soared & actually doubled between 1922 and 1931.

It is frankly absurd to think the comparatively extreme economic success of modernization was either unknown to or ignored by Arabs living in nearby areas such as Egypt, Syria, Lebanon, and Transjordan. 

It’s no wonder that, based on British Mandate census surveys-alone, we know that the Palestinian Arab population nearly doubled from 670,000 to 1.27 million between 1922 and 1946.

Furthermore, the Hope Simpson Enquiry issued in Oct of 1930 noted there was significant immigration from the surrounding Arab territories. This was consistent with demographer Roberto Bachi’s finding of an “unexplained increase in the Muslim population between 1922 and 1931,” which he found was most likely due to unrecorded Arab immigration due to the difficulty in even detecting such immigrants and a degree of undercounting from the 1922 census.”

In fact, most Arab immigration into British Mandate Palestine was, under British Mandate law, technically “illegal.” Therefore, it was almost entirely unreported & unrecorded.

Frankly, nobody was complaining about Arab immigration to British Mandate Palestine at the time.

The only immigration complaints were coming from Arabs who wanted all Jewish immigration stopped.

Furthermore, when John Hope Simpson first arrived in Mandate Palestine in May 1930, he observed Jewish efforts to buy-up as much privately owned land in Eretz Israel as possible, and he noted the Jews were paying “high prices” for land from absentee Arab landlords.

In addition, the demographic data from 1922 and from 1931 shows Arab migration within and from outside of Mandate Palestine had followed – in both direction and magnitude – into the areas where larger Jewish populations were building (with their accompanying Western capital & modern technology).

As further evidence of the sudden influx of Arab immigration, #Golda Meir gave firsthand testimony in her book “My Life.”

About the time Meir first moved to Eretz Israel in 1921 up to the time of the Arab Revolt of 1936-1939, she wrote, “I did not have to look up British census figures to know that the Arab population of Palestine had doubled since the start of the Jewish settlement there. I had seen for myself the rate of growth of the Arab population ever since I had first come to Palestine. Not only did the living standard of the Arabs of Palestine far exceed that of Arabs anywhere else in the Middle East, but, attracted by the new opportunities, hordes of Arabs were immigrating to Palestine from Syria and other neighboring countries all through those years.”

The British Peel Commission Report in 1937 agreed & noted the Jewish immigrants had made major advancements in the Land via agriculture and industry, which in turn had brought large benefits to the Arab population in raising their standard of living with development in the economic, financial, & social spheres. 

The Report noted the “Arab population show[ed] a remarkable increase ... partly due to the import of Jewish capital into Palestine and other factors associated with the growth of the [Jewish] National Home.”

In his memoirs, King Abdullah later wrote, “It is made quite clear to all, both by the map drawn up by the Simpson Commission and by another compiled by the Peel Commission, that the Arabs are as prodigal in selling their land as they are in useless wailing and weeping.” (italics in original).

That said, it is important to realize that there are inherent problems with relying on population statistics during the British Mandate period because mass immigration was technically occurring in a manner inconsistent with British Mandatory law.

That is why Britain’s “The Palestine Blue Book” from 1937 includes a disclaimer that Britain acknowledged there had been significant (though unnumbered) illegal immigration to Mandate Palestine of both Jews and Arabs.

In fact, this coy mention of “illegal Arab immigration” repeatedly shows up in places like the footnotes of British Mandate-era writings, especially given the embarrassment it would have caused the Mandatory Government to freely admit to the sheer massive number of Arab immigrants that had entered the country in those years.

For example, the Royal Institute for International Affairs wrote about the population of Mandate Palestine during the 1920s & 1930s and said, “[t]he number of Arabs who have entered Palestine illegally from Syria and Transjordan is unknown. But probably considerable.”

As another example, C.S. Jarvis, who was the governor of the Sinai from 1923 to 1936 wrote that illegal Arab immigration to Mandate Palestine was coming from the #Sinai, from Trans-Jordan, and from Syria.

Jarvis also noted that, during the Arab Revolt of 1936-1939, the ongoing massive illegal Arab immigration into Mandate Palestine had made it “very difficult to make a case out for the misery of the Arabs if at the same time their compatriots from adjoining states could not be kept from going in to share that misery.”

Winston #Churchill also noted of Eretz Israel in 1939 that “far from being persecuted, the Arabs have crowded into the country.”

At the height of the Arab Revolt in 1938, the British High Commissioner for Palestine, Sir Harold MacMichael, said he believed the Arab landowners were complaining about sales to Jews simply to drive up prices for lands they wished to sell. He further noted that many Arab landowners had been so terrorized by Arab rebels that they decided to leave British Mandate Palestine and sell their property to the Jews.

The Jews, after all, had by that time gone from determined to desperate for their homeland with the rise of Naziism, and were willing to pay truly exorbitant prices to already-wealthy Arab landowners for small tracts of arid land.

In 1944, for example, Jews were paying between $1,000 and $1,100 per acre in Eretz Israel. The land the Jews purchased was almost entirely arid or semiarid land. For comparison-sake, rich black Iowa soil in 1944 was selling for 10% of that cost at about $110 per acre.

Immigration (both Jewish and Arab) to Eretz Israel exploded between the end of World War I & the start of #WorldWarII.

About 37% of the total immigrants were Arabs who wanted to take advantage of the higher standard of living the Jews had made possible.

The Arab population also grew naturally during this timeframe because of the improved living conditions created by the Jews, as they drained malarial swamps & brought improved sanitation & health care to the region. Thus, for example, the Muslim infant mortality rate fell from 201 per thousand in 1925 to 94 per thousand in 1945, & life expectancy rose from 37 years in 1926 to 49 in 1943.

It is not controversial to say that migration flows toward economic opportunities.

To give modern-day examples, since the mid-20th century, millions of North African and East European migrants left their native villages, towns, & cities for the more productive and higher-paying jobs in western Europe. The European Commission estimates that approximately 500,000 migrants enter the #EuropeanUnion illegally each year (almost as many as enter legally).

Similarly, people of #Mexican, #CentralAmerican, and #SouthAmerican descent have illegally crossed into the #UnitedStates for decades for greater opportunities & due to massive wage disparities.

The same logic applies in the Middle East – people follow economic opportunities (just as millions of Arabs have done since at least the 1980s with migration toward countries with oil-rich economies).

Immigration Post-World War II

Following #WWII, the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry went to Mandatory Palestine to study the conditions & report back.

Among other things, the Committee found in November 1945 that during the years of the British Mandate, there had been “unprecedented growth in the size and prosperity of the Arab population of Palestine, as well as the Jews.”

The Committee also noted the “impact of Western science and Western technology upon a semi-feudal civilization.” Arab agriculture had been traditional and far less effective. 

Thus, the Committee stated, “[t]he influx of Western capital and the purchase of modern equipment for agriculture and industry excite in the minds of the Arabs a sense of inferiority and the feeling that they are contending against an imponderable force which is difficult to resist.”

The Arab population between the World Wars increased most in cities with large Jewish populations where new economic opportunities had been created.

Thus, from 1922-­1947, the non-Jewish population increased 290% in #Haifa, 131% in #Jerusalem, and 158% in #Jaffa.

In Arab towns, the population growth was more modest: 42% in #Nablus, 78% in #Jenin, and 37% in #Bethlehem.

Furthermore, demographer Roberto Bachi’s 1974 study included among his findings the fact that there was “great economic development of the coastal plains—largely due to Jewish immigration,” which he found was “accompanied both in 1922-1931 and in 1931-1944 by a much stronger increase of the Muslim and Christian populations in this region than that registered in other regions.”

Bachi noted this dramatic increase resulted from a combination of a strong decrease in mortality of the non-Jewish population in Jewish areas & stronger immigration toward economically developing areas where European Jews were building.

Meanwhile, Jewish landownership had drastically increased.

By 1947, Jewish holdings in Palestine amounted to about 463,000 acres. Approximately 45,000 of those acres were acquired from the British Mandatory government, about 30,000 were purchased from various churches, and the vast majority (about 84%) of Jewish landownership came from purchases made from absentee Arab landowners.

In the pre-State of Israel days, selling land to Jews for exorbitant prices was all the rage among wealthy Arabs.

Among those prominent Arabs who were happy to sell their land to Jews at the insane prices they were willing to pay included: the Arab mayors of Gaza, Jerusalem, & Jaffa; Muslim religious scholar As’ad Shuqeiri (father of first #PLO chairman Ahmad Shuqeiri); King Abdullah himself; & several leaders of the Muslim Supreme Council & Arab nationalist movements.

In April of 1948 – just before the British officially ended their Mandate – a young Robert F. Kennedy went to Eretz Israel to report on what was happening on the ground (bottom right). His dispatches were published amid the early months of the Israeli War of Independence in June of 1948.

One of Kennedy’s dispatches, published on June 3, 1948, noted details of how the Jews had transformed the land. “[W]hat was once arid desert,” Kennedy wrote, had now been turned into “flourishing orange groves. Soils had to be washed of salt, day after day, year after year, before crops could be planted. One can see this work going on in lesser or more advanced stages wherever there are Jewish settlements in Palestine.”

Kennedy pointed specifically to #TelAviv as a modern Jewish marvel, noting it had grown from a “small village of a few thousand inhabitants … into a most impressive modern metropolis of over 200,000.”

As Kennedy summed up the Jewish transformation of the Land: “[the Jews] ha[d] truly done much with what all agree was very little.”

And with that vast, extraordinary improvement in the Land, Kennedy also noted that “[t]he Jews point with pride to the fact that over 500,000 Arabs, in the 12 years between 1932 and 1944, came into Palestine to take advantage of living conditions existing in no other Arab state. This is the only country in the Near & Middle East where an Arab middle class is in existence.”

Kennedy’s findings were later confirmed in Peters’ “From Time Immemorial,” which was a thoroughly researched study of Arab #immigration into Palestine based on information available to her at the time including many accounts of 19th century travelers’ journeys through Eretz Israel.

In documenting the details of how the burgeoning Jewish & Arab populations in the area emerged from the Land’s desolate 19th century beginnings, Peters demonstrated that most “Palestinians” are not tied to the Land by centuries, but rather are the descendants of the Arab economic migrants who arrived in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

text:
Part 1 of 2 - Arab Immigration to Pre-State Israel

What does history say about who the “#Palestinians” are & how many were recent immigrants to Eretz #Israel in the decades prior to Israel’s independence in ’48?

Extensive research shows only 4-5% of today’s “Palestinians” descend from families who lived in Eretz Israel prior to 1831, and most descend from #Arab economic migrants who arrived in the late 19th and early 20th centuries in response to #Jewish immigration & the #British Mandate, both of which boosted job and economic opportunities.

Per historical records, there were only around 100,000 long-term settled #Muslims present in Eretz Israel before 1882 (start of the First Aliyah).

Analysis and details follow (several sources are included, but there are many– so, if you need/want a source for any specific portion of the following, just ask!).

Ethnicity of “Palestinians”

First, we must acknowledge the fallacy that Eretz Israel had a binary population of “#Arabs” and #Jews for centuries.

If that were true, “Palestinians” would include many non-Arabs including, but not limited to, Africans, Armenians, Circassians, & Bosnians – some of whom are Muslims, but none of whom are Arabs.

Circassians, for example, are typically Muslims, but they are not Arabs.

Other than North African & #Ethiopian Jews, the long-term “African” residents of Eretz Israel mainly descend from #slaves “purchased” by Bedouins from #Sudan to work the land around the Negev Desert during #Ottoman rule.

That’s why Africans in Eretz Israel during & after Ottoman rule were (and still are) referred to in the Arab community as “Abid” – which comes from the Arabic word for “slaves.”

And, of course, not all Arab Palestinians are Muslims – some are #Christians, some are Druze, and others are Alawites.

Arab Conquest of Eretz Israel

Arabs (people originating from the Arabian Peninsula) first “ruled” Eretz Israel after Caliph Umar conquered & began colonizing the Land between 636 and 638 CE.

For the previous six centuries, Jews were massacred or exiled from their homeland by the #Romans, the Byzantines, & the Neo-#Persians.

However, when Caliph Umar conquered the Land, he found #indigenous Jews as the majority population with about 300,000-400,000 residents (top left).

The Jews lacked sovereignty (other than a recent three-year rule of Jerusalem from 614-617 CE – fodder for a different deep dive), but they continued to live in their homeland.

In fact, when Caliph Umar conquered Eretz Israel, the Jews had been the majority population in the Land for at least the previous 1,700-2,000 years.

Arab Subjugation of the Indigenous Jewish Majority

Once the Arabs conquered Eretz Israel, they subjugated the indigenous Jewish majority, who were forced into second-class citizenship (“#dhimmis”) under #Islamic law.

In other words, an #imperialist Arab army from Arabia conquered Eretz Israel, colonized the land, & set up quasi-#Apartheid rule since they enforced separate laws meant to subjugate the majority indigenous Jewish population & make Jews legally subordinate to Muslims in every way, including their being forced to pay an extreme yearly tribute (jizya) as a poll tax just for the right to live.

Then, in 717 under Caliph Umar Abd al-Azziz, the Arabs imposed even more oppressive legal restrictions on the indigenous Jews’ public conduct, religious observances, & legal status.

For example, as of 717, Jews in Eretz Israel: (1) could not build new synagogues; (2) were not allowed to ride horses; (3) could not employ Muslims; (4) were forced to wear special clothes to mark them as Jews; (5) could not be witnesses in court; (6) could not carry any weapons; (7) could not marry Muslim women; (8) were responsible for paying the yearly jizya plus additional heavy taxes on things like agricultural land; (9) when they died, Jews’ property automatically passed to Muslims; and (10) in some areas, Jews could be legally robbed by Muslims.

As a result of these increasingly harsh legal restrictions on Jews, many Jewish families were forced to either migrate from rural areas to towns or to move out of Eretz Israel entirely in search of better lives for their families.

While many Jews fled Arab oppression, a significant portion of the Jewish population always remained in Eretz Israel throughout the centuries.

Therefore, when al-Muqaddasi – a medieval Arab geographer – wrote about the population of the Land in 985 CE (about 200 years after Caliph al-Azziz), he noted the vast population of Jews that remained living and working in Eretz Israel.

Forced Conversions & Musta’arabi Jews

In 1005 CE, the Jews of Eretz Israel faced a more extreme Islamic ruler. Caliph al-Hakin (who claimed he was divine & who was first crowned at age 11 in 996 CE) ordered all Jews to convert to Islam or be forced to wear a golden calf around their necks.

Seven years later, in 1012, al-Hakin issued a much harsher decree. The “al-Hakin Edict” forced Jews to convert or face exile from Eretz Israel.

In response to the al-Hakin Edict, most non-#Hebrew origin Christians left, but more than 90% of Jews, Samaritans, & Hebrew-origin Christians decided to stay, meaning most of them “converted” – some actually became Muslims & others pretended to be Muslims – so they would not have to leave the Land.

These “converts” would also become Musta’arabim (Arabized Jews) – accultured into Arab language, custom, and culture.

In fact, some historians believe a large percentage of modern Palestinians with ancient ties to the Land were originally Jews or Hebrew-origin Christians who converted to Islam in 1012, became Musta’arabim, and eventually fully-adopted Arab and Islamic culture.

There are also documents from after the al-Hakin Edict, specifically from 1015 to 1080, which prove many Jews who chose exile over conversion did not go far and settled in Rafah (an area of the southern Gaza Strip). Other Jews chose exile from #Jerusalem over conversion to Islam but managed to resettle among smaller Jewish communities in #Hebron and the coastal cities of Acre, Caesarea, #Jaffa, Ashkelon and Gaza.

Finally, in 1044, the al-Hakin Edict was repealed during reign of Caliph al-Mustansir of Cairo; but only 27% of the Jewish converts to Islam returned to #Judaism openly – although they too would remain Musta’arabi (culturally and linguistically Arab).

Many other Jews who were forcibly converted during the reign of al-Hakin chose to continue living as Muslim #crypto-Jews so their families could continue enjoying the economic advantages of being “Muslims” (such as exemption from paying jizya and kharja, the ability to sell agricultural products to foreign authorities, & the ability to gain employment in the government).

Some of the younger Hebrew-origin people (Jews, Christians, & Samaritans) led dual lives during this time where they maintained their prior faith in secret & acted outwardly Muslim to accrue the material benefits & avoid oppression.

End of Arab rule in Eretz Israel

About 400 years after Caliph Umar first conquered Eretz Israel, in 1071, the Arabs were conquered and replaced by the Seljuks. 

And so began a revolving door of conquerors as the Seljuks were later replaced by Kurdish conquerors, who were replaced by #Crusader conquerors, who were later again replaced by Kurdish conquerors, who were replaced by the Tartars, who were replaced by the Mongols, who were replaced by the #Egyptian Mamelukes (mostly Turkic, #Caucasian, Eastern & Southeastern Europeans), who were replaced by the Ottoman Turks – all of whom were non-Arab peoples.

Jewish Communities in Eretz Israel Continued

While thousands of Jews were slaughtered during the First Crusade by invading Christian armies, the surviving Jewish communities managed to thrive, particularly in Ashkelon, Ramleh, Caesarea, Tiberias, Acre, and Jerusalem.

Thus, when both Benjamin of Tudela and Pethahiah of Regensburg, who visited Eretz Israel in 1160 and 1180 respectively, toured the area, they both took note of the large & prospering Jewish communities in those six towns.

Then, decades later, in 1217, the #Spanish pilgrim Judah al-Harizi similarly wrote about finding a prosperous Jewish community living in Jerusalem.

While some Jewish communities always existed in Eretz Israel and went through ups and downs over the centuries, the constant invasions & conquering armies took their toll on both the Land & the population.

Nachmanides finds Eretz Israel Mostly in Ruin

In 1263, Nachmanides decided to leave an ever-less-welcoming #Spain for Jerusalem, which, by the time he arrived in 1267, he found to be in total ruin.

When he first arrived in Jerusalem, Nachmanides was struck by its desolation. He found the buildings were largely dilapidated & abandoned.

In a letter to his son, Nachmanides wrote, “Many are [Israel's] forsaken places, and great is the desecration. The more sacred the place, the greater the devastation it has suffered. Jerusalem is the most desolate place of all.”

But Nachmanides also expressed hope & recalled #Torah verses in which G-d described Israel during the period of exile: “So devastated will I leave the land, that your enemies who live there will be astonished... Your land will remain desolate, and your cities in ruins.”

Thus, Nachmanides wrote, “That which G-d states here … constitutes a good tiding, proclaiming that during all our exiles, our land will not accept our enemies … For since the time that we left it, it has not accepted any nation or people, and they all try to settle it, but to no avail.”

Indeed, during the centuries of Jewish exile, no conqueror ever succeeded in permanently settling the land or causing the desert to blossom. In the ruins of Jerusalem, Nachmanides saw a fulfillment of God's promise that the land was waiting for the Jews to return.

So, he decided to rebuild some of Jerusalem’s prior Jewish glory. He chose a ruined house outside the Old City walls on Mount Zion – one with marble pillars and a beautiful arch – and began construction of a synagogue. Torah scrolls that had been removed before the Mongol invasion and transported to the city of Shechem (today called “#Nablus”), were returned.

After Nachmanides' death in 1270, the Ramban Synagogue (top right) was moved inside the Old City walls. However, it had to be built below ground-level since, at the time, Muslim law forbade any Jewish place of worship to be taller than any Muslim place of worship.

Ottoman Turkish Rule through 1830

When the Ottoman Turks conquered Eretz Israel under Sultan Selim I in 1516, it was the start of 400 years of Ottoman rule from afar.

After almost 200 years of Ottoman rule, in 1714, the Dutch researcher, scholar, and cartographer Adriaan Reland published an account of his visit to Eretz Israel 7 noted the existence of significant Jewish population centers throughout the country, particularly in Jerusalem, Tzfat (or Safed), Tiberias, Gaza, and Hebron.

Reland wrote, “The names of settlements were mostly Hebrew, some #Greek, and some Latin-Roman. No settlement had an original Muslim-Arab name with a historical root in its location. Most of the land was empty, desolate, and the inhabitants few in number and mostly concentrated in Jerusalem, Acco, Tzfat, Jaffa, Tiberius and Gaza. Most of the inhabitants were Jews and the rest Christians. There were few Muslims, mostly nomad Bedouins. The Arabs were predominantly Christians with a tiny minority of Muslims. In Jerusalem there were approximately 5,000 people, mostly Jews and some Christians.”

Looking for people with the motivation & knowhow to rebuild portions of then-desolate Eretz Israel, in 1740, Ottoman Sultan Mahmud I invited Rabbi Haim Abulafia (Kabbalist & Rabbi of Izmir – 3rd largest city in Turkey), to rebuild the city of Tiberias.

Over the next decade, thousands of Jews immigrated back to Eretz Israel & rebuilt the Jewish city of Tiberias, which began to thrive once again.

Then, toward the end of the 18th century, a severe famine in Egypt led to waves of Egyptian #immigration heading northeast into Eretz Israel.

Also, in the decades after the #French conquest of Algeria in 1830, many Algerians fled and emigrated to Eretz Israel.

Mass Arab Immigration During and After the Egyptian-Ottoman War (1831-1840)

A significant demographic shift occurred during & after the Egyptian-Ottoman War from 1831-1840.

During this war, Egypt’s upstart governor, #Muhammad Ali, briefly dethroned the Ottomans in Eretz Israel.

The total population of Eretz Israel at the time was about 250,000, including Muslims, tens of thousands of Jews, & tens of thousands of Christians.

Under Ali’s nine-year rule, Jews were repeatedly massacred in towns like Tzfat & Hebron.

Also, during his rule, Ali brought thousands of Egyptians to work in Eretz Israel as forced laborers.

In 1840, however, the Ottomans retook Eretz Israel & expelled Ali’s forces. However, during the fighting, massive numbers of Egyptian soldiers deserted & decided to permanently settle in Eretz Israel.

As noted in Joan Peters’ famous book “From Time Immemorial,” the Egyptian-Ottoman War led to a significant demographic shift due to the influx of Arab immigrants from Egypt who chose to stay and settle in the land.

The number of Egyptian immigrants to Eretz Israel just from roughly 1829 to 1841 was at least 20,000-30,000; and they mostly settled in Jaffa, the Coastal plain, #Samaria, and in the Wadi Ara.

Eretz Israel After the Egyptian-Ottoman War

After Ali’s rule ended & Ottoman rule returned, Jerusalem was seen as having increased security. Therefore, the Jewish population of Jerusalem more than doubled in the next four decades before the First Aliyah of modern political Zionism in 1882.

By 1844, Jerusalem once again had a plurality of Jews; and out of 15,510 people, 7,120 were Jews, 5,000 were Muslims, & 3,390 were Christians.

According to Walter Lowdermilk’s “Palestine Land of Promise 1944,” the total population of Eretz Israel in 1850 was about 200,000 and included Jews, Christians, traveling nomadic Bedouins, and settled Muslims.

Then, in 1860, there was significant additional immigration to Tzfat by Moorish (Arab-Berber) tribes from Algeria along with some Kurdish immigrants; and at least 6,000 Arabs from the Beni Sakhr tribe immigrated from today’s Jordan west before settling in Tiberias. Many Turks who had been stationed in Eretz Israel to garrison the land ultimately settled their families there as well.

Bosnian Muslims began immigrating to Eretz Israel in significant numbers largely in 1864. Then in 1878, after the Austro-Hungarian occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, many Bosnian Muslims fled Christian rule.

Most Bosnians who immigrated to & settled in Eretz Israel adopted the surname “Bushnak” – a common surname among “Palestinians” today.

More Bosnian immigrants came to Eretz Israel in the following decades & the population increased to an even greater extent when #Austria-Hungary formally annexed Bosnia in 1908.

Jews in Arab Lands in the 19th Century

Meanwhile, the living situation for Jews living in Arab lands reached a low point in the 1800s. 

Jews in most of North Africa (Algeria, Tunisia, Egypt, Libya, and Morocco) were forced to live in ghettos.

Morocco, which had the largest Jewish community in the Islamic world, forced its Jews to walk barefoot or wear shoes of straw when outside the ghetto.

Muslim children often threw stones at Jews.

And, as anti-Jewish violence increased, many Jews in Arab lands were executed on charges of apostasy.

Furthermore, ritual murder accusations against Jews suddenly became commonplace in the Ottoman Empire.

Additional Arab Immigration to Eretz Israel in the mid-19th Century

Immigration from Egypt to Eretz Israel ratcheted up again in the 1850s & 1860s when the Suez Canal was being built using forced labor. In fact, this era brought many prominent Egyptian-origin “Palestinian” families to Eretz Israel, including the al-Masri, Masarwa, & Fiumi families.

Using just the surnames of certain “Palestinians,” it can be determined the lands from which they came (just like the foregoing Egyptian-origin families).

For example, several prominent “Palestinian” families in Eretz Israel have #Jordanian names (Zarkaw & Kraki families), #Syrian names (al-Hourani & Halabi families), #Lebanese names (Surani, Sidawi and Trabulsi) and #Iraqi names (al-Iraqi) – these are only some examples.

Also, throughout the entirety of Ottoman rule in Eretz Israel, there were considerable increases in immigration of Bedouin tribes (speaking in a #Saudi-Jordanian dialect) from the south & the east, as well as peasant farmers known as “fellahins” who came from Egypt.

The Egyptian fellahins settled mostly in the area around Gaza and received protection from Bedouins in return for goods. The Bedouins, during Ottoman rule, also brought African slaves from Sudan to Eretz Israel to work the land.

Studies on & Observations Made of Eretz Israel in the Mid to Late 19th Century

In 1865, the Palestine Exploration Fund (PEF) was created in London under Queen Victoria by a group of distinguished academics and clergymen. The PEF became the oldest known organization in the world created to study the Land of Israel.

The original mission statement of the PEF was to promote research into the archaeology, history, manners, customs, culture, topography, geology, & natural sciences of Eretz Israel. The PEF conducted many early excavations of biblical and post-biblical sites & prepared studies of the Land’s natural history, anthropology, history, & geography.

Meanwhile, in 1866, the Jews had once again become the majority in Jerusalem.

Three years later, in 1869, Mark Twain wrote “The Innocents Abroad,” which included Twain’s description of his time in Eretz Israel two years earlier in 1867.

Twain found the Land of Israel to be largely desolate and devoid of inhabitants due to centuries of war followed by centuries of neglect under Ottoman rule.

Twain entered Eretz Israel from the north and passed through the Sea of Galilee, the Banias, #Nazareth, #Jenin, and Nablus.

He described Eretz Israel as “...[a] desolate country whose soil is rich enough, but is given over wholly to weeds-a silent mournful expanse … A desolation is here that not even imagination can grace with the pomp of life and action … We never saw a human being on the whole route … There was hardly a tree or a shrub anywhere. Even the olive and the cactus, those fast friends of the worthless soil, had almost deserted the country.”

Then, as Twain was riding on horseback through the Jezreel Valley, he observed, “There is not a solitary village throughout its whole extent – not for 30 miles in either direction. There are two or three small clusters of Bedouin tents, but not a single permanent habitation. One may ride 10 miles, hereabouts, and not see 10 human beings.”

Six years later, in 1875, the Earl of Shaftesbury, told the Annual General Meeting of the PEF that “We have there a land teeming with fertility and rich in history, but almost without an inhabitant – a country without a people, and look! scattered over the world, a people without a country.”

As late as 1880, the #American consul in Jerusalem wrote that Eretz Israel was continuing its historic decline, and the “population and wealth of Palestine ha[d] not increased during the last forty years.”

Population of Eretz Israel During & Just After the First Aliyah (1882-1903)

At the start of the First Aliyah of modern political Zionism (1882-1903), according to Arthur Rupin in “The Jews in the Modern World,” there were fewer than 250,000 Arabs – both Muslims & Christians – living in Eretz Israel; and others, the majority of whom were Jews, made up another 50,000 residents of the Land in 1882.

It was also anecdotally clear to the Jews who had been living there for centuries that most of the Arab population had arrived in recent decades.

Additional anecdotal evidence came from the Jews of the First Aliyah who established Petah Tikvah (bottom) & noted the influx of Arab immigrants from neighboring lands who came specifically to work in the Jewish farming communities.

Arabs from neighboring lands would continue migrating to Eretz Israel to work the land during the decades that followed as more Jews arrived & built sustainable modern agricultural communities.

As Peters noted in, “From Time Immemorial,” “in the Jewish settlement of Rishon l’Tsion [which was] founded in 1882, [had] by the year 1889 … [40] Jewish families … [which] attracted more than four hundred Arab families ... [and m]any other Arab villages had sprouted in the same fashion.”

Peters calculated that in 1882, just the non-nomadic, settled Muslims in Eretz Israel numbered 141,000. And among those 141,000, about 75% of them (about 105,700), lived in Eretz Israel during Ali’s Egyptian invasion in 1831 – meaning about 25% (35,250) of them were recent immigrants since 1831.

Furthermore, according to Daniel Grynglas’ extensive research published in 2015, applying these numbers through a formula using only natural population growth based on the natural growth rates in neighboring #Syria, Egypt, and #Lebanon, only about 453,000 – or a mere 4.3% of the 2015 population of “Palestinians” – trace their ancestry in the Land before 1831. The other 95.7% of 2015’s “Palestinians,” according to Grynglas, are “those Arabs and their descendants who migrated to Israel between 1831 and 2015.”

Of course, Grynglas also recognizes not all of these “Arabs” are of Arab descendance. That said, many of them identify today as Palestinian Arabs since the influx of Arab immigrants led to, after a few generations, the loss of separate identities among the population of non-Jews.

All historical records indicate that only an insignificant number of long-term settled Muslims were present in Palestine before 1882 (at the time of the First Aliyah).

The number of settled Muslim Arabs in Eretz Israel only increased dramatically as Jewish settlements developed infrastructure & provided work and economic opportunities to Arabs from neighboring countries.

Demographer U.O. Schmelz performed an extensive analysis of the Ottoman registration data for the 1905 populations of Jerusalem and Hebron. His analysis showed that of those Arabs living in Jerusalem & Hebron that were born elsewhere, half had moved there from nearby locales with lower economic activity, & the other half was made-up of Arab immigrants into Eretz Israel – 43% from Asia, 39% from Africa, & 20% from Turkey.

As Schmelz concluded, “[t]he above-average population growth of the Arab villages around the city of Jerusalem, with its Jewish majority, continued until the end of the mandatory period. This must have been due—as elsewhere in Palestine under similar conditions—to immigrants attracted by economic opportunities, and to the beneficial effects of improved health services in reducing mortality—just as happened in other parts of Palestine around cities with a large Jewish population sector.”

While Schmelz restricted his research of the 1905 Palestinian census to the official Ottoman registrations & used those registrations with only minor critical comment, he acknowledged that "stable population models assume the absence of external migrations, a condition which was obviously not met by all the subpopulations" that Schmelz enumerated.

From time immemorial my ass.🙄

"Palestine, the land which lies between three continents and borders on the desert, was throughout the ages an arena of conflict between empires and a magnet for invaders and nomads. After the nation of Israel lost its independence, there were many expeditions of conquest, each of which introduced a layer of new settlers into the country's population. The Arab conquest, too, brought new settlers, who imposed the religion of Islam and the Arab language on all the inhabitants. Throughout history there are many instances of conquests whi,ch led, through a process of absorption and assimilation, to the formation of new national entities. Had the Arab conquest led to the formation of a crystallized Arab nation-no matter how small in number-it would have been difficult to contradict the claim of Arab historical continuity in Palestine. But such was not the case. The few Arabs who lived in Palestine a hundred years ago, when Jewish settlement began, were a tiny remnant of a volatile population, which had been in constant flux, as a result of unending conflicts between local tribes and local despots. Malaria and disease had taken a heavy toll of the inhabitants. The numerous factors responsible for the dire state of the Arab community a century ago will be discussed in the course of this investigation. Social paroxysms, wars and destruction prevented the Arab population in Palestine from striking root and from handing down a tradition of permanent settlement from generation to generation. Since the breakdown of the Crusader Kingdom and the subsequent conquest by the Mamelukes, the population of Palestine kept dwindling and reached its nadir after the Black Plague. Western Palestine at that time had a total population of between 140,000 and 150,000: Moslems, Christians and Jews. After the Ottoman conquest, the authorities took a census for tax purposes, and tabulated 49,181 heads of families and single men liable to tax. Professor Roberto Bacchi calculated that in the years 1553-1554 there were 205,000 Moslems, Christians and Jews in Palestine.  During the following 250 years the population growth was minimal. In 1800 the total popUlation was 275,000, of whom 246,300 were Moslems and 21,800 Christians.  In 1890 there were in Palestine 532,000 people: 431,800 Moslems, 57,400 Christians, and 42,900 Jews.  The Christian population was not all Arab. Thus the ChristianArab population at the time is estimated at 42,000,4 and so the total Arab population was about 473,000. From this figure the number of Arabs in Palestine in 1880 can be easily calculated: If we take into account a natural increase in population of between 0.7% and 1% per annum, we find that in 1880, at the beginning of Jewish colonization, there were about 425,000 to 440,000 Arabs III Palestine. Of these, 40,000 to 45,000 were Bedouin nomads. Egyptian Colonization The population in Palestine underwent radical changes in the wake of two destructive wars that swept the country-Napoleon's campaign of 1799, and the invasion by the Egyptian army and the subsequent rule of Ibrahim Pasha between the years 1831-1840. The conquest did establish law and order in the country, but the war, the suppression of rebellions and the subsequent withdrawal caused many old inhabitants to flee and new elements to settle in the land. As a result of the war, the military draft and heavy taxes imposed by the Government, many fellaheen and urban dwellers fled. In addition, the measures taen by the Government to prevent looting and robbery brought about the flight of many Bedouins. The frequent rebellions and their suppression were accompanied by considerable loss of life and flight of large numbers of inhabitants. It was in this period that the Great Earthquake of 1837 occurred, and in its path pestilence and hunger took their toll. On the other hand, there was a limited influx of some thousands of immigrants whom Ibrahim Pasha brought in to settle the empty stretches of the country. Before them, a goodly number of fellaheen had fled Egypt seeking to evade the military draft imposed by Ibrahim Pasha in preparation for the invasion and settled in Palestine. They sought sanctuary with the governor of Akko, Abdullah, who granted it readily. The French scholar, M. Sabry, whose sources were the archives in Cairo writes: "Abdullah, the Governor of Akko, encouraged the migration of fellaheen from Egypt and gave them shelter. Mohammed Ali, the ruler of Egypt, complained to the Porte (the Sultan), who replied that the immigrants were citizens of the Empire and were entitled to settle anywhere they pleased. In 1831, more than six thousand fellaheen crossed the Egyptian border, and Abdullah, in his bountiful mercy, refused to return them (to Egypt). "S After he conquered Palestine, not only did Mohammed Ali refrain from sending back the draft evaders to Egypt, but he sent new settlers to consolidate his rule. The Egyptian settlers scattered to many urban and rural points, appropriated large tracts of land, and lent variety and numbers to the existing population. Some settled in the Hula Valley. They were the Ghawarna tribes, the most disdained and primitive of Bedouin tribes, who suffered greatly from the malaria endemic to the valley. The death rate among their children was so great that the total population diminished from generation to generation. They replenished their ranks by recruiting criminals and army deserters from time to time.  Another Bedouin tribe, Arab ez-Zubeid, (who, in the future, were to sell their lands to the settlers of Yessud-Hama'ala) also came from Egypt, either as refugees or with the encouragement of the Egyptian ruler. In one of the villages of the Hula Valley, Muftahira, the Egyptians established a permanent settlement. Tristram relates that the inhabitants of one of the villages in the Beit-Shean Valley "are Egyptian immigrants and they are grievously oppressed by the neighbouring Bedouin. " The ArabHinadi tribe came to the Jordan Valley, and after some years settled in the village of Delhamiya. The village Ubeidiya in the Jordan Valley was settled by Egyptians, as was Kafer-Miser,in the vicinity of Kaukab el-Hawa. Many Egyptians also settled in Akko and its suburbs. to Members of the Arab el-Ufitribe settled in Wadi Hawarith. They were Egyptian slaves who had been brought by Ibrahim Pasha. II The Egyptian ruler also brought the Bedouin slave tribe Arab ed-Damair to the vicinity of Hadera. They settled in the nearby swamps.  According to the British Palestine Exploration Fund regional map of Jaffa, most of the city was made up of Egyptian-populated districts. "Saknet el-Mussariya," "Saknet Abu Kebir," "Saknet Hammad" and "Saknet Abu Derwish" were all setled by Egyptians who had accompanied the conquering army. 1Another district, "Saknet el-Abid," was settled by freed slaves. The Egyptians settled in the six villages of Fejja, Jaljuliya, Ummlebis, Sumeil, Sheikh-Muwanis and Salame situated on the outskirts of Jaffa, and drove away the indigenous population. A sheikh called Hammed el-Masri occupied a large tract of land by the Yarkon River. 14 Philip Baldensperger states that in 1893 the inhabitants of many villages in the southern part of the country, like Zarnuqa and Kubeiba, were of Egyptian origin; that they were unlike the other Arabs then resident in the country; that the fellaheen used to call them "Masserein"; and that a Palestinian Arab would never give his daughter in marriage to an Egyptian, and would rarely take to wife a woman of Egyptian stockY The dwellers of the village Quttra in the southern part of the country (later the site of Gedera) were originally brought to Palestine from Libya. 16 In a number of villages in Wadi 'Ara-'Ara, 'Ar'ara and Kafer-Kara-and south of the triangle in the villages Kafer-Qasim, Taiyiba and Qalansawa, there are hundreds of families of Egyptian origin who accompanied the conquering forces of Ibrahim Pasha. According to the tradition among these people, their ancestors were the camel riders for the army of occupation and when the Khedive's troops left they remained and settled there.  Similarly, in the cities of Samaria and Judea there are hundreds of families which, to this day, are named Masri. The origin of all of them is traceable to those who left Egypt at the time of Ibrahim Pasha. The Egyptians acquired land in various ways. Jews in Haifa and Jerusalem later negotiated for land with Egyptian landowners-not always successfully. " Two thousand dunam of land in Kafer-Miser in Upper Galilee were purchased from the heirs of the Egyptian nobleman Shedid. 20 Egyptian laborers emigrated or were brought to the country by different factors. Before the First World War they worked on the reclamation of the swamp-lands of Hadera. The engineer in charge of the reclamation project writes: "In view of the dearth of local laborers, capable of working in water and mud, I imported 150 Egyptians to do the work of digging. They participated in the laying of the railroad tracks from Jerusalem to Jaffa that a Belgian company executed, and thereafter remained in the country. " Many of these Egyptians settled in Hadera and (those who survived the malaria) found work in the citrus groves. Zvi Nadav relates: "In Hadera we worked together with about twenty Arabs, most of them blacks and Egyptians. "The Egyptian laborers were skilled in road-building. In 1904, the Jewish Colonization Association (LC.A.) built a road from Yavne'el to Kinneret to bypass the hostile village of Lubiya. The road was built by Jewish and Egyptian labor.  The assimilation of the Egyptians with the indigenous Arab population was a drawn-out process. After his visit to Palestine in 1917, Philip Baldensperger relates that the existing population in Jaffa, though essentially Arab, contained at least twenty-five different nationalities, most of them  Egyptian Arabs. The blacks, with Sheikh el-Abid as their leader, generally lived among the Egyptians, although they originated from countries just north of the equator. The black population was made up of former slaves who had fled their masters, or had been legally freed, or had come as pilgrims but could not return to their native lands. The Egyptians lived in separate areas called Saknat, and though In the middle of the nineteenth century, when whole countries began slipping away from Ottoman rule and falling into the hands of Christian states, the Sultan gave asylum to Moslem refugees who fled their homelands for religious or political reasons. After the French conquest of Algeria in 1830, the Algerians rebelled under the leadership of Abd el-Kader el-Hassani. After a prolonged war the rebellion was put down. Abd el-Kader and many of his followers were captured and imprisoned. In 1856, the French permitted Abd el-Kader to leave Algeria, together with some followers. Some of them went to Syria and others to Palestine. The Algerian Arabs settled in several cities and founded about ten villages. These immigrants, who were called by the natives Mugrabis (Westerners), founded four villages in Lower Galilee- Shara, Ulam, Ma'ader and Kafer-Sabet. They also founded the village Husha, on the site of ancient Usha, near the present Ramat-Yohanan. They established the villages of Delata, 'Alma and Dishon in Upper Galilee, as well as Teleil and Husseiniya on the banks of Lake Hula. The elders of these villages continued to speak the Berber language up to the end of the nineteenth century. 26 H.B. Tristram, the devoutly Christian British traveller-scholar, who in 1863/64 travelled up and down the Holy Land in the footsteps of Jesus, found himself at Mais, an Algerian village near Qedesh and he noted in his diary: it is "a colony of Algerian Arabs, refugees, who still wear the Algerian burnous.Quite a number of Mugrabis settled in Safed, and probably also in Tiberias. We find these facts documented in the reports of the Palestine Exploration Fund. The Mugrabis insulted the members of the Fund delegation, even attacked them, and hindered their work. The delegation sought the intervention of the Emir Abd el-Kader who then resided in Syria. The Emir sent a letter of apology "for the behavior of my people in Safed and Tiberias. " It would seem that the Mugrabis of Safed managed to preserve something of their indentity within the established population. A report by W.J. Masterman, an associate of the Palestine Exploration Fund, dated 1914, describes the Moslem population as being of mixed origin. One of the neighborhoods was called Hareth el-Karad, which denotes a population of Kurdish origin. There were also many families of Algerian origin.  In another part of his report Masterman comments that half the Moslem population of Safed were Mugrabis who had accompanied Abd el-Kader when he went into exile. Other Moslem Arabs were immigrants from Damascus, Bedouins from the Jordan Valley, and sundry village dwellers, all of whom had got to Safed, the commercial center of the region. In the same report to the Palestine Exploration Fund Quarterly, 1893, Baldensperger describes the Mugrabis of Jaffa, who had migrated to the country over the years. They tended to live near the mosques and were employed as watchmen in the citrus groves and in the fields. Some established themselves permanently. Most of them had passed through Jaffa on their way to Mecca and some Mugrabis intermarried with the local Moslems, something that the Egyptians and blacks had not succeeded in doing. Asians from all over the world-Persians, Afghans, Hindus and Baluchis-were engaged in commerce. Baldensperger also tells about North African Arabs in RamIe. There the North Africans lived under the close supervision of their leader and segregated themselves more than in any other place. Whether they were from Tripoli or Morocco, they were known as Mugrabis, and they spoke to one another in the Qebili dialect .In 1878, the Sultan, Abd el-Hamid took under his protection Circassian refugees who had fled the Christian-Russian rule in the Caucasus. Many settled in Trans-Jordan. West of the Jordan they settled in three villages: Kafer-Kamma, Sarona, and Reihaniya. Some Moslems from Bosnia also found refuge in Palestine and settled near Caesarea. Laurence Oliphant writes about one of the Turkoman tribes that pitched their black tents near a Circassian village. They were new immigrants who had arrived from the mountains of Iraq. They knew no language other than Turkish and had hoped that their fellow-tribesmen in the Sharon Plain would receive them. But a sad disappointment awaited them, for such was not the case, and so they had pitched their tents on the slopes of Mount Carmel.  In the winter of 1908, a group of Arabs arrived in Jaffa from Yemen and settled there. Like the Mugrabis, the Turkomans and the Egyptians before them, they assimilated over the years with the general Arab population. Just as the Sultan offered asylum to Moslem refugees, so the Christian communities made an effort to help Christians who sought refuge from Moslem and Druse persecutions. On the initiative of Ludwig Schneller, some German Christians established an orphan asylum in Jerusalem to absorb the surviving victims of the murderous attacks on the Christian population in Deir elKamer and other places in Lebanon. As these children grew up, they were assimilated into the Arab community in Jerusalem.  A few refugee families from the Deir el-Kamer massacre sought safety with the Jews of Safed, who hid them from the Moslems. When the War of Independence was in its early stages in 1947, the elders of the small Christian community in Safed recalled their ancestors' plight, and tried to dissuade the Christian youths from joining in the attack on the Jewish Quarter.  Factors in the Decline of the Arab Population Despite the massive increase through immigration, the total Arab population in the nineteenth century increased only slightly. One of the chief causes for this slow growth lay in the incessant internal strife.

At the end of the nineteenth century and at the beginning of the twentieth, Palestine was a backwater province of the Turkish Empire, in which many political entities sought a foothold. The manifold activities of the Christian churches and the sectarian missions were not only religious in purpose. The German Templars began their colonization project for religious reasons in 1869. At the beginning they were in conflict with the Protestant Church in Germany, but when the Arabs threatened the safety of their new colonies the German Government responded readily. It sent three warships to the shores of Palestine to defend the German citizens and to affirm its presence in the area and its right to intervene in Turkish affairs. In a similar fashion the various societies for the exploration of Palestine and its antiquities were not unaware of their political obligations to their native countries. It was no coincidence that the British Palestine Exploration Fund was established at a time when England was planning to take control of Egypt. Most of the members of the Mission sent by the Fund were army officers of the Engineering Corps. All these external forces were not sufficient to arouse the country from its torpor. The first real stimulus to economic development came from Zionist settlement. The land purchases, the melioration of the land (despite the limitations imposed by the Turkish authorities), the building boom, the planting of vineyards and citrus groves, the increase in commercial and transportation ties with the outside world-all contributed to the creation of new opportunities for employment and subsistence. In addition the activities of the Turkish authorities, such as building railroads, registering land, establishing telegraphic contact with the outside world, paving roads for carriages and building ports-all helped indirectly in the Jewish settlement effort and in the strengthening of the economy. 
Palestine attracted not only Jews who came because of national motivation, but also Arab immigrants from neighboring countries, who hoped to find easier ways to earn a living than prevailed in their native lands. On the other hand the immigration wave to the New World, which swept millions of people from Europe to North and South America, did not by-pass the Palestinian Arabs. Thousands of Arabs, mostly Christians, who despaired of bettering themselves economically in Palestine, left the country and went across the seas. The process of population turnover among the Palestinian Arabs continued but the causes changed: The introduction of a foreign population no longer came in the wake of military conquest, nor was the population any longer diminished as a result of internal strife. Instead, there was migration to and from Palestine usually for economic reasons. We can learn about the extent of the two-way traffic among the Arabs of Palestine from the population figures for the years 1890 to 1915. In 1915, according to Arthur Ruppin,who received his data from official Turkish sources, there were 689,275 persons in Palestine. Among them were 83,000 Jews and 17,000 non-Arab Christians. Thus the Arabs, both Moslem and Christian, numbered 590,000. This figure includes permanent residents and Bedouins. In the twenty-five years between 1890 and 1915 the Arab population increased from 473,000 to 590,000, i.e. by 120,000. This is less than the expected annual increase of 1% through the birth rate. Indeed, the growth was not constant and equal, but as we shall learn further on, it was the result of a simultaneous dwindling of the population within the country and of an infusion from foreign sources. At the beginning of the century there was a constant Arab emigration. Of this Ruppin writes: "There is emigration from the Christian districts, such as Bethlehem, Beit-Jala and Ramallah to North and South America, even though in smaller numbers than from the Lebanon. In many cities of South America are colonies of people from Bethlehem who maintain contact with their homeland, and some of them even go back. They are engaged mostly in trade. The American Consul in Jerusalem Consular Trade Reports  estimates the emigration from the Jerusalem District at 3,000 annually, of whom 30% are Christians, 35% Moslems, and 35% Jews. " Thus, from the Jerusalem District alone 2,000 Arabs emigrated annually. About one town in the Jerusalem area, Bethlehem, there are reliable data on the extent of emigration. In June of 1921 the London Morning Post published a denunciatory article against Zionism, entitled Under the Zionist Yoke. It stated that the Arabs were weary of the contempt in which they were held by the Jews and the Zionist authorities, and that 7,000 Arabs had emigrated from Bethlehem to South America. The Colonial Office in London made inquiries of the High Commissioner in Jerusalem as to the truth of this report. The High Commissioner replied that the population of Bethlehem was estimated to be about 14,000 to 15,000 people. During the ten-year period between 1910 and 1920, 4,500 people emigrated from the town; 393 returned. In the year 1919/20, 245 emigrated and 35 returned. In 1920/21, 185 emigrated and 65 returned. 62 Thus the High Commissioner refuted the libellous story of the Morning Post's correspondent, but the fact remains that during a ten-year period, at a time when the Jews had no political standing, a third of the population of Bethlehem emigrated voluntarily. Masterman reports in 1914 on Jewish and Arab emigration from Safed which, like some other cities, had experienced an exodus of young Jews and Moslems who had emigrated to America, especially to South America. Parenthetically he noted that Safed in those days had the relatively large population of 25,000, of whom 11,000 were Jews. 
The new Jewish settlements that were founded at that time grew and developed. They attracted Arab laborers from nearby villages, but there were also Arab workers who came from distant points and settled in the vicinity of these settlements. Laborers of Egyptian extraction settled or the outskirts of Rishon-Ie-Zion, Ness-Ziona, Rehovot, Gedera, and Ekron, and remained in the country. The building of the Jerusalem-Jaffa railroad inaugurated in 1892 employed many workers from Palestine and from other coutnries. The Belgian company that built the railroad imported Egyptian laborers to do the digging. They remained in the country.65 At the start of the century, work on the railway track between Haifa and Edrei was begun. (It was completed in 1905.) At the outbreak of World War I, the Haifa-Nablus railroad was begun. The local fellaheen and urban labor forces did not have the required skills for building and operating railroads. Many workers were imported from neighboring countries, mainly from Syria and Lebanon. 66 In 1880 Haifa was a small town of 6,000 souls, with fewer than two hundred Jews. In 1910 it had 18,000 inhabitants, of whom 15,000 were Moslems and Christians.  Many of the newcomers to the city were from Lebanon and Syria, as will be detailed further on. Jaffa developed as a port city that absorbed Jewish immigrants, and through which passed pilgrims who entrained from Haifa to Edrei, and then went on to Hejaz. Some of them remained in Jaffa, as reported by Baldensperger. The population doubled in the twenty-year period between 1890 and 1910. In the latter year Jaffa numbered 43,000, of whom 30,000 were Moslems and Christians.  A large number of pilgrims from North Africa settled in Jerusalem amidst their countrymen, who had established a community in earlier times. The North African group developed a broad-ranged program of communal activities; it had a Waqf, mosques, homes for the aged, and residential quarters near the Western Wall. World War I and the Transition to British Rule The eight years between 1914 and 1922 were war and post-war years. During this time the country passed from Turkish to British rule. Arab population Moslems, Christians and Bedouins-numbered 590,000 in 1915. In 1919 there were 515,000 Moslems and about 50,000 Christian Arabs, a total of 565,000. 09 The natural increase of the Arab population for the four years 1915 to 1919 showed an absolute decline of 25,000 people. But the 1922 census showed 643,000 Arabs. * (Moslems, Christians, Druse and Bedouins. As to the errors and distortions of the census, and the rectifications and estimates made by Professor Bacchi more will be said subsequently.) These figures show a sharp decline in the war years, and a quick and unexplained recovery during the ensuing three years. The Claim of Dispossession by Arieh L. Avneri

🚨Comprehensive Report: Charlie Kirk's Views on Marijuana Across Key Video Appearances

Charlie Kirk, conservative commentator and founder of Turning Point USA, has addressed marijuana (cannabis/weed) in multiple videos, podcasts, and campus debates from 2024–2025. 

His stance is overwhelmingly opposed to recreational legalization, federal reclassification (e.g., from Schedule I to III), and loosening restrictions. He views widespread use as detrimental to individual health, societal vitality, and national strength, often refuting pro-legalization claims with data on post-legalization outcomes in states/cities like Colorado, California, and New York. 

While acknowledging limited medical benefits, he prioritizes preventing recreational normalization. Below is a synthesis of his arguments from major appearances.

Major Videos and Discussions

1. The Charlie Kirk Show Monologue (August 2025)

• Kirk delivers his most comprehensive argument against reclassification in a solo episode and X-posted clip.

• Core question: "If more people used marijuana, would America be better?" He answers no, urging policies that decrease usage.

• Refutes four "lies" from the marijuana industry:

—Legalization reduces crime/homelessness (opposite occurred; cities like Denver/Seattle worsened).

—Reduces youth access (usage rose sharply post-legalization due to tacit endorsement and corporate marketing).

—Weakens cartels (they shifted to harder drugs like fentanyl).

—Diminishes allure (normalization increased overall/recreational use).

• Health risks: Modern high-THC strains (20–90% vs. 2–4% in 1970s) linked to psychosis (5x risk), schizophrenia (up to 30% of cases in young men), IQ loss (2–8 points, especially under 18), depression, anxiety, heart issues.

• Societal: Public smell/litter degrades quality of life; more cannabis DUIs than alcohol; invites degeneracy, not virtue or productivity. Geopolitically: Weakens America vs. drug-free China.

https://t.co/K0nQsAGh4D

2. Campus Debate: "Educates Stoner on Dangers of Weed" (September 2024)

• Kirk debates a pro-weed student, calling full legalization a "false promise of liberty."

• Post-legalization failures: Cities messier/dirtier (e.g., Denver, San Francisco); youth ICU visits up; crime rose in Mountain West.

• Personal harm: "Weed is really bad for people... makes you lazier... a less whole human being." Diminishes soul/potential as a lifestyle drug.

• Rejects libertarian "limited government" defense: Laws should promote virtue, not just freedom.

https://t.co/TzXYgDg5D7

3. Campus Hot Take on Cannabis vs. Alcohol (February 2024)

• Kirk tells a student legalization was a "mistake," reversing prior mild support (e.g., reducing prison for possession).

• Harms: Strengthened cartels (pivoted to fentanyl, causing 70,000+ deaths); gateway to harder drugs; expanded government via welfare/social services.

• Vs. alcohol: Both bad (alcohol causes DUIs/domestic issues, 140,000+ deaths/year), but adding marijuana worsens externalities; prefers one mainstream vice over more.

Full clip: https://t.co/uFDD2uLGOl  

Short version: https://t.co/gqIXzXLqLI

4. Club Random Podcast with Bill Maher (April 2025)

• Kirk reveals he has never intentionally used marijuana (abstains from alcohol too).

• Opposes legalization mainly for smell/stench in public and youth brain risks; agrees kids shouldn't use but adults have limits (e.g., no open use).

• Hypothetical curiosity: Wonders if it reveals "corners of your mind," but remains opposed.

• Follow-up clip: Describes secondhand high from Maher's blunt → paranoia, munchies, but stayed "chill."

https://t.co/rIBKvPtMGG (Secondhand marijuana smoke experience highlight)  

https://t.co/TivvavcE4j (Related clip on getting high/paranoia)

5. Other Clips/Related Episodes (2024–2025)

• Consistent themes: Legalization failed promises; high-potency risks; urban decay (e.g., tourism decline from litter/smell); youth perception of safety rose, usage followed.

Consolidated Key Arguments

• Health Impacts: High-THC modern weed causes cognitive decline, mental illness (psychosis, schizophrenia, depression), laziness, addiction. Worst for youth (brain development, IQ loss).

• Societal/Public Impacts: Degrades cities (smell, open use, litter); increases impaired driving, homelessness indicators, and degeneracy. No safer/more pleasant post-legalization.

• Youth Protection: Biggest concern—legalization signals acceptability, raising teen use/psychosis hospitalizations despite promises otherwise.

• Policy/Economic: Corporate marketing would addict more (like junk food); cartels would be stronger via harder drugs; no crime reduction.

• Vs. Alcohol: Alcohol is harmful, but declining (especially Gen Z); better one vice than expanding. Marijuana is more isolating/publicly intrusive.

• Broader Vision: America needs sobriety for purpose, productivity, competitiveness (e.g., vs. China). More use weakens the national project (innovation, family, virtue).

Evolution and Nuance

Kirk once supported decriminalization (no prison for use/sale, ~2018) to avoid over-incarceration/weaken cartels. 

He eventually viewed legalization as a proven failure, hardening against any federal loosening. Accepts narrow medical use (e.g., PTSD) but opposes recreational endorsement.

In summary, Kirk portrays marijuana normalization as a cultural/regressive force eroding personal excellence and national strength. 

He calls for accountability on failed pro-legalization predictions and policies discouraging use, framing opposition as pro-virtue, pro-youth, and pro-American resilience. 

His views spark backlash (especially from younger/libertarian regular users/gamer audiences) but remain data-driven in his presentations.

NIGERIAN STATE SYSTEM: A FAILURE THAT MUST BE DISCONTINUED 
                                                          By Bolarinwa Ayoola

Nigeria began its journey as a modern state in 1914 following the amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates by the British colonial administration under Lord Frederick Lugard. One of the most significant milestones in the country’s history was the creation of regional governments, which were established based on the historical and cultural identities of the constituent peoples.

The three initial regions created were the Western, Northern, and Eastern Regions.
This era of regionalism endured until 1966, when Nigeria’s first democratically elected government was violently overthrown in a bloody coup d'état led by Major Kaduna Nzeogwu on February 15, 1966. 

Following the coup, General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi's military government promulgated the infamous Decree No. 34, which abolished the regional structure and introduced a unitary system of government. This singular act, over the years, has had far-reaching and largely negative consequences for Nigeria’s political, economic, and social development.

Between 1954 and 1966 under the regional system, Nigeria experienced unprecedented growth across the three regions. This period is often referred to as the golden era of Nigerian development.

It featured visionary leadership, economic self-reliance, and progressive policies. Notable regional leaders of this period include Chief Obafemi Awolowo (Western Region), Sir Ahmadu Bello (Northern Region), and Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe (Eastern Region).

Western Region under Chief Obafemi Awolowo
As Premier of the Western Region from 1954 to 1959, Chief Obafemi Awolowo implemented groundbreaking policies that transformed the region socially, economically, and politically. One of his most remarkable achievements was the introduction of free and compulsory primary education in 1955 which was the first of its kind in Nigeria and sub-Saharan Africa.

This led to a dramatic increase in literacy and school enrolment. He also established free health services for children under 18, built modern hospitals, and prioritized rural healthcare.

Awolowo laid the foundation for higher education by initiating the University of Ife (now Obafemi Awolowo University) and pioneered media development by launching Western Nigeria Television (WNTV) in 1959 Africa’s first television station. 

His administration promoted cocoa farming through farm settlements and used revenue from cocoa exports to fund social programs. The Western Nigeria Development Corporation (WNDC) was established to drive industrialization, resulting in investments in infrastructure, electricity, and water supply.

Awolowo's administration was known for its financial prudence, maintaining a debt-free and self-sustaining regional economy, and advocating for federalism and cultural preservation.

Northern Region under Sir Ahmadu Bello
Sir Ahmadu Bello, as Premier of the Northern Region, focused on uniting the diverse ethnic groups while promoting development and preserving traditional Islamic values. Understanding the importance of education, he expanded access to both Qur’anic and Western education, leading to the establishment of Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria in 1962.

This institution became a leading centre of learning in Nigeria.
His administration emphasized agricultural development by modernizing farming techniques and promoting cash crops such as groundnuts and cotton, which were vital to the Northern economy. Infrastructure development, rural electrification, and integration of traditional governance structures such as the emirate system further enhanced the region’s social cohesion and progress.

Eastern Region under Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe
Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe, Premier of the Eastern Region from 1954 to 1959, championed education and economic modernization. He established numerous secondary schools, teacher training colleges, and laid the groundwork for the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, which became a beacon of intellectual advancement.

Through the Eastern Nigeria Development Corporation (ENDC), his administration promoted industrialization and invested in agriculture, manufacturing, and commerce. Cities like Enugu and Onitsha witnessed significant infrastructural improvements, including urban planning and housing developments, which helped elevate living standards and economic prosperity.

Post-1966 Decline and Structural Deficiencies
In over a century of Nigerian history, the 1947–1966 period stands out as an era of true social, economic, and political development. In contrast, the post-regional period has been marked by political instability, infrastructural decay, widespread corruption, and de-industrialization.
On May 27, 1967, Nigeria was reorganized into twelve states.

This number has since expanded to thirty-six, with the creation of six additional states by General Sani Abacha in 1996. However, the current structure has revealed several flaws that have stifled national development.
These flaws include:
Mismanagement and wastage of scarce resources.

Financial irresponsibility at all levels of government.
Insecurity and declining patriotism.
Infrastructure collapse and regression in agricultural and industrial productivity.
Since the return to democratic rule in 1999, Nigeria has struggled to achieve meaningful development. The agricultural backbone of the nation once symbolized by cocoa, rubber, oil palm plantations, and groundnut pyramids has diminished in importance.

Many states are economically unviable and rely heavily on federal allocations, raising questions about the necessity of their creation and the duplication of administrative structures.

Each state maintains an elaborate bureaucracy, including governors, state assemblies, local government officials, and numerous advisers, which significantly drains resources. These bloated administrations divert funding from essential sectors such as education, health, and infrastructure.
Corruption remains rampant in the Fourth Republic. The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) is currently investigating and prosecuting numerous cases involving politicians and senior civil servants accused of looting public funds. This has eroded public trust in the government, leading to widespread disillusionment and loss of national pride.

Many young Nigerians, disconnected from the country's current structure, have turned to illicit activities such as militancy, cybercrime, and insurgency due to lack of opportunities. Cultural and identity crises now plague parts of the North and the entire South-East, further weakening national unity.

The Need for Structural Reforms
The state system, as currently structured, has not been able to drive genuine industrial or agricultural development. The gains made during the regional era have been reversed, and the nation now relies heavily on imports for basic consumer goods. In addition, inefficient state governments are rarely held accountable, as citizens tend to blame the federal government for failures at the state level.
Inter-state cooperation is often hindered by bureaucratic inefficiencies and political rivalries. For example:
Ladoke Akintola University of Technology (co-owned by Oyo and Osun states) suffered repeated disruptions due to unpaid wages and lack of funding cooperation.
Residents along the Isheri River in Lagos and Ogun states endure perennial flooding due to lack of coordinated efforts between the two governments.
This pattern can be observed across many states and different sectors in Nigeria. Nigeria’s post-1966 structural transition from regions to states has produced mixed results, with the drawbacks now far outweighing the benefits. A return to true federalism built on regional autonomy and economic self-reliance promises a viable path to sustainable development and national cohesion. It is imperative for policymakers and citizens alike to critically assess Nigeria’s structural foundations and push for reforms that reflect the country’s historical realities and future aspirations.

Here is the comparative analysis of development in Nigeria during the Regional Government (1954–1966) and the Presidential System (1999–2023) 
Development Indicator
Regional Government (1954–1966)
Presidential System (1999–2023)

Political Structure
Federal parliamentary system with strong regional autonomy; regions had constitutions and premiers.
Centralized presidential system with federal control; state dependence on federal revenue.
